about a subject or person
@@PHRASE0@@about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Toby talks about you all the time.
@@EXAMPLE1@@This leaflet should answer all the questions you have about switching to digital TV.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I'm reading a really good book at the moment - it's about the French Revolution.
@@EXAMPLE3@@What's all the fuss about?
@@THESPROPFORM0@@about what/how/where etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've been thinking about what you said, and I've decided that you're right.
@@PHRASE1@@on
@@DEFINE@@about a particular subject
@@EXAMPLE0@@Lucia Piatti has written several books on the subject.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@advice/opinions/ideas etc on
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you want any advice on where to stay, Jan should be able to help you.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His views on women are really old-fashioned.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@on what/how/where etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Do you have any ideas on where to eat tonight?
@@THESPROPFORM2@@book/programme/film etc on
@@EXAMPLE0@@a book on 19th century English Literature
@@EXAMPLE1@@a lecture on Native American customs and folklore
@@EXAMPLE2@@Did you see that programme on South Africa last night?
@@PHRASE2@@concerning/regarding
@@DEFINE@@about something or someone - use this especially to talk about information, ideas, or questions
@@EXAMPLE0@@For any details concerning a particular country you should check with the embassy.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Richard was called in by the police to answer questions concerning the disappearance of Thomas Ripley.
@@EXAMPLE2@@If you have any questions regarding any of our services, please feel free to call me.
@@EXAMPLE3@@Thank you for your letter regarding the annual subscription to our magazine.
@@PHRASE3@@on the subject of
@@DEFINE@@if you talk or write on the subject of someone or something, you talk or write about them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Marie said nothing at all on the subject of Mr Bertram.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@while we're on the subject
@@GLOSS@@used when you are talking about a subject and want to say more about it
@@EXAMPLE0@@While we're on the subject of money, do you have that $10 you owe me?
@@PHRASE4@@re
@@DEFINE@@used in short business letters, messages etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Re planning meeting on Friday, please bring sales figures.
@@EXAMPLE1@@To: John Deacon. From: Maria Soames. Re: computer system.
@@PHRASE5@@with regard to
@@DEFINE@@used especially to introduce a subject that you want to talk about in a speech, formal report, meeting etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@With regard to the proposed new shopping mall, I would like to add a few remarks to those of the previous speaker.
@@EXAMPLE1@@With regard to your letter concerning my January payment, this matter has now been settled.
@@PHRASE6@@wrt
@@DEFINE@@use this in e-mails to introduce the subject you want to talk about. Wrt is an abbreviation of "with regard to"
@@EXAMPLE0@@Wrt your looking out for a new computer, I saw a good offer in the paper yesterday.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'll be contacting Jean tomorrow wrt the Christmas party - is there anything you'd like me to suggest to her?
to have something as the main subject
@@PHRASE0@@be about
@@EXAMPLE0@@The play is about life in the Deep South in the 1930s.
@@EXAMPLE1@@What's tonight's documentary about?
@@EXAMPLE2@@Have you ever read 'Hideous Kinky'? It's about an English woman and her daughter travelling in Morocco.
@@PHRASE1@@deal with/be concerned with
@@DEFINE@@to be about a particular subject, especially a serious one, and examine it carefully and in detail. Deal with is much more common than be concerned with
@@EXAMPLE0@@The story deals with the psychological conflicts between mother and son.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The earliest films made in India dealt with mythological subjects.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Elton's books are often concerned with environmental issues.
@@PHRASE2@@concern
@@DEFINE@@if a story, report etc concerns someone or something, it is about them and especially about what happens to them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Much of the material in her early letters concerns events which happened some years before.
@@PHRASE3@@focus on
@@VARIANT@@centre on
@@VARIANT@@center on
@@DEFINE@@if something such as a book, article, or discussion focuses on a subject or problem, it is mainly about it and examines it in detail
@@EXAMPLE0@@The next chapter will focus on this problem in greater detail.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a weekly magazine mainly focusing on business-related issues
@@EXAMPLE2@@The controversy centred on the question of illegal arms sales.
approximately a number or amount
@@PHRASE0@@about
@@DEFINE@@a little more or a little less than a number, amount, distance, or time
@@EXAMPLE0@@It should cost about $1500.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The church is about a mile away.
@@EXAMPLE2@@It's been about five years since I've seen Linda.
@@EXAMPLE3@@The chance of men being born colourblind is about 1 in 12.
@@PHRASE1@@approximately
@@DEFINE@@a little more or a little less than a number, amount, distance, or time. Approximately is a little more formal than about and is used especially in written English
@@EXAMPLE0@@Approximately 30% of the community is Polish.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Each disk stores approximately 144 pages of text.
@@PHRASE2@@roughly
@@DEFINE@@approximately - used especially when you are trying to give someone a general idea of the number or amount
@@EXAMPLE0@@A new kitchen would cost roughly $6,000.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The man was roughly my own age.
@@EXAMPLE2@@There were roughly 50 people there.
@@PHRASE3@@or so
@@THESPROPFORM0@@3 days/a minute/fifteen people etc or so
@@DEFINE@@approximately 3 days, a minute etc, or perhaps even more
@@EXAMPLE0@@The baby usually sleeps for an hour or so after breakfast.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He suggested that I take a week or so off work.
@@EXAMPLE2@@There must be thirty people or so in the class.
@@PHRASE4@@odd
@@THESPROPFORM0@@a hundred/forty/thirty etc odd
@@DEFINE@@use this after numbers in tens, hundreds, or thousands
@@EXAMPLE0@@"How old do you think he is?" "Oh, I don't know. Seventy odd."
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's been 30 odd years since I last saw him.
@@PHRASE5@@give or take
@@THESPROPFORM0@@give or take a few miles/a couple of minutes/a pound etc
@@DEFINE@@use this when saying approximately what a number or amount is, when it may be a few miles more or less, a few minutes more or less etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The village is about fifty miles north of here, give or take a few miles.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He's said to be worth $26 million, give or take a few million.
@@EXAMPLE2@@"How long will the meeting last?" "A couple of hours, give or take."
@@PHRASE6@@at a guess
@@DEFINE@@approximately, especially when you do not know the correct number or amount and are guessing what it is
@@EXAMPLE0@@At a guess, I'd say around 3000 people took part in the demonstration.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It was a cold night. About two or three degrees at a guess.
@@EXAMPLE2@@"How much will it cost?" "A hundred and twenty pounds, at a guess."
approximately a large number or amount
@@PHRASE0@@something/somewhere in the region of
@@EXAMPLE0@@The business is worth something in the region of $25m.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The universe is estimated to be somewhere in the region of eleven billion years old.
@@EXAMPLE2@@A typical price would be somewhere in the region of £2,500 per person.
@@PHRASE1@@something like
@@EXAMPLE0@@Smith is already something like $10,000 in debt.
@@EXAMPLE1@@In the USA something like 4000 such accidents occur each year.
@@PHRASE2@@an estimated
@@THESPROPFORM0@@an estimated 3000 people/one million pounds/90% of profits etc
@@DEFINE@@approximately that number or amount - use this when you have no exact or detailed figures on which to calculate the exact number
@@EXAMPLE0@@The event was seen on television by an estimated 250 million people worldwide.
@@EXAMPLE1@@An estimated 10% of new mothers suffer from severe depression.
@@EXAMPLE2@@By the end of the month an estimated 1000 people had been killed and 42,000 left homeless.
@@PHRASE3@@some
@@THESPROPFORM0@@some 100 people/50 years/2000 establishments etc
@@DEFINE@@approximately that number or amount - use this especially when you think it is impressive or surprising
@@EXAMPLE0@@Among the 11 factory sites across Europe, some 2,600 jobs are to be eliminated this year.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He lectured at the Institut Pasteur for some 50 years.
@@PHRASE4@@or more
@@THESPROPFORM0@@5000 people/20%/9 days etc or more
@@DEFINE@@use this when the total may be a lot more, and you want to emphasize that this is a large number or amount
@@EXAMPLE0@@How can you be tired? You slept for ten hours or more last night.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There were a thousand or more fans at the airport to welcome the band.
at approximately a particular time or date
@@PHRASE0@@about
@@VARIANT@@around
@@DEFINE@@a little later or a little earlier than a particular time or date
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's two-thirty. They should be arriving about now.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The cathedral was completed in about the middle of the 16th century.
@@EXAMPLE2@@About six months ago he suffered a major heart attack.
@@EXAMPLE3@@I picked Sue up around eight o' clock.
@@EXAMPLE4@@I don't remember the exact date of the party, but it must have been around the first of December.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@round about
@@EXAMPLE0@@He left the house round about four o'clock.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The job should be finished round about March next year.
@@PHRASE1@@approximately
@@DEFINE@@a little later or a little earlier than a particular time or date. Approximately is a little more formal than about or around and is used especially in written English
@@EXAMPLE0@@The gate will close approximately two minutes before the train leaves.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Tours start approximately every 15-20 minutes in summer.
@@PHRASE2@@some time
@@THESPROPFORM0@@some time after/before/around/between/in etc
@@DEFINE@@at a time in the past - use this when you do not know exactly when or it is not important exactly when
@@EXAMPLE0@@The burglary must have happened some time after 8:00 p.m.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His third symphony was written some time between 1750 and 1753.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The clinic was closed some time in the early nineties.
@@PHRASE3@@or thereabouts
@@THESPROPFORM0@@at 10 o'clock or thereabouts/in the 1950s or thereabouts etc
@@DEFINE@@use this after a time, date etc that is not exact, especially when it is not important to know the exact time, date etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@They're old apartments, built in the 1930s or thereabouts.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The book will be published in May or thereabouts.
@@PHRASE4@@circa
@@THESPROPFORM0@@circa 1920/1850/1492 etc
@@DEFINE@@use this when you are saying when something happened in history
@@EXAMPLE0@@The manuscripts date from circa 400 B.C.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a Robert Adam mansion, built circa 1778
@@EXAMPLE2@@The picture shows Tsar Nicholas, circa 1914.
approximately correct
@@PHRASE0@@roughly
@@EXAMPLE0@@Yes, that's roughly the right answer.
@@EXAMPLE1@@As long as you know roughly how to do it, that's fine.
@@PHRASE1@@more or less
@@DEFINE@@if something is more or less correct, it is good or correct enough to be accepted even if it is not perfect
@@EXAMPLE0@@What she says is more or less true.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Did they have what you were looking for at the hardware store?" "Yes, more or less."
@@PHRASE2@@kind of/sort of
@@DEFINE@@said when you think something is approximately right or true, but not exactly
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's kind of circular-shaped, but not exactly.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Did you finish your homework?" "Well, sort of."
@@PHRASE3@@be in the right ballpark
@@DEFINE@@if you are in the right ballpark , what you have guessed is not exactly correct, but is close to being correct
@@EXAMPLE0@@"I'd think a project like this would take at least five years to complete." "Not quite as long as that, but you're in the right ballpark."
a number or amount that is approximately right
@@PHRASE0@@approximate
@@EXAMPLE0@@The measurements are approximate, but I think they'll do.
@@EXAMPLE1@@An expert could give you the approximate value of the painting.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Approximate journey time to London is four hours.
@@PHRASE1@@rough
@@THESPROPFORM0@@rough guess/calculation/estimate/indication
@@DEFINE@@approximately correct, and therefore not to be used for detailed or important work
@@EXAMPLE0@@The report should give you a rough indication of the company's stock market performance over the past year.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'd say that the whole thing would cost you around $1000, but that's just a rough estimate.
@@PHRASE2@@ballpark figure
@@DEFINE@@a number or amount that is approximately correct - used especially in business
@@EXAMPLE0@@A ballpark figure for the cost of the construction is $4.5 million.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A firm price hasn't been set yet, but the ballpark figure under discussion is $3 million.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@give somebody a ballpark figure
@@EXAMPLE0@@Could you give me a ballpark figure?
@@PHRASE3@@approximation
@@DEFINE@@a number or amount that is approximately correct
@@THESPROPFORM0@@a reasonable approximation
@@EXAMPLE0@@Five thousand dollars seems to be a reasonable approximation of the actual cost.
in a higher position than something
@@PHRASE0@@above
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was a light above the table.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Above his bed is a picture of two old men sitting on a park bench.
@@EXAMPLE2@@During my last year of college, I lived in a little apartment above a grocery store.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@directly above
@@EXAMPLE0@@We looked up and saw a helicopter hovering directly above us.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@the floor/apartment above
@@GLOSS@@above where you are
@@EXAMPLE0@@We could hear noises in the room above.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@from above
@@GLOSS@@seen from above
@@EXAMPLE0@@The light came from above them and to their right.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@above sea level
@@GLOSS@@used when describing how high a place is
@@EXAMPLE0@@Mexico City is 2400 metres above sea level.
@@PHRASE1@@over
@@DEFINE@@directly above something or moving in the air above it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The sign over the door said 'Employees Only'.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A thick layer of smoke hung over the city.
@@EXAMPLE2@@About 400 fans jumped over barricades and invaded the playing field.
@@EXAMPLE3@@As the planes flew over, Selim could see the Russian markings on their wings.
@@EXAMPLE4@@Riot police fired over the heads of the demonstrators.
@@PHRASE2@@overhead
@@DEFINE@@in the sky directly above your head
@@EXAMPLE0@@A flock of birds passed overhead.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Suddenly, they heard the rumble of thunder overhead.
@@PHRASE3@@up
@@THESPROPFORM0@@up in/on/there etc
@@DEFINE@@in a higher position than where you are
@@EXAMPLE0@@I found some old pictures of my mother up in the attic.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Are you able to see up there or do you need a flashlight?
@@PHRASE4@@upstairs
@@DEFINE@@on a higher floor of a building, above where you are
@@EXAMPLE0@@The bathroom is upstairs on your left.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Don't you think the woman upstairs is kind of strange?
@@PHRASE5@@overhang
@@DEFINE@@if something such as a tree or a rock overhangs something, it sticks out over it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The bird was sitting on a branch overhanging the water.
@@EXAMPLE1@@An ancient vine overhangs the terrace.
to accept an offer, invitation, or request
@@PHRASE0@@accept
@@DEFINE@@to say yes to an offer, an invitation, or a chance to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I decided to accept the job.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The president has accepted an invitation to visit Beijing.
@@EXAMPLE2@@If they offered you a place on the course, would you accept it?
@@EXAMPLE3@@We've invited Professor Shaw to come and give a talk and she's accepted.
@@PHRASE1@@take
@@DEFINE@@if you take an opportunity or a job that someone offers you, you accept it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Stephen says he'll take the job if the money's right.
@@EXAMPLE1@@This is a wonderful opportunity -- I think you should take it.
@@PHRASE2@@say yes
@@DEFINE@@if someone says yes , they agree to do what you have asked or invited them to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@We'd really like you to come to France with us this summer. Please say yes!
@@EXAMPLE1@@David doesn't usually lend his car to anyone, so I was surprised when he said yes.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@say yes to (doing) something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Do you really think your parents will say yes to letting you stay out late this Friday night?
@@PHRASE3@@agree
@@DEFINE@@to say you will do what someone has asked you to do, especially something that may be difficult, inconvenient etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@They've asked Tina to work overtime this week, and she's agreed.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@agree to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I wish I had never agreed to teach Paul how to drive.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I've agreed to help Sarah move this weekend.
@@PHRASE4@@take somebody up on/take up somebody's offer
@@DEFINE@@to accept someone's offer to do something for you, especially when you accept the offer some time after it was made
@@EXAMPLE0@@"If you ever need a babysitter, let me know." "Thanks, I might take you up on that some time."
@@THESPROPFORM0@@take up somebody's offer of something
@@EXAMPLE0@@In the end, Rick took up his parents' offer of a loan.
@@PHRASE5@@jump at the chance/opportunity
@@DEFINE@@to eagerly accept an offer to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Marla jumped at the chance to spend a year working in her company's UK office.
to take money or a gift that someone offers you
@@PHRASE0@@take/accept
@@DEFINE@@to take something someone offers you, especially money or a gift. Accept is more formal than take
@@EXAMPLE0@@Mark gave us a lot of helpful advice, but he refused to take any payment for it.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We hope you'll accept this small gift.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@take something from somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@My mother always warned us never to take candy from strangers.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@take bribes
@@EXAMPLE0@@Ochoa was formally accused of taking bribes.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@take it or leave it
@@GLOSS@@said when telling someone that you will not change your offer
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'll give you $500 for the car. Take it or leave it.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@accept something from somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@A Senate candidate can accept up to $2,000 from individual campaign donors.
to accept that something is right
@@PHRASE0@@accept
@@DEFINE@@to agree that a suggestion or idea is right, especially when you did not previously think so
@@EXAMPLE0@@People are beginning to accept the idea that higher taxes may be necessary.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@accept that
@@EXAMPLE0@@The judge accepted that Carter did not mean to harm anyone.
@@PHRASE1@@agree
@@DEFINE@@to accept that a plan or suggestion is good, especially when you have the power to decide whether it will be allowed to happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@I spoke to my boss yesterday about postponing the meeting and she agreed.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@agree to
@@EXAMPLE0@@We want to have a big party, but I don't think my parents will agree to it.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@agree that
@@EXAMPLE0@@The music teacher agreed that Dave should play at the school concert.
@@PHRASE2@@welcome
@@DEFINE@@to think that a plan, suggestion, or decision is very good, and eagerly accept it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some companies have welcomed the idea of employees working from home.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The university's cafeteria welcomes any suggestions for improvement of its menu or service.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be warmly welcomed
@@EXAMPLE0@@The proposal was warmly welcomed by the German Chancellor.
@@PHRASE3@@go with
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that you are willing to accept and support a plan or suggestion that someone has made
@@EXAMPLE0@@"What do you think of Jo's idea?" "I think we should go with it - I can't think of anything better."
@@PHRASE4@@take on board
@@DEFINE@@to realize that a new idea or suggestion is important and that it needs to be thought about seriously
@@THESPROPFORM0@@take something on board
@@EXAMPLE0@@The local government says it has taken much of the public's criticism on board and it promises to make changes.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@take on board something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The management says that it will take on board suggestions from employees about child-care facilities.
@@PHRASE5@@embrace
@@DEFINE@@to eagerly accept ideas, opinions etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@By the end of the last century, Americans had embraced the idea of the right to free public education for all children.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@embrace something wholeheartedly/wholeheartedly embrace something
@@GLOSS@@embrace it completely
@@EXAMPLE0@@The President said he wholeheartedly embraced the need for further talks on the refugee crisis.
to accept something after first refusing or opposing it
@@PHRASE0@@accept
@@DEFINE@@to accept someone's suggestion, offer, or demand, after refusing it for some time
@@THESPROPFORM0@@finally accept something
@@EXAMPLE0@@After a three week strike, the company has finally accepted the workers' pay demands.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The owners finally accepted our offer of £62,000.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@(finally) have to accept something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The President finally had to accept that there was little support for his health care initiatives.
@@PHRASE1@@give in
@@DEFINE@@to unwillingly agree to accept someone's demands after they have argued with you, asked you repeatedly, or threatened you

@@PHRASE2@@back down

@@PHRASE4@@accede to

@@PHRASE5@@cave in

@@THESPROPFORM0@@cave in to
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's unlikely that the government will cave in to the rebels' demands.

to officially accept a new law or proposal
@@PHRASE0@@pass
@@DEFINE@@if a parliament or similar group passes a law or proposal, the members vote to accept it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The State Assembly passed a law which banned smoking in public places.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@pass by
@@EXAMPLE0@@The bill was passed by 197 votes to 50.
@@PHRASE1@@approve
@@DEFINE@@to officially accept something that has been planned to happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Medical Research Council said it could not approve the use of the new drug without further tests.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Congress voted not to approve the President's plans for cutting the arms budget.
@@PHRASE2@@ratify
@@THESPROPFORM0@@ratify an agreement/treaty

@@PHRASE3@@be carried
@@DEFINE@@if a suggestion, proposal etc is carried , most of the people at an official meeting vote in favour of it and it is accepted

@@EXAMPLE0@@The motion to restrict handgun sales was carried by 76 votes (=76 more people voted for it than voted against it ).

@@THESPROPFORM0@@uphold by

@@DEFINE@@if an official committee or someone in authority rubber-stamps a decision, they approve it immediately without thinking about it or discussing it because they have no real power of their own

when the real situation is different from what people think
@@PHRASE0@@actually
@@DEFINE@@used to tell or ask someone what the real situation is, when they think it is something different
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Here's the $10 I owe you." "Actually, you owe me 20."
@@EXAMPLE1@@Did he actually hit you or just threaten you?
@@EXAMPLE2@@It turns out that one of the children I thought was a girl was actually a boy.
@@PHRASE1@@in fact
@@DEFINE@@used to tell someone what the real situation is, when they think it is something different. Actually is more informal and is used more in conversation than in fact . Actually is also used more in questions than in fact . Actually is often used at the beginning of a sentence that answers a question, but in fact is not.
@@EXAMPLE0@@He said it would be cheap but in fact it cost over £200.
@@EXAMPLE1@@No, I'm not offended at all. In fact, I'm glad you asked the question.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@in actual fact/in point of fact
@@EXAMPLE0@@They seem to think that building a new road will improve the traffic problem, whereas in point of fact it will make it worse.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There are almost 200,000 possible combinations of symbols. In actual fact, only a small number of these are used.
@@PHRASE2@@really
@@DEFINE@@used to say what the truth is, especially because something about the situation may make people believe something that is wrong
@@EXAMPLE0@@He failed his tests, but he's quite a bright guy, really.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Are you sure she's really a lawyer? She doesn't act like one.
@@EXAMPLE2@@They're asking £600,000 for the house. That's more than it's really worth.
@@PHRASE3@@in reality/the reality is
@@DEFINE@@used to introduce the second part of a statement when you want to show that the first part is not true or exact
@@EXAMPLE0@@It seems like just yesterday, but in reality it was five years ago.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Nowadays owning a car may appear to be a necessity, but in reality it isn't.
@@EXAMPLE2@@They say that the economy is already coming out of the recession, but the reality is that there has been no improvement at all.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@the reality of the situation is
@@EXAMPLE0@@The reality of the situation is that by sending drug users to jail, the government may be discouraging people from seeking treatment.
@@PHRASE4@@the truth/fact is
@@DEFINE@@used to show what the real truth or fact is in a situation, when this is surprising or different from what people believed was true
@@EXAMPLE0@@The truth was that she did not enjoy getting together with the rest of her family.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The fact is he was murdered. He didn't commit suicide at all.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I may make it all look easy, but the truth is I work very hard.
@@PHRASE5@@in practice
@@DEFINE@@used to show the difference between what is supposed to happen according to a rule or law, and what does happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@Teenagers are not allowed to drink in bars, but in practice they often do.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Economic predictions are highly theoretical. It's what they mean in practice that is important.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@in theory ... in practice
@@EXAMPLE0@@The law seemed like a good idea in theory, but in practice it has proved far too expensive.
@@PHRASE6@@in effect/effectively
@@DEFINE@@used to show what really happens, even though this was not clear from what was said or done
@@EXAMPLE0@@Foreign companies have been effectively running the country for decades.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Management seems to be saying, in effect, that if we don't like the offer, we can all quit.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Can you give me some advice? I'm thinking of buying a computer.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@give advice on/about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Ask your bank to give you some advice about special student packages.
what you say when you are advising someone
@@PHRASE0@@you should do something/you ought to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@You should go to the doctor with that cough.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I think you should stay here until you've sobered up.
@@EXAMPLE2@@That new restaurant's great -- you really ought to try it.
@@EXAMPLE3@@Do you know what you ought to do? You ought to tell her exactly what you think of her.
@@PHRASE1@@if I were you
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are giving someone friendly advice
@@EXAMPLE0@@I wouldn't do that if I were you.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Here's your money -- if I were you I'd put it in the bank right now.
@@PHRASE2@@you'd be better off
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are advising someone how to do something in a better way
@@EXAMPLE0@@The ferry takes about eight hours! You'd be better off going by plane.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I think you'd be better off using a knife rather than scissors for that job.
@@PHRASE3@@take my advice
@@DEFINE@@say this when you think that someone should do something because you know from your own experience how unpleasant or difficult something can be
@@EXAMPLE0@@Take my advice - don't go into teaching unless you're absolutely committed.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Divorces are a nightmare. Take my advice and stay single.
@@PHRASE4@@take it from me
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are telling someone that they should trust the advice you are giving them because it is based on your personal experience
@@EXAMPLE0@@Take it from me, you'll regret it if you waste your time at school.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Love affairs with colleagues never work out -- take it from me.
@@PHRASE5@@you'd be well advised to do something/you would do well to do something
@@DEFINE@@use this when you are strongly advising someone to do something, especially because they may have trouble if they do not do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Before your interview you'd be well advised to have another look at what you put on the application form.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There are parts of Detroit you'd be well advised to avoid.
@@PHRASE6@@on no account/not on any account
@@DEFINE@@use this when you are strongly advising someone not to do something because it would be dangerous or stupid
@@EXAMPLE0@@On no account should you attempt this exercise if you're pregnant.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@not on any account
@@EXAMPLE0@@You shouldn't sign the contract unless you are sure you understand it. Not on any account.
@@PHRASE7@@make sure (that) you ...
@@DEFINE@@say this when you do not want someone to make a mistake, for example by forgetting to do something or losing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Make sure that you take your passport.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Make sure you lock all the doors and windows at night.
@@PHRASE8@@the best thing is to ...
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are telling someone what you think the best way of dealing with a particular situation is, based on your own experience
@@EXAMPLE0@@The best thing is to just ignore her. She'll soon take the hint.
@@PHRASE9@@a word of advice ...
@@DEFINE@@say this especially when you are warning someone to be careful about something
@@EXAMPLE0@@A word of advice: when you're at the interview don't mention that you used to work in a bar.
to ask someone for their advice
@@PHRASE0@@ask somebody's advice
@@DEFINE@@to ask someone to advise you about something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Can I ask your advice? I need to find somewhere to stay in London.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@ask sb's advice on/about
@@EXAMPLE0@@I always ask my brother's advice about computers.
@@PHRASE1@@seek advice
@@DEFINE@@to ask someone to advise you or to try to find someone to advise you, especially someone who has special or professional knowledge
@@THESPROPFORM0@@seek advice from somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@The best thing to do is to seek advice from an expert.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@seek somebody's advice on
@@EXAMPLE0@@Carla sought her grandmother's advice on all personal matters.
@@PHRASE2@@get/obtain advice
@@VARIANT@@take advice
@@THESPROPFORM0@@get legal/medical/professional etc advice
@@DEFINE@@to ask someone who has special knowledge to advise you about a problem that you cannot deal with by yourself
@@EXAMPLE0@@If the debt is not paid within seven days, we will take legal advice.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Pregnant women should get medical advice before taking any kind of drug.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@get legal etc advice on
@@EXAMPLE0@@She had told her employers that she would be getting professional advice on her rights.
@@PHRASE3@@consult
@@DEFINE@@to get advice from someone who is trained in a particular profession, for example a lawyer or a doctor
@@EXAMPLE0@@If the symptoms persist, consult your doctor.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I want to consult my lawyer before I say anything.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@consult somebody about something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Tonight the President will consult his military observers about the likelihood of an attack.
to do what someone advises you to do
@@PHRASE0@@take somebody's advice/follow somebody's advice
@@DEFINE@@to do what someone advises you to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've decided to take your advice and go to art school.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If she had followed my advice, this would never have happened.
@@PHRASE1@@do what somebody says
@@DEFINE@@to do what someone has told or advised you to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you'd done what I'd said, none of this would have happened.
@@PHRASE2@@listen to
@@DEFINE@@to do what someone advises you to do, especially because you respect them and trust their judgement
@@EXAMPLE0@@You tell him Dad - I'm sure he'll listen to you.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Bob warned us about this. I wish I'd listened to him.
@@PHRASE3@@on somebody's advice/on the advice of somebody
@@DEFINE@@if you do something on someone's advice , you do it because they have advised you to do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@On her doctor's advice, she took a few days off work.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He decided not to take the exam, on the advice of his professor.

to make someone angry
@@PHRASE0@@make somebody angry
@@VARIANT@@make somebody mad
@@EXAMPLE0@@Sophie tried not to do anything that would make Henry angry.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It always makes me mad when people drive up behind me and start flashing their lights.
@@PHRASE1@@annoy
@@DEFINE@@to make someone fairly angry
@@EXAMPLE0@@The only reason she went out with Charles was to annoy her parents.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Jane's constant chatter was beginning to annoy me.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Are you doing that just to annoy me?
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it annoys somebody that/when
@@EXAMPLE0@@It annoys me that Kim never returns the books she borrows.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@I find it annoying when...
@@EXAMPLE0@@I find it annoying when people eat smelly foods on public transport.
@@PHRASE2@@irritate
@@DEFINE@@to keep annoying someone
@@EXAMPLE0@@That silly smile of hers always irritated me.
@@EXAMPLE1@@After a while, the loud ticking of the clock began to irritate me.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Jean Paul's attempts to apologize just irritated me even more.
@@PHRASE3@@piss somebody off
@@VARIANT@@tick somebody off
@@DEFINE@@an impolite expression meaning to annoy someone
@@EXAMPLE0@@Shut up, Bernie, before you really start to piss me off.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it pisses somebody off the way
@@EXAMPLE0@@Doesn't it piss you off the way your husband sits in front of the TV every night while you cook dinner?
@@PHRASE4@@infuriate
@@DEFINE@@to make someone very angry especially by doing something that they cannot control or change
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her racist attitudes infuriated her co-workers.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Kramer's stubborn refusal to answer any questions infuriated the officers.
@@PHRASE5@@anger
@@DEFINE@@to make someone angry
@@EXAMPLE0@@The police department's handling of the affair has angered many in the community.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The decision to again allow logging in the area angered environmentalists.
@@PHRASE6@@bug
@@DEFINE@@if something bugs you, it annoys you because it is always there or is always happening, so that you cannot stop thinking about it or noticing it
@@EXAMPLE0@@It really bugs me when I can't remember someone's name.
@@EXAMPLE1@@You know what bugs me? Getting a call from a telephone salesman right when I sit down to dinner.
@@PHRASE7@@get on somebody's nerves
@@DEFINE@@if someone or something gets on your nerves , they annoy you, especially by continually saying or doing something that you do not like
@@EXAMPLE0@@The noise from the apartment upstairs was beginning to get on my nerves.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I hope Emma isn't going to be there - she really gets on my nerves.
@@PHRASE8@@it makes me sick
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that something makes you very angry, especially an unfair situation
@@EXAMPLE0@@It makes me sick, the way they treat old people here.
@@PHRASE9@@be like a red rag to a bull
@@VARIANT@@be like waving a red rag in front of a bull
@@DEFINE@@if something is like a red rag to a bull , it will always make a particular person angry
@@EXAMPLE0@@Whatever you do, don't mention his ex-wife. It's like a red rag to a bull.
to deliberately make someone angry
@@PHRASE0@@provoke
@@EXAMPLE0@@The dog wouldn't bite you for just petting her. You must have provoked her.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@provoke somebody into (doing) something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Paul tried to provoke Fletcher into a fight.
@@PHRASE1@@wind somebody up
@@DEFINE@@to deliberately say or do something in order to make someone angry, especially because you enjoy making them angry
@@EXAMPLE0@@She's married again? You're winding me up!
@@EXAMPLE1@@He only pretends to be sexist in order to wind me up.
@@PHRASE2@@antagonize
@@DEFINE@@to make someone feel angry with you by doing something that they do not like
@@EXAMPLE0@@The White House does not want to antagonize Beijing.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The police department antagonizes the black community here on an almost regular basis.
making you angry
@@PHRASE0@@annoying
@@EXAMPLE0@@Jason is one of the most annoying people I have ever met.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Just as I stepped into the shower the phone rang. It was so annoying.
@@PHRASE1@@irritating
@@DEFINE@@annoying, especially because something keeps happening that makes you a little angry
@@EXAMPLE0@@Sammy has an irritating habit of leaving the refrigerator door open while he's fixing something to eat.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's so irritating how Ellen always tries to finish people's sentences for them.
@@PHRASE2@@infuriating
@@VARIANT@@maddening
@@DEFINE@@making you very angry and impatient
@@EXAMPLE0@@Jill's attitude towards the people who work under her is infuriating.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I can't believe she's been reading our mail. How infuriating!
@@PHRASE3@@be a pain in the neck
@@VARIANT@@be a pain in the ass/butt
@@DEFINE@@to be very annoying. Be a pain in the ass/butt are impolite expressions
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's such a pain in the neck to have to drive downtown every day.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Bobby's being a real pain in the butt today. I wish he'd just go home.
@@PHRASE4@@stupid
@@DEFINE@@used when you are talking about something that makes you feel very annoyed or impatient, for example because it does not work properly
@@EXAMPLE0@@I have to stay late and finish this stupid report.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The stupid gate won't open properly.
@@PHRASE5@@frustrating
@@DEFINE@@a situation that is frustrating is annoying and makes you feel very impatient by making it impossible for you to do what you want
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's so frustrating when you're in a hurry and the traffic isn't moving.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Learning a new language can be a frustrating experience.
to behave in a very angry way
@@PHRASE0@@have/throw a tantrum
@@DEFINE@@if someone, especially a child, has or throws a tantrum , they shout angrily and cry, especially because they cannot have what they want
@@EXAMPLE0@@Whenever it's time for bed she throws a tantrum.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Almost all two-year-olds have tantrums from time to time.
@@PHRASE1@@make a scene
@@DEFINE@@to start a loud angry argument with someone, especially in a public place and in a way that is embarrassing
@@EXAMPLE0@@Please don't talk so loudly. You're making a scene.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I hate it when people make a scene in public.
@@PHRASE2@@outburst
@@DEFINE@@a sudden expression of very strong angry feelings, especially because you cannot control your anger any longer
@@EXAMPLE0@@I was embarrassed by my husband's outburst.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Corbin apologized for his outburst at the meeting.
@@PHRASE3@@shake your fist
@@DEFINE@@to hold up your hand with the fingers tightly closed and shake it in order to show that you are angry
@@EXAMPLE0@@The old man shook his fist angrily at the nurse.
@@PHRASE4@@stamp your foot
@@DEFINE@@to bring your foot down hard on the ground because you are angry about something
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Louis, get over here!" Margret demanded, stamping her foot.
often behaving in an angry, unfriendly way
@@PHRASE0@@bad-tempered
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her father was a bad-tempered man who sat alone drinking beer and watching TV most nights.
@@EXAMPLE1@@As Aunt Matilde's pain grew worse, she became too bad-tempered to see anyone.
@@PHRASE1@@grumpy/grouchy
@@DEFINE@@angry and unfriendly, and often complaining about things
@@EXAMPLE0@@a grumpy old man
@@EXAMPLE1@@Sandy is always grouchy in the mornings.
@@PHRASE2@@disagreeable
@@DEFINE@@someone who is disagreeable is bad-tempered and very unfriendly and behaves in an unpleasant way towards people
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's impossible to have a normal conversation with your father - he's always so disagreeable.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The landlord is an extremely disagreeable man. Have as little to do with him as possible.
@@PHRASE3@@moody
@@DEFINE@@often becoming annoyed or unhappy, especially when there seems to be no good reason to
@@EXAMPLE0@@Tammy's been moody and emotional all day.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a moody teenager
@@PHRASE4@@uptight
@@DEFINE@@behaving in a bad-tempered way towards other people, especially because you are always nervous or worried about something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I wish you would stop being so uptight.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@uptight about
@@EXAMPLE0@@My parents have always been uptight about me dating boys.
@@PHRASE5@@cantankerous
@@DEFINE@@an old person who is cantankerous is bad-tempered and complains and quarrels a lot
@@EXAMPLE0@@As Ethel grew older, she became more cantankerous.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Brooks is the committee's cantankerous chairman.
@@PHRASE6@@misery
@@DEFINE@@use this about someone who is always complaining and never seems to enjoy anything
@@EXAMPLE0@@Stop grumbling, you old misery.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Don't invite her. She's such a misery!
@@PHRASE7@@surly
@@DEFINE@@someone who is surly behaves in a bad-tempered, rude, and unhelpful way when dealing with people
@@EXAMPLE0@@Passengers complained about the dirty lavatory and surly staff.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Kevin can be really surly sometimes.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I declined to tip the porter, who left with a surly expression.
unfriendly and quiet because you are angry
@@PHRASE0@@sullen
@@DEFINE@@someone who is sullen behaves in a bad-tempered, unfriendly way and does not smile or talk much to people
@@EXAMPLE0@@Dick just sat there with a sullen expression on his face, refusing to speak.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The secretary was sullen and uncooperative.
@@PHRASE1@@sulky
@@DEFINE@@someone who is sulky has an angry, unhappy look on their face and does not talk much, especially because they think they have been treated unfairly
@@EXAMPLE0@@On the drive home, Maria was sulky and said very little.
@@EXAMPLE1@@William was a sulky little boy who seemed to care for nothing except his video games.
@@PHRASE2@@sulk
@@VARIANT@@be in a sulk
@@DEFINE@@if someone sulks , they are deliberately silent and bad-tempered for a period of time, because something has annoyed them, or because they think that they have been treated unfairly
@@EXAMPLE0@@Cindy always sulks when I won't buy her any candy.
@@EXAMPLE1@@You can't sit around sulking all day.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@sulk about something
@@EXAMPLE0@@What are you sulking about now?
easily annoyed
@@PHRASE0@@irritable
@@DEFINE@@easily annoyed by unimportant things, especially because you already feel bad-tempered about something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Since Steve quit smoking, he's been really irritable.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Zoe hadn't had much sleep and was feeling tired and irritable.
@@EXAMPLE2@@You're turning into an irritable old man.
@@PHRASE1@@touchy
@@DEFINE@@someone who is touchy is easily offended and made angry by things, so you have to be careful what you say to them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Saiid's a little touchy about how you pronounce her name.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@touchy about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Try not to look at his scars - he can be really touchy about it.
@@PHRASE2@@crotchety
@@DEFINE@@an old person who is crotchety becomes angry about unimportant things and complains a lot
@@EXAMPLE0@@a crotchety old man
@@EXAMPLE1@@When we were in Germany, we rented a room from a crotchety old woman named Brunhilde.
@@PHRASE3@@short-tempered/quick-tempered
@@DEFINE@@someone who is short-tempered gets angry quickly and easily
@@EXAMPLE0@@Jackie can be very short-tempered when she's hungry.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Her father is a quick-tempered man.
@@PHRASE4@@have a short fuse
@@DEFINE@@to often get angry quickly and easily
@@EXAMPLE0@@They say the judge has a very short fuse.
angry feelings

@@THESPROPFORM0@@feel anger towards

@@EXAMPLE0@@I've said some things in anger that have almost cost my marriage.

@@DEFINE@@a very strong feeling of anger that someone has that is either very difficult for them to control or is expressed very suddenly or violently
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fly into a rage
@@GLOSS@@to suddenly became very angry
@@EXAMPLE0@@When we accused him of lying, he flew into a rage.

@@GLOSS@@to be so angry, you shake
@@EXAMPLE0@@Vera's hands shook with rage as she read the letter.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@in a blind/jealous/terrible rage
@@EXAMPLE0@@Brown killed his wife in a jealous rage.
@@PHRASE4@@frustration
@@DEFINE@@the feeling of being annoyed, caused especially by a difficult or unpleasant situation that you are unable to change or control
@@EXAMPLE0@@Students have spoken of their growing frustration with school administrators.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The discussion sessions help patients deal with some of the frustrations they may be feeling.
@@PHRASE5@@resentment
@@DEFINE@@a feeling of anger because you feel that you are being treated badly or unfairly, and cannot do anything about it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Patricia stared at the other girls with resentment.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Resentment and jealousy can often build up in relationships.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@resentment at/against/of
@@EXAMPLE0@@She couldn't let go of her resentment over the divorce.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Any attempts to lessen his prison sentence will cause public outrage.
@@PHRASE7@@irritation
@@DEFINE@@the feeling of being annoyed, caused especially by someone or something that is repeatedly annoying
@@THESPROPFORM0@@irritation with
@@EXAMPLE0@@Bailey expressed irritation with the inaccurate reports in the media.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@a source of irritation
@@GLOSS@@something that causes irritation
@@EXAMPLE0@@The heavy traffic is a constant source of irritation.
@@PHRASE8@@exasperation
@@DEFINE@@the feeling of being very annoyed because you cannot control a situation, learn to do something, or understand something, even though you are trying very hard
@@THESPROPFORM0@@exasperation with
@@EXAMPLE0@@Many people express exasperation with the National Health Service, but most seem to prefer it to a private system.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@in exasperation
@@EXAMPLE0@@He pounded the desk in exasperation.

@@DEFINE@@if you say or do something in reply to what someone has said, you say or do it as a way of answering their question, request, remark etc

@@DEFINE@@an answer to a question in a test or competition
@@EXAMPLE0@@Write your answers on the form and send it to this address.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@the answer
@@GLOSS@@the correct answer
@@EXAMPLE0@@And the answer is ... Budapest!
@@THESPROPFORM1@@answer to
@@EXAMPLE0@@What's the answer to question 4?
@@THESPROPFORM2@@give your answer
@@EXAMPLE0@@Think carefully before you give the answer.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@the right/wrong answer
@@EXAMPLE0@@The first person to call with the right answer will win 10 CDs of their choice.
@@PHRASE1@@result
@@DEFINE@@an answer that you have found after calculating or doing tests
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've tried three different ways of adding these figures and each time I get a different result.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We have completed our experiments and we are now analyzing the results.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The results of our accountant's calculations show that we are on the verge of bankruptcy.
@@PHRASE2@@solution
@@DEFINE@@the correct answer to a complicated problem in a test or competition
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was a difficult equation, but it took her only five minutes to work out the solution.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@solution to
@@EXAMPLE0@@The solution to this week's puzzle will be published in next week's magazine.

@@THESPROPFORM0@@answer a question
@@EXAMPLE0@@You have 20 minutes to answer all the questions.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@answer correctly
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you answer correctly, you could win a video camera.
to find or calculate the answer to a question
@@PHRASE0@@solve
@@DEFINE@@to find the correct answer to a question, problem, or sum by thinking about it carefully or doing calculations
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm never going to solve this puzzle - it's impossible.
@@EXAMPLE1@@According to Greek legend, it was Oedipus who solved the riddle of the Sphinx.

@@EXAMPLE0@@It's all right, I don't need a calculator. I can work it out in my head.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'm sure they owe me more money than that - I'll have to sit down and figure it out.

any of a group of things
@@PHRASE0@@any
@@DEFINE@@use this to talk about each one of the things in a group, when it is not important to say exactly which one
@@EXAMPLE0@@You can buy the magazine at any good bookstore.
@@EXAMPLE1@@This remote control can be used with any television set.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@any of the/these/my/them etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@I told Debbie she could borrow any of my books.
@@EXAMPLE1@@So, do you like any of your new classes?
@@PHRASE1@@anything
@@DEFINE@@everything that you may want, need etc, especially when there is a very big choice
@@EXAMPLE0@@I was going to throw all these things away anyway, so please take anything you like.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Do you know anything about computers?
@@EXAMPLE2@@Paul goes to all the auctions in the area looking for anything in Art Deco style.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@anything else
@@EXAMPLE0@@The one thing he wanted more than anything else was a glass of cold water.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@anything at all
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you have any questions, feel free to ask me anything at all.
@@PHRASE2@@whatever
@@DEFINE@@anything at all -- use this to emphasize that it does not matter which object, action, idea etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Can I have a cake, Mummy?" "You can have whatever you want, darling."
@@EXAMPLE1@@We'll do whatever we can to help.
@@EXAMPLE2@@You should find whatever you need in the cupboard under the sink.
@@EXAMPLE3@@Here was an audience eager to listen to whatever I had to say.
@@PHRASE3@@you name it
@@DEFINE@@you say you name it when you are telling someone that there is everything that they want, or need, or can think of
@@EXAMPLE0@@World-class museums, great theater, outdoor sports -- you name it, this city's got it.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I had so many different jobs while I was a student: waiter, sales clerk, bartender -- you name it.
any one of the people in a group or in the world
@@PHRASE0@@any
@@DEFINE@@use this to talk about each person in a group of people when it is not important to say exactly which one
@@THESPROPFORM0@@any/man/child/teacher etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Ask any teacher and they'll tell you I'm right.

@@THESPROPFORM2@@any of you/them/us
@@EXAMPLE0@@Have any of you seen my glasses?
@@PHRASE1@@anyone/anybody
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't worry about it. It can happen to anybody.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Did anyone call while I was out?
@@EXAMPLE2@@If anybody needs more information, come and see me after class.
@@EXAMPLE3@@Sarah liked him more than anyone else she knew.
@@EXAMPLE4@@This would be an ideal job for anyone who speaks French and Italian.
@@PHRASE2@@any Tom, Dick or Harry
@@DEFINE@@anyone in the world, used especially when you mean that you should be more careful about who you choose or allow to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Any Tom, Dick, or Harry could have written something just as good.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If you don't have someone at the door, any Tom, Dick or Harry could turn up at the party and walk straight in.

@@DEFINE@@any person -- use this when the identity of the person is not important or is not known
@@EXAMPLE0@@Whoever you ask, you will get the same answer.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Sam wanted to feel that others, no matter who they were, agreed with him.
@@EXAMPLE2@@If someone comes to your door you should always ask for some form of identification, no matter who they say they are.
@@PHRASE4@@any fool/idiot
@@DEFINE@@if you say that any fool or any idiot can do something, you mean that anyone can do it because it is extremely easy, and if someone cannot do it they must be very stupid
@@EXAMPLE0@@Any fool could see that the child was unhappy.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Astronomers say that over the next few weeks the comet will be coming into view.

@@PHRASE5@@loom/loom up
@@DEFINE@@if a large person or thing looms or looms up , they suddenly appear in a way that makes you feel nervous or frightened, especially in a situation in which you cannot see clearly
@@EXAMPLE0@@As we rounded the curve, the mountain loomed up in front of us.

@@PHRASE6@@reappear
@@DEFINE@@to appear again after a short time of not being there or not being able to be seen

@@DEFINE@@to say that there is a difference between two things and argue about this, when really the difference is too small to be important
@@EXAMPLE0@@Batard is a little sweeter than Chevalier but perhaps that's splitting hairs; both these wines are excellent.

@@PHRASE0@@start an argument
@@EXAMPLE0@@I didn't want to start an argument, so I kept quiet.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Phil got into an argument with a guy at the bar.

@@EXAMPLE0@@A lot of young people take drugs. Personally, I can't see the attraction.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@attraction of
@@EXAMPLE0@@For many mothers, one of the attractions of childcare in the workplace is the chance to be near their children.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@a tourist attraction
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Galapagos Islands are one of Ecuador's main tourist attractions.
@@PHRASE1@@appeal
@@DEFINE@@a quality that someone or something has that makes people like it, want it, or feel interested in it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Much of Corfu's appeal lies in its lively night life.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Fink writes with eloquence about the appeal of the Jewish faith for her.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The film is flawed, although it has a certain nostalgic appeal.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@have popular/universal/mass appeal
@@GLOSS@@be interesting to most people
@@EXAMPLE0@@While animation has universal appeal, audiences have become increasingly insistent on high standards.
@@PHRASE2@@the lure of something
@@DEFINE@@a strongly attractive quality that makes you want something very much, even though you know it may be bad for you
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's hard to escape the lure of credit cards and the access they provide.
@@EXAMPLE1@@In public housing projects, the lure of gangs is strong for teenagers.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I tried hard to settle down, but the lure of travel and adventure was too much for me.
@@PHRASE3@@temptation
@@DEFINE@@something that makes you want to do or have something, even though you know you should not
@@EXAMPLE0@@Life in New York has so many temptations.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@temptation to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@When life was hard, the temptation to start drinking again was strong.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@resist (the) temptation
@@GLOSS@@not do something that you would really like to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@She thought of taking a day off work, but resisted the temptation.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@give in to (the) temptation
@@GLOSS@@do something that you would really like to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@I finally gave in to temptation and ate a huge piece of cheesecake.
@@PHRASE4@@charm
@@DEFINE@@a pleasant quality that someone has that makes people like them, feel attracted to them, or be easily persuaded by them. Charm is also used about the special qualities that a place or thing has that make people like it
@@EXAMPLE0@@With her charm and good looks, she's sure to be a success.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She was a leader of great character and tremendous personal charm.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The book captures Savannah's old Southern charm and its eccentric citizens perfectly.
available for someone to have or use
@@PHRASE0@@available
@@DEFINE@@if something is available , you can get it, buy it, or use it
@@EXAMPLE0@@There's no room for more books - we've used up all the available space.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@available to
@@EXAMPLE0@@Grants are available to students who have high grades.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@available from
@@EXAMPLE0@@The publication is available from the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@available at/in
@@EXAMPLE0@@Tickets are available at all Ticketmaster locations.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@have something available
@@EXAMPLE0@@Do you have a room available for this weekend?
@@THESPROPFORM4@@readily/freely available
@@GLOSS@@very easy to get
@@EXAMPLE0@@Drugs like heroin are readily available on the streets.
@@THESPROPFORM5@@make something available
@@EXAMPLE0@@These statistics are never sold or made available to the public.
@@PHRASE1@@free
@@DEFINE@@a room or seat that is free is not being used by anyone now, and no one has asked for it to be kept for them to use later
@@EXAMPLE0@@Is this chair free?
@@EXAMPLE1@@The only free seats on the train were in a smoking compartment.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@have something free
@@EXAMPLE0@@The hotel never has any rooms free over the Christmas period.
@@PHRASE2@@spare
@@DEFINE@@something that is spare is not being used now, but it can be used if someone needs it
@@EXAMPLE0@@I need 50 cents for the parking meter - do you have any spare change?
@@EXAMPLE1@@We're using the spare bedroom as a storage space.
@@EXAMPLE2@@a spare tyre
@@PHRASE3@@empty
@@DEFINE@@something such as a room or seat that is empty has no one using it at the moment and is therefore available for someone else to use
@@EXAMPLE0@@They have three empty rooms now that the kids have moved out.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I think there's an empty seat in the back row.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The house was empty for two months before it was sold.
@@PHRASE4@@vacant
@@DEFINE@@a building, home, room, or office that is vacant is available because it is not owned or rented by anyone
@@EXAMPLE0@@There don't seem to be any vacant rooms in the whole of London!
@@EXAMPLE1@@If you're looking for somewhere to rent, I think there's a vacant apartment in my building.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Of the buildings the company owns, only 3% are vacant.
@@PHRASE5@@to be had/found
@@DEFINE@@something that is to be had or to be found is available to anyone who knows where to get it from
@@EXAMPLE0@@When no work was to be had, he borrowed money from friends.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We looked all over, but there were no fast food restaurants to be found.
@@EXAMPLE2@@She knew of a place where designer clothes were to be had at bargain prices.
@@PHRASE6@@be going
@@DEFINE@@if something is going , it is available for anyone who wants it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Is there any more wine going?
@@EXAMPLE1@@There aren't many jobs going in this part of the country.
@@PHRASE7@@at your disposal
@@DEFINE@@if something is at your disposal , someone has provided it for you to use whenever you want or in any way that you want
@@EXAMPLE0@@We have ample money at our disposal to do this job right.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A limousine and driver were put at her disposal for the entire week.
@@PHRASE8@@be on tap
@@DEFINE@@if something that you like or enjoy is on tap , it is available to you all the time so that you can have it whenever you want it
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's a great place for a rest: food, music, alcohol - everything's on tap.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Some three hundred free outdoor shows are on tap during the weekend festival.

@@THESPROPFORM0@@be a bad influence on
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her new boyfriend has been a very bad influence on her.
a situation that you think is wrong or immoral
@@PHRASE0@@bad
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's very bad that tons of food are going to waste while people are starving.
@@EXAMPLE1@@What's really bad is the way the government promises new housing and never provides it.
@@PHRASE1@@wrong
@@DEFINE@@morally unacceptable, unfair, and against accepted ideas about what should be allowed to happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@I was taught that abortion is wrong, even though it's not illegal.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's wrong the way they treat that poor animal.
@@PHRASE2@@disgusting
@@DEFINE@@something that is disgusting makes people feel shocked and angry, because it is completely immoral, evil, or unfair
@@EXAMPLE0@@The attitude toward immigrants and racial minorities in this country is disgusting.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's disgusting the way politicians use their position to their personal advantage.
@@PHRASE3@@shocking/scandalous
@@DEFINE@@very immoral, unfair, or cruel, in a way that people think is unnecessary and unacceptable
@@EXAMPLE0@@The state of the country's health system is scandalous.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a shocking waste of human life
@@EXAMPLE2@@The amount of money spent on nuclear weapons is shocking.
@@EXAMPLE3@@It's scandalous that a lawyer who holds a position of trust would be involved in this kind of embezzlement.
@@PHRASE4@@outrageous
@@DEFINE@@a situation that is outrageous is extremely bad and unfair in a way that makes people very angry
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've always thought it outrageous that the poor have to pay for tax cuts for the rich.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The President accused the writer of an outrageous personal attack on his wife.
@@PHRASE5@@be a disgrace
@@DEFINE@@if you say something is a disgrace , you think it should not be allowed to happen, because it is very unfair or unkind
@@EXAMPLE0@@The way they treat their workers is a disgrace.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it's a disgrace (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's a disgrace that the only hospital in the town has been closed.
@@PHRASE6@@be a crime/be a sin
@@DEFINE@@you say that a situation is a crime or is a sin when you mean it is very bad, especially because it is not fair and could easily be prevented
@@EXAMPLE0@@No one should be in such a bad way that they have to beg. It's a sin.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The condition of the inner cities in this country is nothing short of a crime.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it's a crime/sin to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Mrs Clark said it would be a sin to evict them just because they hadn't paid their rent.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It would be a crime not to take this opportunity to reconstruct our educational system.
@@PHRASE7@@criminal
@@DEFINE@@a situation that is criminal is morally wrong, but not illegal
@@EXAMPLE0@@I think keeping animals locked up in cages is criminal.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Having such beautiful paintings and not letting the public see them is a criminal waste of the nation's art treasures.
@@PHRASE8@@deplorable
@@DEFINE@@a situation that is deplorable is very bad, especially when it is unnecessary and could easily be prevented
@@EXAMPLE0@@Something must be done about the deplorable state of our roads.
@@EXAMPLE1@@In addition to their harsh sentences, the prisoners have been exposed to deplorable prison conditions.

@@PHRASE0@@boring
@@DEFINE@@something that is boring is not interesting in any way and makes you feel tired and annoyed
@@EXAMPLE0@@I don't want some boring job in an office!
@@EXAMPLE1@@a long boring lecture on economic planning
@@EXAMPLE2@@What a boring way to spend an evening!

@@DEFINE@@very ordinary and not really interesting or enjoyable

@@PHRASE2@@dull
@@DEFINE@@boring because nothing different, interesting, or exciting happens
@@EXAMPLE0@@We spent a dull afternoon with some of Harold's business associates.
@@EXAMPLE1@@This kind of mindless work can become very dull very quickly.
@@PHRASE3@@monotonous
@@DEFINE@@something that is monotonous is boring because it always continues in the same way and it never changes
@@EXAMPLE0@@Life on the farm was slow and monotonous.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The teacher's low monotonous voice almost put me to sleep.
@@PHRASE4@@tedious
@@DEFINE@@something that is tedious is boring and tiring because it continues for too long
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was one of the most tedious plays I've ever had to sit through.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Doing all those calculations without a computer would be extremely tedious.
@@PHRASE5@@banal
@@DEFINE@@stories, books, remarks etc that are banal , are ordinary and uninteresting, especially because they do not contain anything new, exciting, or original
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was just another banal newspaper story.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I was expecting an interesting interview but he only asked a few banal questions about the weather.
@@PHRASE6@@mundane
@@DEFINE@@a job, event, or activity that is mundane is boring and ordinary and gives you very little pleasure, especially because you do it every day
@@EXAMPLE0@@The play is about the mundane existence of factory workers.
@@EXAMPLE1@@My initial job was pretty mundane, but later I was given more responsibility.
@@PHRASE7@@repetitive
@@DEFINE@@if something such as a job, speech, or a piece of writing or music is repetitive , it is boring because parts of it keep repeating again and again
@@EXAMPLE0@@As children we suffered through schoolwork that was dull and repetitive.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He has some good ideas, but his lectures can get a little repetitive.
@@PHRASE8@@uninspiring
@@DEFINE@@something that is uninspiring has nothing exciting or new about it, and makes you feel bored
@@EXAMPLE0@@The restaurant's dessert selection was somewhat uninspiring.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Both candidates turned in uninspiring performances in last night's debate.
@@PHRASE9@@humdrum
@@THESPROPFORM0@@humdrum existence/life/job

@@EXAMPLE0@@Occasional holidays abroad were the only things that brightened up her otherwise humdrum life.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Going to night school might improve your chances of getting out of that humdrum job.
@@PHRASE10@@soul-destroying
@@DEFINE@@a job or an experience that is soul-destroying is extremely boring and makes you very unhappy because you feel that you are a useless person and your life has no meaning
@@EXAMPLE0@@They spend all day sticking paper labels on toy cars - it's soul-destroying.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Going to the unemployment office and having to wait there for hours is a soul-destroying experience.
@@PHRASE11@@send you to sleep
@@VARIANT@@put you to sleep

@@EXAMPLE0@@All his talk about his financial problems just sends me to sleep.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Isn't there anything else to watch? This movie's putting me to sleep.

@@EXAMPLE0@@A pile of branches was burning in the yard.
@@EXAMPLE1@@At one end of the room a coal fire burned brightly.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The candle flickered briefly, then burned with a steady flame.
@@PHRASE1@@be on fire
@@DEFINE@@if a building, vehicle, or piece of clothing is on fire , it is burning
@@EXAMPLE0@@Large areas of the forest are reported to be on fire.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Before long the neighboring houses were on fire too.
@@PHRASE2@@be in flames
@@VARIANT@@be ablaze
@@DEFINE@@to be on fire with a lot of flames, causing serious damage
@@EXAMPLE0@@When the fire department arrived the whole school was in flames.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Twelve hours after the bombing raid, many parts of the city were still ablaze.
@@PHRASE3@@blazing
@@DEFINE@@burning very brightly with a lot of flames and heat
@@EXAMPLE0@@They sat on the sofa in front of a blazing fire.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The heat from the blazing car could be felt several metres away.
@@PHRASE4@@smoulder
@@VARIANT@@smolder
@@DEFINE@@to burn slowly, producing smoke but no flames
@@EXAMPLE0@@The fire in the chemical factory was so intense that it was still smouldering a week later.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A cigarette smoldered in the ashtray.
@@EXAMPLE2@@a pile of smoldering leaves
@@PHRASE5@@flicker
@@DEFINE@@if a fire or flame flickers , it burns unsteadily
@@EXAMPLE0@@A welcoming fire flickered in the grate.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Inside the shrine candles flicker next to statues of saints.
when something starts burning
@@PHRASE0@@catch fire
@@VARIANT@@catch on fire
@@DEFINE@@to start burning accidentally
@@EXAMPLE0@@Two farm workers died when a barn caught fire yesterday.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The car turned over, but luckily it didn't catch fire.
@@EXAMPLE2@@There was an explosion, and the whole garage caught on fire.
@@PHRASE1@@burst into flames
@@DEFINE@@to suddenly start burning and produce a lot of flames that cause serious damage
@@EXAMPLE0@@The plane crashed into the side of the mountain and burst into flames.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Without warning the toaster burst into flames.
@@PHRASE2@@go up (in flames)
@@DEFINE@@if a building or vehicle goes up or goes up in flames , it starts burning very quickly and usually is destroyed by fire
@@EXAMPLE0@@Be careful with those matches, or the whole place will go up in flames!
@@EXAMPLE1@@The fire spread slowly until it reached the gas cylinders, then the factory went up in flames.
@@EXAMPLE2@@If the oil tanker goes up, it could burn for weeks.
@@PHRASE3@@break out
@@DEFINE@@if a fire breaks out , it starts burning accidentally and spreads very quickly
@@EXAMPLE0@@Over £20,000 worth of damage was caused when a fire broke out in the cellar.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Would you know what to do if a fire broke out in your school?
@@PHRASE4@@flare up
@@DEFINE@@to suddenly begin to burn, or suddenly burn much more strongly than before, with a strong, bright flame
@@EXAMPLE0@@The spilled gasoline suddenly flared up in a sheet of flame.
@@EXAMPLE1@@They threw some dry wood onto the bonfire and it flared up, showering sparks into the night sky.
@@PHRASE5@@ignite
@@DEFINE@@to start burning
@@EXAMPLE0@@Scientists could not explain why the gas had suddenly ignited.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The compound ignites at 450 degrees Celsius.
to be destroyed by fire
@@PHRASE0@@burn down
@@DEFINE@@if a building burns down , it is completely destroyed by fire
@@EXAMPLE0@@Charlene has lived with relatives since her house burned down.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The hotel burnt down in 1990.
@@PHRASE1@@gutted
@@DEFINE@@a building that is gutted is still standing, but its inside has been completely destroyed by fire
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Was there anything worth saving after the fire?" "No, the place is completely gutted."
@@EXAMPLE1@@a street full of gutted buildings
@@PHRASE2@@burnt-out
@@VARIANT@@burned-out
@@DEFINE@@a building or a vehicle that is burnt-out or burned-out has had everything inside it destroyed by fire
@@EXAMPLE0@@In the main square the burnt-out shell of the Palace of Justice still smouldered.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The van was burned-out and completely blackened by smoke.

@@EXAMPLE5@@"Gone with the Wind' was a great movie, but it was a little long.
@@EXAMPLE6@@In the US it is normal for the police to carry guns, but not in Britain.
@@PHRASE1@@however/nevertheless/nonetheless
@@DEFINE@@use this when saying something that is surprising after what you have just said, or that is very different from it
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was a terrible accident. Nevertheless, air travel is still the safest form of transport.
@@EXAMPLE1@@December saw a more than average rainfall; however, the possibility of a drought is still strong.
@@EXAMPLE2@@War is never welcome, nonetheless, I believe that we must defend our country.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@but nevertheless/nonetheless
@@EXAMPLE0@@The leaves aren't particularly dangerous, but nevertheless they are not something you'd want your child or pet to eat.
@@PHRASE2@@on the other hand
@@DEFINE@@use this at the beginning of a sentence when you have just mentioned one side of an argument or situation and you are going to mention the opposite side
@@EXAMPLE0@@Nuclear power is relatively cheap. On the other hand, you could argue that it's not safe.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The hamburger was tough and overcooked. The fries, on the other hand, were terrific, and well worth the money.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@but on the other hand
@@EXAMPLE0@@You want to help your kids as much as you can, but on the other hand, you've got to be careful to help them learn on their own.
@@PHRASE3@@still/all the same/then again
@@VARIANT@@mind you
@@DEFINE@@use this when you have just said one thing and you now want to say something very different about it, for example when you give an advantage and then a disadvantage
@@EXAMPLE0@@Teaching is an interesting job. Then again, it can be very stressful too.
@@EXAMPLE1@@This trip is going to be very expensive. Still, we don't go away very often.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I'd love to travel around the world. Mind you, I wouldn't want to go on my own.
@@EXAMPLE3@@My parents are happy to lend me the money. All the same, I do feel guilty about it.
@@PHRASE4@@yet
@@DEFINE@@use this to introduce a fact that seems surprising after what you have just said
@@EXAMPLE0@@The sun was shining, yet it was quite cold.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Last summer there was a drought, yet some people were still watering their lawns every day.
@@PHRASE5@@whereas/while
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that although something is true of one person, thing, or situation, it is not true of another
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some house plants thrive if placed near a window with plenty of sunlight while others prefer to be in a more shaded spot.
@@EXAMPLE1@@American cars are generally too large for the Japanese market, whereas Japanese cars are popular in the US.
@@PHRASE6@@though/although
@@DEFINE@@use this to introduce a fact or opinion that makes what you have just said less strong or definite
@@EXAMPLE0@@Dan's been very ill, although he's better now.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I don't really like classical music, though I did enjoy that Pavarotti concert.
@@EXAMPLE2@@They're a very nice couple, although I very seldom see them these days.
@@PHRASE7@@though
@@DEFINE@@use this at the end of a sentence to add a fact or opinion that makes what you have just said seem less important , or to add a different fact or opinion
@@EXAMPLE0@@I think she's Swiss. I'm not sure, though.
@@EXAMPLE1@@George did say one nice thing, though.
@@PHRASE8@@even so
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that something is true in spite of the fact that you have just mentioned
@@EXAMPLE0@@Try to run on a soft surface, such as grass. Even so, you may start having knee problems.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@but even so
@@EXAMPLE0@@She had only seen Matthew Godden once before, but even so she recognized him instantly.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The fines for speeding are large, but even so, they are not always a deterrent.
@@PHRASE9@@only/except
@@DEFINE@@use this for introducing the reason why something is not possible
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'd like to come and live here, only it's too expensive.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I would have asked them to stay with us, except we don't have enough room.
