when things are done, chosen etc by chance
@@PHRASE0@@at random
@@DEFINE@@if you do or choose things at random , you do or choose them without using any plan or system
@@EXAMPLE0@@The forms were distributed at random to people passing by.
@@EXAMPLE1@@While he waited, he picked up a magazine, turned to a page at random, and started reading.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Twenty students were chosen at random to take part in the experiment.
@@PHRASE1@@random
@@DEFINE@@something that is random is done or chosen without using any plan or system
@@EXAMPLE0@@The union believes that the random drug testing of employees is an invasion of their privacy.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A few random shots were fired, but the battle was over.
@@PHRASE2@@arbitrary
@@DEFINE@@something that is arbitrary is decided or arranged without any reason, plan, or system, especially in a way that seems unfair
@@EXAMPLE0@@The way the programme of events is organized seems completely arbitrary to me.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The fans complained about the apparently arbitrary distribution of tickets for the next game.
when you have the chance to do something
@@PHRASE0@@chance
@@DEFINE@@a situation in which it is possible for you to do something enjoyable, useful, or exciting, or something that you want to do
@@THESPROPFORM0@@chance to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I never got the chance to thank him for all his help.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's a beautiful building - you should go and see it if you have a chance.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@give somebody a/the chance to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I wish he'd just give me the chance to explain.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@take the chance to do something
@@GLOSS@@use a chance when you have it
@@EXAMPLE0@@You should take the chance to travel while you are still young.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@chance for somebody to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Back to School Night" will be a chance for parents to meet their child's teacher.
@@THESPROPFORM4@@somebody's last chance
@@GLOSS@@when you will not have another chance
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was her last chance to see him before she left town.
@@PHRASE1@@opportunity
@@DEFINE@@a chance to do something, especially something that is important or useful to you, or something that you want to do very much
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was too good an opportunity to pass up.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@opportunity to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@All he needs is an opportunity to show his ability.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@opportunity of doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@After they had refused him the opportunity of improving his position, he resigned.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@opportunity for somebody to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@We see this as an exciting opportunity for our companies to work together.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@have an/the opportunity (to do something)
@@EXAMPLE0@@She was delighted to have an opportunity to talk with someone who shared her interest in classical music.
@@THESPROPFORM4@@equal opportunities
@@GLOSS@@the same opportunities as other people
@@EXAMPLE0@@All over the world women are demanding equal opportunities.
@@PHRASE2@@break
@@DEFINE@@a sudden or unexpected chance to do something, especially to be successful in your job
@@EXAMPLE0@@Gary wants to work in television. He's just waiting for a break.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@lucky break
@@EXAMPLE0@@Seeing that advertisement in the paper was a lucky break for me.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@big break
@@EXAMPLE0@@Nimoy's big break in television came in the mid-'60s, when he won the role of Spock on "Star Trek".
@@PHRASE3@@golden opportunity
@@EXAMPLE0@@I got a grant from my university to study in the USA for a year. It's a golden opportunity!
@@THESPROPFORM0@@a golden opportunity (for somebody) to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The management course is being paid for by the company and it's a golden opportunity to improve your skills.
@@PHRASE4@@chance of a lifetime
@@DEFINE@@the chance to do something very exciting or important that you might never be able to do again
@@EXAMPLE0@@This job is the chance of a lifetime. You'd be a fool not to take it.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If you don't hurry up and make a decision, you could miss the chance of a lifetime.
@@PHRASE5@@room/scope
@@DEFINE@@a chance to do things you want to do, in the way that you want to do them. Scope is more formal than room
@@EXAMPLE0@@He refused the post because he felt it didn't offer him much scope.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@room/scope for
@@EXAMPLE0@@There will always be room for debate and disagreement in this class.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I have two jobs, which doesn't leave much room for socializing.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Despite our recent success, there is still scope for improvement.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@room/scope to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@We've left the course deliberately vague, so there's room to concentrate on your particular areas of interest.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Better paid labour means greater scope to increase the company's profits.
@@PHRASE6@@prospects
@@DEFINE@@the chance of being successful at something in the future, especially your job
@@EXAMPLE0@@He had no job, no family, no home, no prospects.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Employers are now offering more jobs with quality training and excellent career prospects.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@prospects for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The prospects for an alliance between the two nations do not look good.
@@PHRASE7@@possibility
@@DEFINE@@the chance to do something
@@THESPROPFORM0@@possibility for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The possibilities for improvement are endless.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We need to investigate all possibilities for helping these children.
@@PHRASE8@@open doors for/open the door for
@@DEFINE@@to give someone an opportunity to do something, for example the opportunity to do a particular job
@@EXAMPLE0@@My experience in the Peace Corps really opened doors for me when I started looking for a job.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Alice Coachman's Olympic success opened the door for generations of African-American track athletes.
to use an opportunity
@@PHRASE0@@take the opportunity
@@THESPROPFORM0@@take the opportunity to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I would like to take this opportunity to thank you all for your help.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@take the opportunity of doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm going to take every opportunity of going to see Brian while he's living in Germany.
@@PHRASE1@@grab the chance
@@DEFINE@@to quickly use an opportunity to do something, especially when you think you might not get another chance
@@EXAMPLE0@@It may be the last time he offers you the job so I'd grab the chance while you can.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@grab the chance to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Knowing how difficult it is to find a job I grabbed the chance to be trained as an electrician.
@@PHRASE2@@jump at the chance/opportunity
@@DEFINE@@to eagerly and quickly use an opportunity to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The early retirement plan is excellent and I'm surprised that people haven't jumped at the opportunity.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@jump at the chance/opportunity to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@When the resort was put up for sale, the Millers jumped at the chance to buy it.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She thought Lewis would jump at the opportunity to make some extra money on weekends.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@jump at the chance/opportunity of doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Who wouldn't jump at the chance of spending a month in Australia?
@@PHRASE3@@strike while the iron is hot
@@DEFINE@@to do something quickly, while you are in a situation in which you are most likely to be successful
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't wait until tomorrow before you tell him, strike while the iron is hot!
@@PHRASE4@@make hay while the sun shines
@@DEFINE@@to take the opportunity to do something now while the conditions are good, because you might not be able to do it later
@@EXAMPLE0@@Let's make hay while the sun shines and finish this project before I start falling asleep.
@@PHRASE5@@opportunist
@@DEFINE@@someone who always looks for and takes opportunities that might make them more successful -- used to show disapproval
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is difficult to tell whether he really wants to help May or whether he is just an opportunist.
@@EXAMPLE1@@As the finance company started to fail a few opportunists managed to make more money out of it.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Jerry's already sold the car to someone else. You've missed your chance.

@@DEFINE@@to not use the chance to do something enjoyable or useful, especially when this is not a good thing
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you don't come to the picnic you'll miss out on all the fun.

@@EXAMPLE1@@I was afraid I'd blown my chance but she agreed to go out again on Saturday night.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@blow your chances of doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@She started running much too fast at the beginning and blew her chances of winning the race.
@@PHRASE3@@miss the boat
@@DEFINE@@to be too late to use an opportunity to do something good
@@EXAMPLE0@@Buy your shares in the company now or you'll miss the boat.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He didn't get his application in early enough so he missed the boat.
@@PHRASE4@@let something slip through your fingers
@@DEFINE@@to not use a good opportunity when you are able to, especially an opportunity that you will not get again
@@EXAMPLE0@@We had an opportunity to win the championship last season and we let it slip through our fingers.
@@PHRASE5@@lost opportunity
@@DEFINE@@an opportunity that you wasted by not using it to become successful, enjoy yourself etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you don't take the job it'll just be another lost opportunity in your life.
to become different
@@PHRASE0@@change
@@EXAMPLE0@@She's changed a lot since she went to college.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's amazing how much things have changed since we were young.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Her expression did not change, and she answered me calmly.
@@EXAMPLE3@@"The telecommunications industry is changing at lightning speed," said Richard Miller, the company's chief financial officer.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@change into
@@EXAMPLE0@@The caterpillar eventually changes into a beautiful butterfly.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@change from something to/into something
@@EXAMPLE0@@In the 18th century, Britain changed from a mainly agricultural society to an industrial one.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@change to
@@EXAMPLE0@@The lights changed to green, and the motorbike sped off.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@change colour
@@VARIANT@@change color
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was the end of September, and the leaves on the trees were starting to change color.
@@THESPROPFORM4@@change out of all recognition
@@GLOSS@@change completely
@@EXAMPLE0@@The town I grew up in has changed out of all recognition.
@@PHRASE1@@changing
@@DEFINE@@becoming different
@@EXAMPLE0@@I find it hard to keep up with changing fashions.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His book is concerned with the changing role of fathers.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Ansel Adams loved wide landscapes and changing light.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@constantly/rapidly changing
@@EXAMPLE0@@Businesses need to be flexible enough to adapt to changing conditions in a rapidly changing world.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@fast-changing/ever-changing
@@GLOSS@@changing quickly or frequently
@@EXAMPLE0@@Job insecurity is widespread in the fast-changing American workplace.
@@PHRASE2@@alter
@@DEFINE@@to change - use this especially about someone's feelings or behaviour, or about a situation
@@EXAMPLE0@@His mood suddenly altered and he seemed a little annoyed.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His defence lawyer said that Wilson's lifestyle had altered dramatically since the offences three years ago.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Her face hadn't altered much over the years.
@@PHRASE3@@turn into something
@@DEFINE@@to become something completely different
@@EXAMPLE0@@In fairy tales when the princess kisses a frog, it turns into a handsome prince.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A trip to the beach turned into a nightmare for a local family yesterday.
@@PHRASE4@@turn cold/nasty/violent etc
@@DEFINE@@to suddenly become cold, unpleasant etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The ink-black nights were turning cold, and the stars were frosty and fewer.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The protest turned violent when groups of demonstrators stormed the parliament building.
@@PHRASE5@@go from ... to ...
@@DEFINE@@to stop being one thing and start being something else, especially something very different
@@EXAMPLE0@@In less than five years, he went from being a communist to being a member of the military government.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His face went from pink to bright red.

@@THESPROPFORM0@@go from bad to worse
@@GLOSS@@change from being bad to being even worse
@@EXAMPLE0@@After Kathy lost her job, things went from bad to worse, and eventually she and Ed split up.
to change all the time or often
@@PHRASE0@@keep changing
@@EXAMPLE0@@His ideas about what he wants keep changing.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'll check the regulations for you - they keep changing.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The police strongly suspected that she had been involved - her story kept changing and was filled with inconsistencies.
@@PHRASE1@@vary
@@DEFINE@@to change often
@@DEFINE@@if something varies , it changes according to what the situation is
@@EXAMPLE0@@Ticket prices to New York vary, depending on the time of year.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@vary from....to
@@EXAMPLE0@@Driving regulations vary from state to state.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@vary considerably/enormously/greatly
@@GLOSS@@change a lot
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her income varies considerably from one month to the next.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@vary in price/quality/size etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Vegetables vary in quality according to the season.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@it varies
@@EXAMPLE0@@"How much milk do you use a day?" "Oh, it varies."
@@THESPROPFORM4@@vary from day to day/week to week etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@It hadn't been established where we'd all sleep - the location seemed to vary from night to night.
@@PHRASE2@@fluctuate
@@DEFINE@@if something such as a price or amount fluctuates , it changes very often from a high level to a low one and back again
@@EXAMPLE0@@The car industry's annual production fluctuates between 5.1 million and 9.2 million vehicles.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Cholesterol levels in the blood fluctuate in the course of a day.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fluctuate wildly
@@EXAMPLE0@@Share prices on the New York Stock Exchange often fluctuate wildly.
@@PHRASE3@@be in flux/be in a state of flux
@@DEFINE@@if something such as a system or a set of ideas is in flux or in a state of flux , it is changing a lot all the time, especially in a confusing way, so that you do not know what it will finally be like
@@EXAMPLE0@@The computer industry is in constant flux, responding all the time to changes in technology.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Our education programme is in a state of flux, as new approaches are being developed.
often changing or likely to change
@@PHRASE0@@changeable
@@DEFINE@@feelings or conditions that are changeable change frequently so that it is difficult to know what they will be like in a short time
@@EXAMPLE0@@You love him now, but at your age feelings are changeable.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'm a changeable sort of person.
@@EXAMPLE2@@changeable weather
@@PHRASE1@@erratic
@@DEFINE@@behaviour, processes, or services that are erratic change suddenly in an unexpected and surprising way, when it would be better if they remained the same
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her behaviour was becoming more and more erratic.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Heating was difficult owing to erratic supplies of gas, electricity and water.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The company's erratic performance is a cause for some concern.
@@PHRASE2@@volatile
@@DEFINE@@a volatile situation or character is likely to change suddenly and unexpectedly
@@EXAMPLE0@@The political situation in the Balkans is still extremely volatile.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She formed enduring friendships with women and more intense, volatile ones with men.
@@PHRASE3@@unstable
@@DEFINE@@a person, situation, or system or government that is unstable is likely to change suddenly and become worse, because there is something wrong with their character or the way things are organized
@@EXAMPLE0@@Regimes governed by violence are always unstable.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Was it safe to trust someone who was so emotionally unstable?
@@PHRASE4@@variable
@@DEFINE@@changing according to the situation - use this about amounts, prices, speeds, temperatures etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Demand for the company's products is variable.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The weather here is likely to be very variable.
@@PHRASE5@@inconsistent
@@DEFINE@@inconsistent behaviour or work changes too often from good to bad, and you cannot trust it to be good all the time
@@EXAMPLE0@@People feel threatened when decision-making is inconsistent and arbitrary.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A succession of injuries produced an inconsistent season for one of our best players.
@@PHRASE6@@unsettled
@@DEFINE@@conditions or situations that are unsettled change frequently so that it is impossible to make plans or know what will happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is dangerous to visit there while the political situation is so unsettled.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The weather has been very unsettled lately.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Eliot led a strangely unsettled life, drifting from place to place and job to job.

@@EXAMPLE0@@These old teachers tend to have very fixed ideas.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@have fixed ideas about
@@EXAMPLE0@@He has very fixed ideas about the way a wife should behave.
@@PHRASE1@@reactionary
@@DEFINE@@strongly opposed to change, especially social or political change, in a way that you think is unreasonable
@@EXAMPLE0@@The seventy-year-old president has been condemned as reactionary by his radical opponents.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He is known for his reactionary views on immigration and the reintroduction of the death penalty.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Cultural attitudes to women were more reactionary than in most of Western Europe.
@@PHRASE2@@entrenched
@@DEFINE@@entrenched attitudes are ones that people have had for a long time and are very difficult to change
@@THESPROPFORM0@@entrenched in
@@EXAMPLE0@@The unequal treatment of men and women in the labour market is deeply entrenched in our culture.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@firmly/deeply entrenched
@@EXAMPLE0@@In the small towns racial prejudice was deeply entrenched.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@entrenched attitudes/habits/beliefs etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The attitudes of adults to the mentally handicapped tend to be firmly entrenched, and difficult to change.
@@PHRASE3@@stick in the mud
@@DEFINE@@someone who has old-fashioned attitudes and is unwilling to change or try something new
@@EXAMPLE0@@Come on, don't be such an old stick in the mud.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She accused him of being a stick in the mud.
@@PHRASE4@@diehard
@@DEFINE@@someone who still refuses to change their beliefs even when most other people have changed them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Apart from a few union diehards most of the men have accepted the new productivity agreement.
@@PHRASE5@@hidebound
@@DEFINE@@a group of people or an institution that is hidebound has very old-fashioned ideas and attitudes and is unwilling to change them
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was predictable that the medical establishment, so hidebound and reactionary, would reject Dr Stone's ideas.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The hidebound attitudes of Russia's powerful aristocracy made any kind of progress impossible.
unwilling to change the way you do things
@@PHRASE0@@inflexible
@@DEFINE@@not willing to change the way you think or the way you do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Although many students adored Albers, others found him inflexible and stifling.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Union negotiators criticized the employers for being too inflexible on the issues of pay and working conditions.
@@PHRASE1@@be set in your ways
@@DEFINE@@to be unable to change the way you do things because you have done them that way for a long time
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm too old and set in my ways to try living in a foreign country now.
@@PHRASE2@@rigid
@@DEFINE@@someone who is rigid will never change their mind about what is right or wrong or about how things should be done
@@EXAMPLE0@@Our manager was so rigid, he'd never listen to our ideas.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Any major changes were prevented by the rigid conservatism of the Church.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@rigid in your ideas/opinions/attitudes etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Andrew was even more rigid in his attitudes towards child-rearing than his father, who was himself quite strict.
when something that has been decided cannot be changed
@@PHRASE0@@final
@@DEFINE@@a decision that is final cannot be changed, especially because it has been made officially by someone in authority
@@EXAMPLE0@@They thought carefully before making a final commitment to buy.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@final approval/decision etc

@@EXAMPLE1@@The officials have final authority when making decisions.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@and that's final!
@@GLOSS@@used to say that you will not change your mind about something, and do not want to hear any more about it

@@THESPROPFORM2@@have the final say
@@GLOSS@@be the person who makes the final decision
@@EXAMPLE0@@My boss has approved the project, but it's the Chief Executive who has the final say.

@@DEFINE@@a decision or choice which is irrevocable cannot be changed after it has been made

@@EXAMPLE1@@I posted the letter, then realized that what I had done was irrevocable, and that I couldn't change my mind now.

someone's character
@@PHRASE0@@character
@@DEFINE@@the combination of qualities that makes someone a particular kind of person, for example a good or bad, honest or dishonest person
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her behavior last night revealed a lot about her character.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A candidate's character and qualifications are more important than past experience.
@@EXAMPLE2@@What strikes me most about Hamlet is his noble character.
@@PHRASE1@@personality
@@DEFINE@@someone's character - use this especially about how someone behaves towards other people, for example whether they are friendly or unfriendly, confident or easily frightened etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's true he can be emotional at times but that's just part of his personality.
@@EXAMPLE1@@This election should be about issues and policies, not about the personalities of the candidates!
@@THESPROPFORM0@@friendly/nice/warm etc personality
@@EXAMPLE0@@Yun has a lovely, warm personality.
@@PHRASE2@@nature

@@EXAMPLE0@@Kindness and sympathy were in his nature.

@@EXAMPLE2@@She was surprised to learn he had a romantic side to his nature.

@@THESPROPFORM1@@it's not in somebody's nature
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was not in his nature to take risks.

@@THESPROPFORM0@@the right temperament

@@PHRASE4@@a nervous/jealous etc disposition

@@PHRASE5@@make-up
@@VARIANT@@makeup
@@DEFINE@@someone's character - use this especially to say that someone's character is completely fixed and they cannot change it or control it
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's not in their make-up to accept defeat.

@@THESPROPFORM0@@be part of somebody's make-up
@@EXAMPLE0@@Stubbornness has always been a significant part of his makeup.

@@DEFINE@@if you know what makes someone tick , you understand their character, desires, and what makes them behave in the way they do

@@EXAMPLE1@@As a teacher, you need to get to know your students, find out what makes them tick.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Permission to use firearms is conditional on the consent of the Chief of Police.

@@PHRASE0@@unconditional

@@EXAMPLE1@@They are campaigning for the unconditional release of all political prisoners.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Before you accept the loan you'd better make sure that there are no strings attached.

@@THESPROPFORM0@@unrelated to something/unconnected with something
@@EXAMPLE0@@A spokesperson claimed that Hoyle's dismissal was completely unrelated to his recent criticism of the club.
@@PHRASE2@@have no connection with
@@DEFINE@@to not be connected with something in any way
@@EXAMPLE0@@His comment had absolutely no connection with what we were talking about.

@@DEFINE@@to not be connected with something or someone in any way
@@EXAMPLE0@@Those boxes are nothing to do with me. Sally left them there.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Your age has nothing to do with your ability to do the job.
not connected with the subject you are talking about
@@PHRASE0@@irrelevant
@@EXAMPLE0@@Chris continued to annoy her with questions on totally irrelevant subjects.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"But I didn't know it was illegal to park here." "That's completely irrelevant."
@@THESPROPFORM0@@irrelevant to
@@EXAMPLE0@@To many young people, the church seems outdated and irrelevant to modern times.

@@DEFINE@@say this when you think that what someone has said does not have any real connection with what you are arguing about

@@PHRASE2@@be/have nothing to do with
@@DEFINE@@if something has nothing to do with a subject, it is not connected with it in any way
@@EXAMPLE0@@My back was bothering me a little bit, but that had nothing to do with how badly I played.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I don't know what's the matter with Billy -- he says it's nothing to do with school.

@@PHRASE3@@what has that got to do with ...?
@@VARIANT@@what does that have to do with ...?
@@DEFINE@@say this when someone has mentioned something and you cannot understand how it is connected with the subject you are talking about
@@EXAMPLE0@@I realize you didn't get home until after midnight but what does that have to do with coming in late for work?
@@PHRASE4@@doesn't come into it/doesn't enter into it
@@DEFINE@@say this about something that someone has mentioned that does not influence or affect what you are talking about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Whether the applicant is a man or a woman doesn't come into it.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'm afraid this is company policy, and your own views on the matter simply don't enter into it.

@@EXAMPLE1@@It's true we're not friends but that's neither here nor there. We're still able to work together.
@@PHRASE6@@have no bearing on something
@@DEFINE@@if something has no bearing on the situation that you are talking about, it does not affect that situation or help to explain it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The president's age has no bearing on whether or not I will vote for him.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A suspect's previous criminal record should have no bearing on the trial.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Rescuers are working round the clock to find survivors of the blast.
@@PHRASE2@@twenty-four-hour/24-hour
@@THESPROPFORM0@@twenty-four-hour service/guard/care etc
@@DEFINE@@a service etc that is done or provided continuously, all day and all night
@@EXAMPLE0@@Twenty-four-hour medical care is provided.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The police cannot provide 24-hour protection for everyone.
@@PHRASE3@@24/7
@@DEFINE@@happening, done, or existing 24 hours a day and seven days a week and never stopping
@@EXAMPLE0@@The hotline is open 24/7 to teenagers who need someone to talk to.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Do you think about this guy 24/7?

@@DEFINE@@the person in charge of a court, who knows a lot about the law and makes the official decision about what the punishment for a crime should be
@@EXAMPLE0@@Everyone stood up as the judge entered the courtroom.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Judge Butler gave the defendant a six-month jail sentence.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The judge advised the governor that the law violated the First Amendment rights of teachers.
@@PHRASE1@@jury
@@DEFINE@@a group of ordinary people, who listen to the people speaking at a trial, and then decide whether or not someone is guilty of a crime
@@EXAMPLE0@@The jury was made up of seven women and five men.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Have you ever been on a jury?
@@EXAMPLE2@@The jury awarded Hayes $3.5 million in damages.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@jury duty/service
@@GLOSS@@a period of time during which you must be ready to be part of a jury if necessary
@@EXAMPLE0@@I have been called for jury duty twice.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@hung jury
@@GLOSS@@a jury that cannot make a decision about whether someone is guilty or not
@@EXAMPLE0@@Broderick's first trial last year ended in a hung jury.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@sit on a jury
@@GLOSS@@be a member of a jury
@@EXAMPLE0@@Are people with criminal records allowed to sit on a jury?
@@PHRASE2@@lawyer
@@VARIANT@@attorney
@@DEFINE@@someone who is trained in the law and who represents people in court
@@EXAMPLE0@@You have to study for a long time to become a lawyer.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He refused to answer any questions until his lawyer came.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@defence lawyer
@@THESPROPFORM1@@defense laywer
@@GLOSS@@a lawyer who tries to prove that a person is not guilty of a crime
@@EXAMPLE0@@Defense lawyer Charles Grieshammer said he was not surprised by the verdict.
@@PHRASE3@@defendant
@@DEFINE@@the person in a trial who is being judged guilty or not guilty of a crime
@@EXAMPLE0@@The defendant pleaded not guilty.
@@EXAMPLE1@@According to the defendant, the heroin was destined for the New York City area.
@@PHRASE4@@the accused
@@DEFINE@@someone who is trying to prove that they are not guilty of a crime that they are on trial for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The accused is being held in the Pelham County Jail on charges of assault and battery.
@@EXAMPLE1@@According to the sixth amendment, the accused has the right to a fair and public trial.
@@PHRASE5@@the defence
@@VARIANT@@the defense
@@DEFINE@@the lawyers in a court who try to prove that someone is not guilty of a crime
@@EXAMPLE0@@The defence plans to call only one witness to testify.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Today, the defence makes its final presentation to the jury.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Peres said the defense team would appeal the sentencing by Judge Bernardo Tirado.
@@PHRASE6@@the prosecution
@@DEFINE@@the lawyers in a court who try to prove that someone is guilty of a crime
@@EXAMPLE0@@The prosecution's first witness is expected to be one of the defendant's co-workers.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Speaking for the prosecution, Lipscomb said that both men should go to prison for the rest of their lives.
@@PHRASE7@@witness
@@DEFINE@@someone who tells what they know about a crime in court
@@EXAMPLE0@@Police have appealed for witnesses to come forward.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The witness was asked to identify the defendant in the courtroom.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@call somebody as a witness
@@EXAMPLE0@@The congressman was called as a witness for the prosecution today.
to bring someone to court to be judged
@@PHRASE0@@prosecute
@@DEFINE@@to officially say that someone has broken the law and bring them to a court of law to be judged

@@EXAMPLE0@@Baldwin was prosecuted in 1998 for distributing child pornography online.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@prosecute a case
@@EXAMPLE0@@Last year, Napolitano's office prosecuted 115 child abuse cases, the highest number in the nation.
@@PHRASE1@@put somebody on trial
@@DEFINE@@to officially bring someone to a court of law to be judged
@@EXAMPLE0@@A month after the murder, a man was arrested by police and put on trial.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@put sb on trial for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The couple were put on trial for fraud and found guilty.
to be judged in a court of law
@@PHRASE0@@be tried
@@EXAMPLE0@@The suspect will be tried within the next few weeks.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Patterson is being tried for the murder of a 30-year-old Oakland hairdresser.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be tried for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The two women are being tried for drug smuggling.
@@PHRASE1@@be on trial
@@DEFINE@@if someone is on trial , a court of law is trying to decide whether they are guilty or a crime or not

@@EXAMPLE1@@The accused was extradited to Miami earlier this year, and is currently on trial there.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be on trial for
@@EXAMPLE0@@Three men are on trial for illegally smuggling tropical birds into the country.

@@EXAMPLE0@@The judge ruled that Pinochet was too ill to stand trial in Spain.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Brady stood trial for the killings late last year.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@stand trial on

when a legal case is judged in court
@@PHRASE0@@come to trial
@@DEFINE@@if a serious legal case comes to trial , it is judged in a court of law
@@EXAMPLE0@@The case won't come to trial until next summer.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The British press is not permitted to comment on a case until it comes to trial.
@@PHRASE1@@come/be brought before the court
@@DEFINE@@if a legal case or a criminal comes or is brought before the court , they go to a court of law so it can be officially decided what further legal action should be taken
@@EXAMPLE0@@He thinks his case will come before the court within the next few months.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The case was brought before the court by farmer Brad Morgan.
@@PHRASE2@@be heard
@@DEFINE@@if a court case, a problem, or a complaint is heard , a judge or lawyer listens to it to decide what legal action should be taken
@@EXAMPLE0@@Last year 2,047 cases were heard in the Hillbrow small claims court.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Yesterday counsel for both parties agreed the case should be heard on March 12.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Stansfield would never have knowingly become involved in political espionage.
@@PHRASE4@@consciously
@@DEFINE@@if you do something consciously , you do it carefully and you think about it as you are doing it, especially because you know what the result of your actions might be
@@EXAMPLE0@@I don't think she was consciously trying to hurt your feelings.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Most school teachers do not consciously discriminate between their students.
@@PHRASE5@@wilfully
@@VARIANT@@willfully
@@DEFINE@@if you wilfully do something, you do it deliberately or do not try to stop it even though you know it is wrong or it will cause harm -- used especially in legal contexts
@@EXAMPLE0@@The mother could face a charge of wilfully neglecting her children.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The defendants were convicted of wilfully promoting racial hatred.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The new evidence was either not available or was willfully ignored.
@@PHRASE6@@pointedly
@@DEFINE@@said or done in a way that will make other people notice you, especially to show them that you think they should do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Miss Phillips looked at the clock pointedly and I realized that it was time for me to leave.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The shopkeeper made a rude comment about shoplifters and looked pointedly at the boy standing next to me.
@@PHRASE7@@make a point of
@@DEFINE@@to deliberately do something because you think it is important to do it, or because you want other people to notice that you have done it
@@THESPROPFORM0@@make a point of doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Kramer made a point of looking very bored while the colonel was speaking.
@@EXAMPLE1@@You should make a point of arriving fifteen minutes early at the office every morning -- show that you're keen.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@make a point of something
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Did you complain about it?" "Yes, I made a point of it."

when what happens is influenced by other facts or events
@@PHRASE0@@depend
@@DEFINE@@if something depends on a fact, result, decision etc, it is not fixed or decided because it will change if the fact, result, decision etc changes
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it depends how/where/what etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@I might not be able to go to France - it depends how much it costs.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@it depends/that depends
@@GLOSS@@say this when your decision may change according to what happens
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Are you going to apply for that job?" "Well, it depends."
@@THESPROPFORM2@@it all depends
@@GLOSS@@say this to emphasize that you cannot be certain about something
@@EXAMPLE0@@We still don't know whether we'll have to move to a new house or not - it all depends.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@depend on
@@EXAMPLE0@@The amount I earn depends on the kind of work I'm doing.
@@PHRASE1@@according to
@@DEFINE@@if something is done according to particular facts, a particular situation etc, these affect the way it is done
@@EXAMPLE0@@Telephone charges vary according to the time of day.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The students were grouped according to age and ability.
@@PHRASE2@@depending on something
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that what will happen or what you do will change according to what happens in another situation
@@EXAMPLE0@@Inflation goes up and down depending on the state of the economy.
@@EXAMPLE1@@In many languages there are different words for "you' depending on who you are talking to.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I kept getting different answers depending on who I asked.
@@PHRASE3@@be determined by
@@DEFINE@@if the quality or nature of something is determined by other things, it depends on those things for how it is made
@@EXAMPLE0@@The colour of the rock is determined by the type of mineral present in it.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The ultimate flavor of the cheese variety is determined by the length of time it is allowed to mature.
@@EXAMPLE2@@An individual's metabolism is generally determined by his or her genetic make-up.
@@PHRASE4@@be dictated by
@@DEFINE@@if a decision, choice, or result is dictated by something, it depends very strongly on it, and leaves no choice for the people involved
@@EXAMPLE0@@A country's choice of export products is dictated by geography, climate, and natural resources.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Any development in the city center is dictated by the city's historic preservation laws.
@@PHRASE5@@be based on
@@DEFINE@@if one decision, situation, calculation etc is based on another, the second is the main thing upon which the first decision etc depends
@@EXAMPLE0@@Your pension will be based on the amount that you are earning when you retire.
@@EXAMPLE1@@This year's funding for the program is based on the number of applications that we received last year.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The jury's decision must be based on the evidence heard in court.
@@PHRASE6@@be dependent on
@@DEFINE@@to depend on something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The speed of the plane is dependent on the efficiency of the engines.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Benefits paid will be dependent on length of service with the company.
@@PHRASE7@@hinge on/hang on
@@DEFINE@@if a result, especially an important result, hinges on or hangs on something happening, it depends on it completely
@@EXAMPLE0@@The future prospects of a student can hinge on his or her performance in these exams.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The case hinged on whether the jury believed the defendants had planned to kill anyone when they broke into the house.
@@PHRASE8@@be riding on
@@DEFINE@@if something important such as money or success is riding on the result of something else, it depends on it
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's really stressful when you know that your whole future may be riding on this one interview.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Boxing has become big business, with a huge amount of money riding on the outcome of a fight.
@@PHRASE9@@be decided by
@@DEFINE@@if what someone does or what happens is decided by something else, it depends on it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The future of the school will be decided by the results of this survey.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Your choice of tool will be decided by the hardness of the wood you are working on.

@@DEFINE@@if someone is up to something they are probably doing something bad, but you do not know exactly what
@@EXAMPLE0@@I know he's lying - what do you think he's up to?
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be up to something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The kids have been whispering and giggling all day - I think they're up to something.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@be up to no good
@@GLOSS@@be doing something bad
@@EXAMPLE0@@She was beginning to suspect that the handsome stranger was up to no good.
@@PHRASE1@@get up to
@@DEFINE@@to do something that other people disapprove of, especially because you think it is funny or because you enjoy it
@@EXAMPLE0@@She peeped into the bedroom to see what mischief her grandson was getting up to.
@@EXAMPLE1@@When we were students, we used to get up to all sorts of things.
@@PHRASE2@@commit
@@DEFINE@@to do something that is a crime, especially a serious crime
@@THESPROPFORM0@@commit a crime/murder/robbery etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Women commit far fewer crimes than men.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The murder must have been committed between 7 and 10pm.
@@PHRASE3@@indulge in
@@DEFINE@@to do something that you enjoy, even though there is a reason you should not do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@I was downtown, so I decided to indulge in a little shopping.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Most people indulge in harmless fantasies to relieve the boredom of their lives.
@@PHRASE4@@stoop to
@@DEFINE@@to do something that you know is morally wrong because you think it is the only way that you can achieve what you want to achieve
@@EXAMPLE0@@"She even tried to get him fired." "I can't believe she'd stoop to that."
@@THESPROPFORM0@@stoop to doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@They ended up stooping to hair-pulling and name-calling.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His lawyers even stooped to using the children to gain public sympathy.
ways of asking what someone is doing
@@PHRASE0@@what is somebody doing?
@@EXAMPLE0@@What are you two doing?
@@EXAMPLE1@@He's been in the yard a long time - what's he doing out there?
@@PHRASE1@@what is somebody up to?
@@DEFINE@@say this when you think someone is secretly doing something bad
@@EXAMPLE0@@You look guilty, Stuart. What have you been up to?
@@EXAMPLE1@@They've been locked in there all morning - what are they up to?
@@PHRASE2@@what is somebody playing at?
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are angry and think someone has done something wrong or stupid
@@EXAMPLE0@@She shouldn't have told him what I said. What was she playing at?
@@EXAMPLE1@@You boys! What on earth do you think you're playing at? Stop it at once!
when someone is doing something
@@PHRASE0@@active
@@DEFINE@@always doing things or ready to do things, especially physical activities or activities within an organization
@@EXAMPLE0@@They're both in their seventies, but they're still very active.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@active in
@@EXAMPLE0@@In Washington Harriman quickly became active in Democratic Party affairs.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@active member
@@EXAMPLE0@@Today there are over 5,000 active members in the Accra church.
@@PHRASE1@@in action
@@DEFINE@@if you see someone in action , you see them doing the job or activity that they are trained to do or usually do
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've heard a lot about his dancing - I'd love to see him in action.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The advertisement shows two firefighters in action putting out a blaze.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I had seen him in action during the San José strike, and I was very impressed.
something that someone does
@@PHRASE0@@thing
@@DEFINE@@something that someone does - always use this with the verb do
@@EXAMPLE0@@The first thing you should do is connect the printer to the computer.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@a nice/stupid/nasty etc thing to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@That was a really nice thing to do - I know Leona enjoys your visits.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I know I shouldn't have hit him - it was a dumb thing to do.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@the right/best/smart/only etc thing to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@He gave her half the money because it was the right thing to do.
@@PHRASE1@@action
@@DEFINE@@something that someone does
@@EXAMPLE0@@You can't be blamed for the actions of your parents.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Bedell's financial problems do not excuse his actions.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@course of action
@@GLOSS@@something that you could do in order to deal with a situation
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was only one possible course of action - he had to resign.
@@PHRASE2@@activities
@@DEFINE@@things that people do, especially as an organized group - use this especially about illegal things that people do
@@EXAMPLE0@@The FBI is investigating the company's business activities.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There is growing evidence of drug-smuggling activities in and around the port.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Alberts created false documents to hide his activities from his employers.
@@PHRASE3@@activity
@@DEFINE@@when people are doing things, moving around, and looking busy
@@EXAMPLE0@@There's a lot of activity downstairs - do you know what's going on?
@@EXAMPLE1@@Military activity was secretly taking place for weeks before the invasion.
@@PHRASE4@@act
@@DEFINE@@a particular kind of action
@@THESPROPFORM0@@act of courage/stupidity/cruelty/kindness etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Saving the boys from the river was an act of great courage.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We condemn all acts of violence, no matter what the reason.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The whole nation is very grateful for the numerous acts of kindness rendered in this time of crisis.
@@PHRASE5@@deed
@@DEFINE@@something very brave, very good or very bad that someone does - used especially in literature
@@EXAMPLE0@@One day he will pay for his evil deeds.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He grew up reading the tales and legends of heroic deeds.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@good deed
@@EXAMPLE0@@Well, that's my good deed for the day.
@@PHRASE6@@feat
@@DEFINE@@something that someone does that is admired because it is very difficult and you need a lot of skill or strength to do it
@@THESPROPFORM0@@feat of
@@EXAMPLE0@@Using the code requires incredible feats of memory.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@perform/accomplish/achieve a feat
@@EXAMPLE0@@The circus acrobats perform amazing feats on the trapeze.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He led his team to victory for the tenth time, a feat no captain had achieved before.
@@PHRASE7@@exploits
@@DEFINE@@brave or exciting actions that people are told about and admire
@@EXAMPLE0@@The children loved to hear their father tell stories of his wartime exploits.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Powell's exploits on the Colorado River made him a hero of the old West.
something that people do for enjoyment
@@PHRASE0@@activity
@@EXAMPLE0@@What kind of activities do you enjoy?
@@THESPROPFORM0@@outdoor/indoor activities
@@EXAMPLE0@@Rebecca has always loved hiking and other outdoor activities.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@leisure/social/cultural etc activities
@@EXAMPLE0@@The retirement home arranges social and cultural activities for its seniors.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@lay on activities
@@GLOSS@@provide them
@@EXAMPLE0@@In the afternoon, there will be plenty of activities laid on for the kids.
@@PHRASE1@@pursuits
@@DEFINE@@things that people do because they enjoy them
@@THESPROPFORM0@@leisure/outdoor/artistic etc pursuits
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her husband never gave her much support in her artistic pursuits.
@@EXAMPLE1@@After he retired, my grandfather was able to devote his time to literary pursuits.
@@PHRASE2@@pastime
@@DEFINE@@an activity that is pleasant, relaxing and usually not very difficult, that you do when you are not working, because you enjoy it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Our cat's favourite pastime is sitting at the window and watching the people walk by.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Watching talk shows has become a national pastime in this country.
@@PHRASE3@@something to do
@@DEFINE@@something that you can do and that will stop you feeling bored when you have nothing to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@I don't mind helping - it'll give me something to do.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He really needs something to do in his spare time to keep him out of trouble.
@@PHRASE4@@hobby
@@DEFINE@@something that you do for interest and enjoyment regularly over a long period of time, for example, collecting things or making models
@@EXAMPLE0@@My hobbies are wind-surfing and playing the guitar.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I never saw my song-writing as anything more than a hobby until recently.
to do something in order to deal with a bad situation
@@PHRASE0@@do something
@@DEFINE@@to do something to deal with a problem, especially one that is urgent
@@EXAMPLE0@@Quick, do something - there's water all over the kitchen floor.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We need to do something before everyone gets fed up and quits.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@do something about
@@EXAMPLE0@@When are you going to do something about this broken window?
@@EXAMPLE1@@Teenagers were dropping out of school in huge numbers, until a group of parents and teachers decided to do something about it.
@@PHRASE1@@take action
@@DEFINE@@to do something to stop a bad situation from happening or continuing - use this to talk about people who have a clear plan for dealing with a problem
@@EXAMPLE0@@Unless governments take action, the Earth's atmosphere will continue to heat up.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@take action against
@@EXAMPLE0@@The school will take strong action against any students using illegal drugs.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@take action on
@@EXAMPLE0@@Congress is expected to take action on campaign finance reform soon.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@take action to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The President may step in and take action to lower energy prices.
@@PHRASE2@@act
@@DEFINE@@to use your power or authority to deal with an urgent problem
@@EXAMPLE0@@We must act before the situation gets out of control.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Despite the crisis, the Commission seems unwilling to act.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Critics accuse the company of acting too slowly in notifying residents of the chemical leak.
@@PHRASE3@@take steps/take measures
@@DEFINE@@if a government or someone in a position of power takes steps or measures , they do what is necessary to improve a situation or to deal with a problem
@@EXAMPLE0@@The governor has not yet decided what measures should be taken.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@take steps/take measures to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@All departments must take measures now to reduce costs.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We apologize for the error and have taken steps to see that it does not happen again.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@take drastic measures
@@EXAMPLE0@@Drastic measures will be taken against those who engage in terrorism.
@@PHRASE4@@move
@@DEFINE@@if a person or organization moves to do something, they start to take action, especially in order to deal quickly with an urgent matter
@@EXAMPLE0@@If anyone wants to put in a bid on the property they'll have to move quickly.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@move to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Airport authorities are moving fast to improve security following a series of bomb threats.
@@EXAMPLE1@@In the past year the leadership has moved to strengthen their control over the party.
@@PHRASE5@@intervene/step in
@@DEFINE@@to get involved in a difficult situation in order to stop a fight or deal with someone else's problem
@@EXAMPLE0@@The referee intervened when two of the players started to fight.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The situation was allowed to continue for several months before the local authorities stepped in.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@intervene in something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The UN was not authorized to intervene in a country's internal affairs.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@intervene/step in to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Soldiers intervened to prevent further bloodshed.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Thomas had listened to the argument for long enough and he stepped in to defend Miss Price.
something that someone does in order to deal with a situation
@@PHRASE0@@action
@@DEFINE@@what someone does when they use their power to deal with a problem or to achieve something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Strong action is needed to restore law and order.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's been politics as usual - all talk and no action.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@action on
@@EXAMPLE0@@The agency has promised action on the pollution problem for years, but nothing has happened.
@@PHRASE1@@step
@@DEFINE@@one of a series of things that someone does in order to deal with a problem or to achieve success
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her first big step towards a career in movies was her move to Hollywood.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Now that we've identified the problem, what's the next step?
@@EXAMPLE2@@These steps are necessary if the company is to succeed in the European market.
@@PHRASE2@@measure
@@DEFINE@@an action taken by a government or someone in authority to deal with a problem or improve a situation, for example by making a new law or rule
@@EXAMPLE0@@Government officials refused to say what measures were being planned to deal with the refugee crisis.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@measure to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Lawmakers are searching for the best measures to strengthen Social Security.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@drastic measures
@@EXAMPLE0@@Drastic situations require drastic measures.
@@PHRASE3@@move
@@DEFINE@@something that you decide to do in order to achieve a particular result, especially as one of a series of planned actions
@@THESPROPFORM0@@somebody's move
@@EXAMPLE0@@The management have offered less money than we wanted so what's our next move?
@@EXAMPLE1@@His first move after taking office was to appoint four communists to his cabinet.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@move to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The UN's latest move to stop the fighting has ended in failure.
to do something skilfully or carefully
@@PHRASE0@@do (something) well
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't worry about the test - I'm sure you'll do well.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She enjoys her job and does it very well.
@@EXAMPLE2@@If a firm does a job well, we use them again.
@@PHRASE1@@do a good job
@@DEFINE@@to do something well, especially a job that you have been asked to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@You can always rely on Brian to do a good job.
@@EXAMPLE1@@You're doing a good job there, Sally. I don't know what we'd do without you.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@do a good job of doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@They did a really good job of decorating my bathroom.
@@PHRASE2@@make a good job of
@@DEFINE@@to do something well, especially a piece of practical work, so that it looks good or works well
@@EXAMPLE0@@The hairdresser made a good job of your hair. It looks lovely.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We've just had a new heating system installed, but unfortunately they didn't make a very good job of it.
@@PHRASE3@@excel
@@DEFINE@@to do something much better than most other people, especially because you have a natural ability to do it well
@@EXAMPLE0@@I didn't exactly excel academically and I left school as soon as I had the chance.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@excel at/in
@@EXAMPLE0@@He played cricket for Middlesex but it was football that he really excelled at.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Many parents put too much pressure on their children to excel in school.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@excel yourself
@@GLOSS@@do even better than usual
@@EXAMPLE0@@Costner has excelled himself in this movie - definitely his best performance yet.
@@PHRASE4@@outdo
@@DEFINE@@to be better or more successful than someone else at doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Canadian hockey team has outdone all its rivals.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@outdo somebody in something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Each state seems to be trying to outdo its neighbors in cutting health services.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@outdo yourself
@@GLOSS@@do even better than usual
@@EXAMPLE0@@The singer outdid himself at the festival, singing for almost three hours to noisy applause.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@not to be outdone
@@GLOSS@@so that no one else does better than you
@@EXAMPLE0@@Not to be outdone, Stern went on television and made a speech of his own.
@@PHRASE5@@distinguish yourself
@@DEFINE@@to do something very well, so that people notice you, praise you, and remember you
@@EXAMPLE0@@Bradley has distinguished himself as the top scorer on the team.
@@EXAMPLE1@@After joining the newspaper, she quickly distinguished herself with a series of hard-hitting exposés.
to do something in a careless or unskilful way
@@PHRASE0@@do (something) badly
@@EXAMPLE0@@I think I did pretty badly in the exam today.
@@EXAMPLE1@@They packed the glass and china for us, but they did it very badly and a lot of stuff got broken.
@@PHRASE1@@mess up
@@DEFINE@@to do something badly because you have made mistakes, often so that you do not get the result you wanted
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've practiced all week, but I'm still afraid I'll mess up.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@mess something up
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't ask Terry to do it - she'll probably just mess it up.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@mess up something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Danny messed up three plays and made us lose the game.
@@PHRASE2@@make a mess of
@@VARIANT@@make a hash of
@@DEFINE@@to do something badly and make a lot of mistakes, especially when it is important that you do it well
@@EXAMPLE0@@Let's be honest. Most people make a mess of handling money.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She picked herself up and started the dance again, determined not to make a hash of it this time.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@make a complete hash of something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I made a complete hash of the interview - I don't stand a chance of getting the job.
@@PHRASE3@@screw up
@@DEFINE@@to spoil something you are trying to do, by making stupid mistakes
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you screw up too many times, they'll kick you off the team.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@screw something up
@@EXAMPLE0@@I was so nervous about the driving test that I screwed the whole thing up.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@screw up something
@@EXAMPLE0@@My audition was going really well until I screwed the last part up.
@@PHRASE4@@do a bad job
@@DEFINE@@to do something badly, especially a job you have been asked to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most people think the mayor is doing a pretty bad job.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@do a bad job of doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@He did such a bad job of labeling these envelopes I don't think I'll ask for his help again.
@@PHRASE5@@bungle
@@DEFINE@@if an organization or someone in authority bungles what they are trying to do, they fail to do it successfully because of stupid or careless mistakes
@@EXAMPLE0@@The plan seemed simple enough, but the CIA managed to bungle the operation.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Analysts agree that the company bungled its response to the crisis.
@@PHRASE6@@botch/botch up
@@DEFINE@@to do something badly, especially a practical job such as making or repairing something, as a result of being too careless or not having enough skill
@@EXAMPLE0@@They were supposed to fix the roof, but they completely botched the job.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@botch something up
@@EXAMPLE0@@We hired someone to fix the computer system, but he botched it up even more.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@botch up something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I wouldn't take your car to that garage - they botch up the simplest jobs.
@@PHRASE7@@mismanage
@@DEFINE@@if someone who is in charge mismanages a system or planned piece of work, they do it badly because they did not organize and control it properly
@@EXAMPLE0@@The whole project was seriously mismanaged from the beginning.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Many people accused the government of mismanaging the environment and indirectly causing the flooding.
@@PHRASE8@@fluff
@@DEFINE@@to do something badly because you are not paying enough attention, especially when it is your turn to do something in a play or in a game
@@EXAMPLE0@@I was so nervous that I fluffed my lines.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It should have been an easy catch, but he fluffed it.
@@PHRASE9@@not do yourself justice
@@DEFINE@@to do something less well than you could, in an examination, game etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@My grandfather was very intelligent, but he never did himself justice at school.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There were a couple of good performances, but most of the players didn't really do themselves justice.
to not do something that you should do
@@PHRASE0@@not do
@@EXAMPLE0@@I haven't done my taxes yet and they're due next week.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The electrician came round yesterday, but he didn't do all the jobs I asked him to do.
@@EXAMPLE2@@She was afraid that if she didn't do what her boss told her she would be fired.
@@PHRASE1@@do nothing/not do anything
@@DEFINE@@to not try to help someone or prevent a bad situation, even though you know it is happening
@@EXAMPLE0@@How could neighbors listen to her scream and do nothing?
@@THESPROPFORM0@@do nothing/not do anything about
@@EXAMPLE0@@We told the police months ago, but they still haven't done anything about it.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@do nothing/not do anything to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@No one did anything to stop the purse snatcher.

@@DEFINE@@to escape from a prison or from a place where someone is keeping you
@@EXAMPLE0@@Guards have been ordered to shoot anyone trying to escape.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@escape from
@@EXAMPLE0@@He escaped from prison in June, but was rearrested by police a month later.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@escape into/through/out etc.
@@EXAMPLE0@@Grant had escaped through a bathroom window while in police custody.
@@PHRASE1@@break out/get out
@@DEFINE@@to escape from a prison or from a building or room where you are being kept
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some of the men were planning to break out.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The doors and windows are all firmly locked - I don't know how we're going to get out.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@break out/get out of
@@EXAMPLE0@@In 1998 the two men broke out of jail and murdered a police officer.
@@EXAMPLE1@@No one has ever managed to get out of this prison alive.
to succeed in escaping from someone who is chasing you
@@PHRASE0@@escape
@@DEFINE@@to succeed in escaping from someone who is trying to catch you
@@EXAMPLE0@@It looks as if they've escaped. They're probably over the border by now.
@@EXAMPLE1@@So far the terrorists have managed to escape the police.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@escape from
@@EXAMPLE0@@He ducked down an alley to escape from the mob that was chasing him.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@escape into/across/over etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Criminals generally know their neighborhood well, so it's not difficult for them to escape into the back streets.
@@PHRASE1@@get away
@@DEFINE@@to escape from someone who is chasing you, especially when there is no chance that you will be caught afterwards
@@EXAMPLE0@@How could you let him get away!
@@EXAMPLE1@@Police believe the gunmen got away in a white Ford pickup.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@get away from
@@EXAMPLE0@@Follow that car and don't let it get away from you.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@get clean away
@@GLOSS@@get away completely
@@EXAMPLE0@@Detectives followed the man as far as the harbour, but then he jumped into a speedboat and got clean away.
@@PHRASE2@@give somebody the slip
@@DEFINE@@to escape from someone who is chasing you by tricking them or doing something unexpected
@@EXAMPLE0@@Watch him very carefully - he might try and give us the slip.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I wanted to talk to her before she left the hotel, but she gave me the slip.
@@PHRASE3@@throw somebody off the scent
@@DEFINE@@to escape from someone who is chasing you or trying to find you by cleverly doing something that makes it impossible for them to know where you are
@@EXAMPLE0@@He made the calls from different pay phones around the city to throw the police off the scent.
@@PHRASE4@@shake off
@@DEFINE@@to escape from someone, especially someone who has been chasing you for a long time, for example by hiding or by going faster than them
@@THESPROPFORM0@@shake off somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@Mailer disappeared into a dark basement, hoping to shake off the gang.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@shake somebody off
@@EXAMPLE0@@You're going to have to drive faster if you want to shake them off.
@@PHRASE5@@make your getaway/make a getaway
@@DEFINE@@to successfully escape after a crime, leaving no signs to show where you are
@@EXAMPLE0@@Police have found the helicopters that the terrorists used to make their getaway.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@make a clean getaway
@@GLOSS@@to escape leaving no signs to show where you are
@@EXAMPLE0@@The robbers hopped into a waiting car and made a clean getaway.
@@PHRASE6@@elude
@@DEFINE@@to cleverly avoid being found or caught by someone, especially for a long time
@@EXAMPLE0@@Despite a $25,000 reward on his head, he continues to elude the authorities.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@elude capture
@@EXAMPLE0@@Lt. Forney managed to elude capture by enemy forces for several weeks.
when someone escapes
@@PHRASE0@@escape
@@DEFINE@@when someone escapes from prison, from danger, or from someone who is chasing them
@@EXAMPLE0@@They had planned their escape very carefully.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Tunnel to Tanto Grande" is the story of a daring escape staged by political prisoners in Peru.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@escape from
@@EXAMPLE0@@Until his escape from the camps, he was beaten nearly every day by his captors.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@narrow escape
@@GLOSS@@when you only just escape from danger
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was a narrow escape - a couple of minutes later the whole place went up in flames.
@@PHRASE1@@breakout
@@VARIANT@@jailbreak
@@DEFINE@@an escape from a prison, especially one that involves several prisoners and is done using violence
@@EXAMPLE0@@Prison governors met today to discuss ways of preventing similar breakouts in the future.
@@EXAMPLE1@@As many as 20 guards may have been involved in the jailbreak.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@breakout from
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was a mass breakout from a city center prison yesterday.
someone who has escaped
@@PHRASE0@@escaped
@@DEFINE@@use this to describe someone who has escaped , especially from a prison
@@EXAMPLE0@@Police are on the lookout for three escaped prisoners.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Sherwood, an escaped convict, hunted down his ex-girlfriend and killed her.
@@PHRASE1@@be on the loose/be at large
@@DEFINE@@someone who is on the loose or at large has escaped from the police or from a prison and is likely to be dangerous
@@EXAMPLE0@@There's a killer on the loose, and we've got to find him.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Carillo's murderer remained at large yesterday as investigators continued their search.
@@PHRASE2@@be on the run
@@DEFINE@@someone who is on the run is trying to hide or escape from someone who is chasing them, especially the police
@@EXAMPLE0@@After the train robbery he spent three years on the run.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be on the run from
@@EXAMPLE0@@Dean was a drug addict who was constantly on the run from the police.
@@PHRASE3@@fugitive
@@DEFINE@@someone who has escaped from the police or from danger, who has to keep moving from one place to another so that they will not be caught
@@EXAMPLE0@@Porter escaped in 1995 and remains a fugitive.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fugitive from
@@EXAMPLE0@@a fugitive from Stalin's oppressive regime

@@EXAMPLE0@@Once they realized that I had been lying, it was almost impossible to extricate myself.

@@EXAMPLE0@@At that time, the US was on the verge of extricating itself from the unpopular war.

@@EXAMPLE0@@I don't know how she's going to talk her way out of this one.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Phil never does his homework, but he always manages to talk his way out of it.

@@DEFINE@@to be unable to escape, or feel too frightened to escape, from the place where you are or from an unpleasant situation

@@DEFINE@@to be unable to escape, for example from a place, an unpleasant situation, or your own thoughts and opinions, so that you feel you cannot do anything to change things
@@EXAMPLE0@@The door was locked from the outside, and suddenly they realized they were prisoners.

@@EXAMPLE0@@In some respects I'm a prisoner of my past - I don't feel I can just start over.

@@DEFINE@@use this to emphasize that something is more important or happens more with one particular thing than any others

@@DEFINE@@use this when you are giving an example
@@EXAMPLE0@@There are lots of famous buildings in Kyoto, for example the Golden Pavilion and the Tyoanyi Temple.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There are some tasks which are your responsibility. For instance, it's up to you to dismantle furniture and take down curtains.
@@PHRASE1@@e.g./eg
@@DEFINE@@use this when you are giving an example or a series of examples. In British English, people usually write eg ; in American English people usually write e.g.
@@EXAMPLE0@@Make sure you eat foods that contain protein, e.g. meat, cheese, fish, milk, or eggs.
@@EXAMPLE1@@This course includes a study of basic language skills (eg speaking and listening).
@@PHRASE2@@such as
@@DEFINE@@used when you want to give one or two typical examples of something but not all the examples that are possible
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is difficult to get even basic foods such as sugar and bread.
@@EXAMPLE1@@People's ability to do the tests is influenced by factors such as age, sex, and ethnic background.
@@PHRASE3@@like
@@DEFINE@@used in spoken English when you are giving a example which is typical of what you mean
@@EXAMPLE0@@We could cook something easy, like pasta.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We still haven't settled a number of problems, like who is going to be in charge here while I'm away.
@@PHRASE4@@take
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are talking about something and you want to give an example of a certain type of situation, person etc, in order to prove what you are saying is correct
@@EXAMPLE0@@I can think of lots of people who got worse grades than you and still have good jobs. Take Julie.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@take somebody/something for example
@@EXAMPLE0@@Take me for example. I've never relied on other people for help.
@@PHRASE5@@be a case in point
@@DEFINE@@a particular person, situation etc that is a case in point , is a very good or typical example of what you have just mentioned
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some birds have returned to England after once being extinct here. The return of the osprey is a case in point.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Some women have managed to achieve success in football. A case in point is Anne Spencer.
@@PHRASE6@@by way of illustration
@@DEFINE@@if you name a particular situation, person etc by way of illustration , you want to use them as a way of explaining what you mean
@@EXAMPLE0@@Other countries have totally different laws on abortion. By way of illustration let us look at the cases of Germany and Japan.
@@PHRASE7@@to name but a few
@@DEFINE@@if you say to name but a few after giving several examples of something, you mean that these are just a few examples of what you mean and there are many more
@@EXAMPLE0@@So many industries have been hit in the recession. Steel, coal, construction, to name but a few.
not including someone or something
@@PHRASE0@@except/except for
@@DEFINE@@not including the person or thing that you mention. At the beginning of a sentence, always use except for , not just except
@@EXAMPLE0@@Everyone's going except Donald.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The house was silent except for a clock chiming in the living room.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Except for a small part in an obscure movie years ago, Depardieu had never before acted in an English-language picture.
@@PHRASE1@@except
@@DEFINE@@use this when you have made a statement that is true, but then you want to introduce a fact that does not match what you have said
@@THESPROPFORM0@@except (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Celia looks just like her sister, except that her sister has shorter hair.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's similar to Paris, except the people look a lot poorer.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@except do something
@@GLOSS@@that is the only thing it cannot do
@@EXAMPLE0@@a computer that can do everything except talk
@@PHRASE2@@apart from
@@VARIANT@@aside from
@@DEFINE@@use this when you mention one or two things that do not fit the main thing that you are saying
@@EXAMPLE0@@This is an excellent piece of work, apart from a couple of spelling mistakes.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Aside from its mineral resources, Mongolia's major assets are its 25.5 million livestock.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@apart from doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Apart from going swimming occasionally, I don't get much exercise.
@@PHRASE3@@but
@@DEFINE@@use this especially after the words any, none, nothing, all, anyone, or everyone to show that you mean everything except the thing, person etc you are mentioning
@@EXAMPLE0@@I can come and see you any day but Tuesday.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There was nothing left but a few dried up sandwiches.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Anyone but Tommy would have realized I was trying to apologize.
@@PHRASE4@@other than
@@DEFINE@@use this in a negative sentence to show that the thing, person etc that you mention is the only person or thing that is not included in your statement
@@EXAMPLE0@@Other than at football matches, people sing less than they used to.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@other than to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Sam refused to discuss the argument, other than to say that Diane had called him 'gutless'.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@other than that
@@EXAMPLE0@@You should get a little stiffness, but other than that, there should be no side effects.
@@PHRASE5@@with the exception of
@@DEFINE@@not including one thing, person, or group - use this when saying something about the whole of a group
@@EXAMPLE0@@The whole school, with the exception of the youngest class, had to attend the ceremony.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@with the possible exception of
@@GLOSS@@but possibly not that person or thing
@@EXAMPLE0@@I think they should all pass the test, with the possible exception of Fauzi.
@@PHRASE6@@bar
@@DEFINE@@use this to introduce the only thing, person, or group about which your statement is not true
@@EXAMPLE0@@I get hardly any mail, bar the occasional postcard from my mother.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He died with no possessions bar a small piece of land in Ireland.
@@PHRASE7@@but for
@@DEFINE@@use this to introduce the only thing that makes a description of something not completely true - used especially in writing
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was complete silence but for the occasional sound of distant traffic.
someone or something that is not included
@@PHRASE0@@exception
@@DEFINE@@someone or something that is not included in a general statement, or does not do what most others in the same situation do
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most of the students did well, though there were one or two exceptions.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@notable exception
@@GLOSS@@one that is very famous or special
@@EXAMPLE0@@Women do not usually get to the top in politics, but there have been a few notable exceptions.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@major/minor exception
@@GLOSS@@an important/not very important one
@@EXAMPLE0@@With a few minor exceptions, the legal system in the two countries is very similar.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@exception to the rule
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most couples who break up seem to find it hard to remain friends. Kim and Gerry are exceptions to that rule.

@@THESPROPFORM0@@do a swap with somebody

@@THESPROPFORM0@@change something for something

@@PHRASE6@@barter

@@EXAMPLE0@@In the local market, meat and vegetables are bartered for electrical goods.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@barter with
@@EXAMPLE0@@She had some success in bartering with her guards.
@@PHRASE7@@switch
@@DEFINE@@to exchange something so that two or more things or people change the places that they are in
@@EXAMPLE0@@He was accused of switching the price labels on goods.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Professor Rigby's talk may be switched to the main hall.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@switch seats/places
@@EXAMPLE0@@We switched seats halfway through the show.
@@PHRASE8@@change places
@@DEFINE@@to exchange the place you are standing or sitting on with another person
@@THESPROPFORM0@@change places with
@@EXAMPLE0@@Would you mind changing places with me?
@@PHRASE9@@change partners
@@DEFINE@@if a group of people who are dancing change partners , they stop dancing with one person and dance with another person in the group
@@EXAMPLE0@@We agreed to change partners after a couple of dances.

@@DEFINE@@say this when someone is not sure what you mean and you are going to try to explain in a way that will help them to understand, especially by saying something humorous or direct

@@PHRASE0@@pointless
@@DEFINE@@something that is pointless is unlikely to have a very useful or successful result, so it would be better not to do it or try it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The argument was completely pointless.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Most people think the project is a pointless waste of money.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@pointless exercise
@@EXAMPLE0@@Speculating like that was always a pointless exercise, but he did it nevertheless.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@it is pointless to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's pointless to take notes and then never look at them again.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@it is pointless doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@She decided it was pointless trying to work while her mind was on other things.
@@PHRASE1@@be a waste of time
@@DEFINE@@something that is a waste of time is unlikely to achieve any useful result, so you would be wasting your time if you tried to do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Many people think that complaining about bad service is a waste of time.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@a complete/total waste of time
@@EXAMPLE0@@These meetings are a complete waste of time. Nothing ever gets decided.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@it is a waste of time doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's a waste of time going to the doctor - he'll just tell you to get plenty of rest.
@@PHRASE2@@there's no point/what's the point
@@DEFINE@@say this when you think that it is useless to do something because you will not achieve anything useful by doing it
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Why don't you try to explain things to him?" "There's no point, he never listens."
@@EXAMPLE1@@I was going to buy a new car, but what's the point when my old one's perfectly all right?
@@THESPROPFORM0@@there's no point (in) doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@There's no point getting a new carpet until the decorating's done.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@what's the point in/of doing something?
@@EXAMPLE0@@What's the point of giving a signal when there are no other cars around to see it?
@@PHRASE3@@doomed
@@DEFINE@@not having any chance at all of succeeding
@@EXAMPLE0@@Attempts to clean up the environment are doomed unless businesses take a leading role.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Within a few months she realized that her marriage was doomed.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@doomed to failure
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you refuse to provide any information to the user, then your computer program is doomed to failure.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@doomed from the start
@@EXAMPLE0@@Their business venture was doomed from the start, as they did not have the necessary capital.
@@PHRASE4@@lost cause
@@DEFINE@@something that you try to make successful, although it seems very clear to other people that it cannot succeed
@@EXAMPLE0@@At first it seemed the attempt to save the species was a lost cause.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The miners' strike of 1984 turned out to be a lost cause.
@@PHRASE5@@non-starter
@@DEFINE@@an idea or plan that will definitely not be successful
@@EXAMPLE0@@Everybody would prefer a lower rate of tax, but that that is a non-starter economically.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The project would have been a non-starter without the help of Judith Glyn.
when an event or product is unsuccessful
@@PHRASE0@@be a failure
@@EXAMPLE0@@The latest model seems likely to be a failure since cheaper versions are now available.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be a complete/total failure
@@EXAMPLE0@@It takes a little while for an author to realize that his book has been a complete failure.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@be a commercial failure
@@GLOSS@@to not make enough profit
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her first film was praised by the critics, but was a commercial failure.
@@PHRASE1@@be a fiasco
@@DEFINE@@to be completely unsuccessful, in a way that makes people feel disappointed and embarrassed
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was a fiasco! Nobody knew what they were doing and everything went wrong.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The show turned into a fiasco when members of the audience invaded the stage.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be a complete/total fiasco
@@EXAMPLE0@@Lamont's attempts to prop up the pound were a complete fiasco.
@@PHRASE2@@be a disaster
@@DEFINE@@if an event, especially a social event, is a disaster , it makes people feel angry, disappointed, or embarrassed, instead of being enjoyable
@@EXAMPLE0@@Our first date was a disaster.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The whole visit was something of a disaster, and he was still recovering from it months later.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be a total/complete disaster
@@EXAMPLE0@@Even the host would have to admit that the evening had been a complete disaster.
@@PHRASE3@@be a shambles
@@DEFINE@@if a situation or event is a shambles , it is completely unsuccessful because it has been very badly planned or organized
@@EXAMPLE0@@The whole conference was a shambles because half the speakers did not come.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The way this school is run is a shambles.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be a complete/total shambles
@@EXAMPLE0@@Let's hope this year's celebrations aren't a complete shambles like last year's.
@@PHRASE4@@flop/be a flop
@@DEFINE@@if a product, play, or performance flops or is a flop , it is not successful because people do not like it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The movie flopped and Laughton never got the chance to direct again.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It was just another so-called "wonder product' that flopped when people failed to buy it.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Despite all the publicity, the show was a flop.
@@EXAMPLE3@@It is the public who decide whether a film will be a hit or a flop.
@@PHRASE5@@bomb
@@DEFINE@@if a product, play, or performance bombs , it is not successful because people do not like it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Although the show was a hit in London it bombed on Broadway.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She has had few offers of work since her last movie bombed so spectacularly.

@@EXAMPLE0@@We expected her to pass easily, but she failed by 15 marks.

@@EXAMPLE0@@You either pass and get your degree or flunk out.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@flunk out of college/school etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was extremely humiliating to flunk out of law school like that.
@@PHRASE3@@bomb
@@DEFINE@@to fail very badly
@@EXAMPLE0@@I bombed the English test yesterday.
when a relationship or marriage fails

@@EXAMPLE0@@If your marriage fails it can be difficult to make a new start in life.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She was trapped in a failing relationship.
@@PHRASE1@@go wrong
@@DEFINE@@if a marriage or other relationship goes wrong , or something about it goes wrong ,something happens or changes to make it fail after it had started well

@@EXAMPLE1@@Only the two of you know what went wrong.
