when a company, shop, or business fails
@@PHRASE0@@fail
@@EXAMPLE0@@A large number of businesses failed when interest rates rose.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Several thousands of small businesses fail each week.
@@PHRASE1@@go out of business
@@DEFINE@@if a company goes out of business , it stops existing because it is no longer making a profit
@@EXAMPLE0@@Many small farms are going out of business.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be put/forced out of business
@@EXAMPLE0@@As the recession hit, many traders were forced out of business.
@@PHRASE2@@go under
@@DEFINE@@if a business, bank, or company goes under , it fails - used especially in newspapers and business contexts
@@EXAMPLE0@@When the company went under, some of our workers found positions with Ford.
@@PHRASE3@@close down
@@DEFINE@@if a shop, factory, or business closes down, it stops making or selling goods
@@EXAMPLE0@@If the factory closes down, 600 people will lose their jobs.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Coal mines are closing down all over the country.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Not long ago, the orchestra was the pride of the city. Now it is on the verge of closing down.
@@PHRASE4@@closure
@@VARIANT@@closing
@@DEFINE@@when a shop, factory, or business fails and closes
@@EXAMPLE0@@Further factory closures have been announced.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@closure of
@@EXAMPLE0@@The closing of the Minton Savings and Loan was a great loss to the town.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@face/be threatened with closure
@@GLOSS@@to be going to close down
@@EXAMPLE0@@Penrhyn is now the largest quarry in the world, yet 5 years ago it faced closure.
@@PHRASE5@@go bankrupt/go bust
@@DEFINE@@if a person or company goes bankrupt , they are legally forced to sell their property and possessions to pay their debts
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her father went bankrupt in 1984.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He bought a small printing firm that had gone bankrupt.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The company went bust last year, owing £12 million.
@@PHRASE6@@fold
@@DEFINE@@to fail and be unable to continue in business
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most of the companies dependent on the steelworks folded within weeks.
@@PHRASE7@@go to the wall
@@DEFINE@@to fail and be unable to continue in business, especially because of difficult economic conditions
@@EXAMPLE0@@Over 300 small firms have gone to the wall in the past year.
@@EXAMPLE1@@High interest rates will force many businesses to go to the wall.
a time when an economy is not successful
@@PHRASE0@@recession
@@DEFINE@@a period when a country's economic growth stops and there is less trade, so that many companies have to reduce the number of workers they employ
@@EXAMPLE0@@The car industry, like most other industries, is feeling the effects of the recession.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@severe recession
@@GLOSS@@very bad recession
@@EXAMPLE0@@In times of severe recession companies are often forced to make massive job cuts in order to survive.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@in recession
@@GLOSS@@suffering from a recession
@@EXAMPLE0@@The economy is in recession and will remain so for at least another year.
@@PHRASE1@@slump
@@DEFINE@@a period when there is a big reduction in trade so that many companies fail and a lot of people lose their jobs
@@EXAMPLE0@@The post-war slump sent the unemployment figures to twice the expected level.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@slump in
@@EXAMPLE0@@The slump in the property market is making it difficult for people to sell their homes.
@@PHRASE2@@depression
@@DEFINE@@a period of time continuing for several years when greatly reduced business activity severely affects a country's economic growth, and a lot of people lose their jobs - use this especially when this affects many countries across the world
@@EXAMPLE0@@In Germany the depression in the late 1920s helped Hitler's rise to power.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Hartnell blamed his financial difficulties on the worldwide depression.
@@PHRASE3@@crash
@@DEFINE@@a sudden and unexpected fall in the value of shares in companies, with the result that many companies have to close and a lot of people lose their jobs
@@EXAMPLE0@@Luckily, I sold my shares just before the crash.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The Wall Street Crash was disastrous for many American businessmen.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@stock market crash
@@GLOSS@@crash in the organizations that buy and sell shares in companies
@@EXAMPLE0@@The stock market crash made me suspicious of those types of insurance schemes.
treating people in a way that is reasonable and equal
@@PHRASE0@@fair
@@DEFINE@@treating everyone equally, or treating people in a way that most people think is right
@@EXAMPLE0@@The old system of student funding seemed much fairer.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Everyone has the right to a fair trial.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Observers will be present to ensure a free and fair election.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it is fair that
@@EXAMPLE0@@Do you think it's fair that she gets paid more money than me?
@@THESPROPFORM1@@it's only fair
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her husband should help take care of the baby - it's only fair.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@be fair to somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@In order to be fair to everyone, ticket sales are limited to two for each person.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@to be fair
@@GLOSS@@say this when you are giving a reason why someone should not be criticized too strongly
@@EXAMPLE0@@To be fair, these are complicated, serious issues, and the department has only been discussing them for a short time.
@@PHRASE1@@just
@@DEFINE@@a situation, decision etc that is just gives someone what they rightly deserve or have a right to expect
@@EXAMPLE0@@Many of us did not feel that the court's decision was just.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a just and lasting peace
@@THESPROPFORM0@@just decision/punishment/settlement etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Attorney General called the sentence a fair and just punishment for someone who had committed such a dreadful crime.
@@PHRASE2@@reasonable
@@DEFINE@@if an agreement, offer, or what someone does is reasonable , most people would agree that it is fair and sensible
@@EXAMPLE0@@The company made every reasonable effort to correct the problem.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The students' goals in the protest seem so reasonable that the university is setting up a committee to consider them.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it is reasonable to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Do you think it's reasonable to expect people to work more than 60 hours a week?
@@PHRASE3@@balanced
@@DEFINE@@giving fair and equal treatment to all sides of an argument or subject
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Newsweek" gave a reasonably balanced report on the crisis.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Recently historians have taken a far more balanced view of the Irish question.
@@PHRASE4@@even-handed
@@DEFINE@@treating everyone equally and not showing special favour to anyone
@@EXAMPLE0@@Local magistrates are expected to respect the law and provide even-handed justice.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The BBC has the reputation of being even-handed in its coverage of election news.
@@PHRASE5@@fair's fair
@@DEFINE@@use this to tell someone that they should do something because it is right and fair, especially after you have done something for them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Come on, fair's fair. It's your turn to mind the kids.
@@PHRASE6@@play fair
@@DEFINE@@to do something in an honest and fair way
@@EXAMPLE0@@The film company says that it played fair in all its contract dealings with the actors' unions.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A mystery novel should play fair with the reader, providing all the clues necessary to solve the crime.
words for describing someone who is always fair
@@PHRASE0@@fair
@@EXAMPLE0@@Kelson has a reputation as a fair and compassionate judge.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Despite the discrimination they suffered, my grandparents remained fair, decent, good people.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be fair to somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've always tried to be fair to all my children.
@@PHRASE1@@just
@@DEFINE@@someone who is just treats people in a way that is fair and right - use this especially about leaders, rulers, and other people in authority, especially in historical descriptions
@@EXAMPLE0@@He was the perfect choice for Emperor -- just, patient, merciful and of royal blood.
@@EXAMPLE1@@No just government would allow this kind of treatment of its own citizens.
@@PHRASE2@@fair-minded
@@DEFINE@@someone who is fair-minded is able to see situations in a fair and reasonable way and always considers other people's opinions
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Chairman is a fair-minded man, so will listen to any criticism of his proposals.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She remained maddeningly fair- minded, even about her greatest opponents.
able to be fair because you are not involved in a situation
@@PHRASE0@@objective

@@EXAMPLE2@@The disease is still fairly common in many countries.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Investigators searched through the plane's wreckage for several hours before locating the flight recorder.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If you have difficulty locating a particular book, please ask one of the librarians for assistance.
@@PHRASE2@@dig out
@@DEFINE@@to find something you have not seen for a long time, or that may not be easy to find, especially in order to give it to someone who has asked for it
@@THESPROPFORM0@@dig out something
@@EXAMPLE0@@It seems like every time Grandma comes over we have to dig out the family photos.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I took the opportunity to dig out a few facts and figures about this remote island.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@dig something/it/them out
@@EXAMPLE0@@I have her address somewhere -- I'll dig it out for you when I get time.
difficult to find
@@PHRASE0@@be difficult to find/hard to find
@@DEFINE@@if someone or something that you need is difficult to find or hard to find , you cannot easily find them because there are not many of them or they are well hidden
@@EXAMPLE0@@Taxis are hard to find at that time of night.
@@EXAMPLE1@@What we wanted was a house with a big garden -- something that was difficult to find in the middle of a city.
@@PHRASE1@@elusive
@@DEFINE@@an elusive person or animal is difficult to find, often because they do not want to be found
@@EXAMPLE0@@The gray fox is a very shy elusive creature.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A cure for the disease has proven to be elusive.
@@EXAMPLE2@@We repeatedly tried to contact the manager, an elusive man who was never in his office.

@@DEFINE@@to bend a piece of paper or cloth, so that one part of it covers another
@@EXAMPLE0@@He folded his newspaper and handed it to me.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Before getting into bed, I usually fold my clothes and put them on the chair.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fold something in two/in half
@@GLOSS@@across the middle
@@EXAMPLE0@@Tom folded the letter in half and stuck it in his pocket.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@fold something into a square/triangle etc
@@GLOSS@@so that it has the shape of a square or triangle
@@EXAMPLE0@@The napkins were folded into neat triangles.
@@PHRASE1@@fold up
@@DEFINE@@to fold something, usually several times, in order to make it into a smaller or neater shape
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fold up something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Rachel folded up the ironing board and put it in the closet.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@fold something up
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't just leave your clothes on the floor like that - fold them up.
@@PHRASE2@@turn down
@@THESPROPFORM0@@turn down a sheet/blanket/collar etc
@@DEFINE@@fold it back so that the top or corner of it is pressed down
@@THESPROPFORM1@@turn down something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I turned down a corner of the page I was reading and shut the book.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The maid always turns down the bedclothes and places a mint on the pillow.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@turn something/it/them down
@@EXAMPLE0@@Button up your jacket and turn the collar down.
a piece of furniture or equipment that can be folded
@@PHRASE0@@folding/collapsible
@@DEFINE@@a folding or collapsible bed, chair, bicycle etc is one that is specially designed so that it can be folded up and easily carried or stored
@@EXAMPLE0@@You'll have to sleep on a folding bed in the living room.
@@EXAMPLE1@@By the window stood a large collapsible table with drawings and pencils all over it.
@@PHRASE1@@fold/fold up
@@DEFINE@@able to be folded
@@EXAMPLE0@@My umbrella folds up and fits into my handbag.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I want a push chair that folds easily and weighs very little.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fold up into something
@@GLOSS@@fold into the shape of something else
@@EXAMPLE0@@This portable bath folds up into a carrying case that is perfect for storing baby clothes.
the straight line where something has been folded
@@PHRASE0@@fold
@@DEFINE@@a straight line where something, especially paper or cloth, has been folded
@@EXAMPLE0@@Cut the paper along the fold.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She lay there in the narrow bed, her chin resting on the fold of the sheet.
@@PHRASE1@@crease
@@DEFINE@@a straight fold made carefully, especially in clothing
@@EXAMPLE0@@I folded the paper back into its original creases and put it into the drawer.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@sharp crease
@@EXAMPLE0@@The defendant wore a blue blazer, a white shirt, and gray pants with a sharp crease.
when something gets folds in it
@@PHRASE0@@crease
@@DEFINE@@if clothes crease , they get unwanted folds or lines in them when you leave them somewhere, or when you wear them
@@EXAMPLE0@@These trousers will crease if you don't hang them up properly.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Linen is a beautiful fabric but it creases very easily and needs to be pressed regularly.
@@PHRASE1@@creased
@@DEFINE@@clothes that are creased have unwanted folds or lines in them because you have left them somewhere or been wearing them
@@EXAMPLE0@@His shirt was creased at the back where he had been lying down on it.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Professor Haines finally showed up wearing a badly creased suit with stains on the front.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@get creased
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't put your shirts in there - they'll get creased.
@@PHRASE2@@crumpled
@@DEFINE@@if papers or clothes are crumpled , they have a lot of unwanted lines and folds, and look old and untidy
@@EXAMPLE0@@She reached into her pocket and handed the clerk a crumpled ten-dollar bill.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I spent the night under a bridge, using a crumpled blanket as a bed.
to open something that is folded
@@PHRASE0@@unfold
@@EXAMPLE0@@He took out his handkerchief, unfolded it, and blew his nose.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Eileen struggled to unfold a large map.
@@EXAMPLE2@@"I must lay the table," she said, unfolding a clean white linen tablecloth.
to follow someone
@@PHRASE0@@follow
@@DEFINE@@to walk, drive, run etc behind someone else, going in the same direction as them, especially because you are going somewhere together
@@EXAMPLE0@@Follow me and I'll show you where the library is.
@@EXAMPLE1@@You drive on ahead and I'll follow.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@follow somebody around
@@GLOSS@@to follow someone wherever they go, especially when this is annoying
@@EXAMPLE0@@My little brother's been following me around all day.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@followed by somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@The woman entered the room, followed by three young children.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@follow somebody out/down/across etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@She didn't notice that Jack had followed her into the kitchen.
@@PHRASE1@@follow on
@@DEFINE@@to follow someone to the place where they are going but at a later time
@@EXAMPLE0@@You go ahead. I'll follow on later.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@follow on behind
@@EXAMPLE0@@The bus set off first and we followed on behind in the car.
to closely follow a person or animal in order to watch them
@@PHRASE0@@follow
@@EXAMPLE0@@He followed her home to find out where she lived.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Did you make sure you weren't followed on the way over here?
@@EXAMPLE2@@She complained to the police officer that she was being followed by two strangers.
@@PHRASE1@@tail
@@DEFINE@@if someone such as a police officer tails someone, they secretly follow that person to find out where they are going or what they are doing
@@EXAMPLE0@@That police car has been tailing us for the last 5 miles.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A group of photographers tailed the couple all over London.
@@PHRASE2@@be/sit on somebody's tail
@@DEFINE@@to follow close behind someone, especially in order to watch or catch them
@@EXAMPLE0@@A police car was on their tail within seconds of the alarm going off.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We sat on their tail for about an hour until we lost them in traffic.
@@PHRASE3@@shadow
@@DEFINE@@to follow someone or something very closely in order to watch all their movements without them realizing that they are being followed
@@EXAMPLE0@@I want you to shadow him for the next three days and find out who he hangs out with.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Consumed with jealousy, he shadowed her for three days, hoping to catch her with her lover.
@@PHRASE4@@track/trail
@@DEFINE@@to follow a person or animal closely, especially by looking for signs showing that they have gone in a particular direction
@@EXAMPLE0@@Undercover agents have been tracking him for weeks.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It would be impossible to trail anyone across this type of ground.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@track/trail somebody to something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The police trailed the gang to their hideout.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Dogs are used to track the wolves to their lair in the forest.
@@PHRASE5@@hound
@@DEFINE@@to keep following someone and asking them questions about their activities, personal problems etc, in a way that is annoying or threatening
@@EXAMPLE0@@After the court case she was hounded relentlessly by the press.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The couple found themselves hounded by photographers as they left the church.
@@PHRASE6@@stalk
@@DEFINE@@to follow a person or animal quietly in order to catch, injure, kill them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Polar bears stalk seals that are resting on the ice.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The killer would stalk his victim, overpower her and then brutally murder her.
@@PHRASE7@@stalker
@@DEFINE@@a criminal or mentally ill person who continuously follows and watches someone in a threatening way, especially someone famous or someone they are attracted to
@@EXAMPLE0@@Women's groups are demanding that Congress toughen the law against stalkers.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The stalker's reappearance has led to increased security around the actress.
to follow a person or animal quickly in order to catch them
@@PHRASE0@@run after
@@DEFINE@@to run or walk quickly behind someone in order to catch them or talk to them, when they are going away from you
@@EXAMPLE0@@A group of little boys ran after him to ask for his autograph.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She's left her briefcase. Quick! Run after her!
@@PHRASE1@@chase
@@DEFINE@@to run after someone in order to catch them, when they are trying to escape from you
@@EXAMPLE0@@I didn't have the energy to chase him any more.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@chase somebody across/up/down etc something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The farmer chased the children across the field.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@chase after
@@EXAMPLE0@@We chased after him for about five blocks but then we lost him and had to turn back.
@@PHRASE2@@pursue
@@DEFINE@@to chase someone in a very determined way - used especially in stories and news reports
@@EXAMPLE0@@Police pursued the gunman into an abandoned building.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The ship was being pursued by enemy submarines.
@@PHRASE3@@in pursuit
@@DEFINE@@if you are in pursuit of someone, you chase them because you want to catch them -- used especially in stories and news reports
@@EXAMPLE0@@The robbers sped off in a stolen car with three police vehicles in pursuit.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@in pursuit of
@@EXAMPLE0@@Cheng raced through a crowded shopping mall in pursuit of the man who had grabbed her purse.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@in hot pursuit
@@EXAMPLE0@@A deer suddenly sprang across the road, with a pack of hunting dogs in hot pursuit.
@@PHRASE4@@be on/at somebody's heels
@@DEFINE@@to follow very closely behind someone who is trying to escape from you, especially when you want to catch or attack them - used especially in stories
@@EXAMPLE0@@The rebels headed for the border but government troops were still at their heels.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be hard/hot/close on somebody's heels
@@EXAMPLE0@@Just 15 minutes into the race Lawson was already hot on the champion's heels.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@on/at somebody's heels
@@EXAMPLE0@@He rushed out of the theatre with a pack of reporters at his heels.
@@PHRASE5@@go after
@@DEFINE@@to follow someone quickly especially because you want to talk to them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't go after him now. Let him calm down first.
@@PHRASE6@@give chase
@@DEFINE@@to start to chase someone who is trying to escape from you - used especially in stories and descriptions
@@EXAMPLE0@@Police spotted the car speeding on Dumbarton Bridge and quickly gave chase.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Anyone can make a mistake, but to ignore basic safety regulations is quite inexcusable.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it is inexcusable that
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is inexcusable that the government has never paid a cent to the widows of these brave men.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Many of our great works of art are being sold and exported.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There's some debate as to what constitutes great poetry.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The Renaissance period produced some of the greatest architecture of all time.
@@PHRASE2@@classic
@@THESPROPFORM0@@classic film/book/album etc
@@DEFINE@@a film, book etc that is one of the best of its kind
@@EXAMPLE0@@2001 is a classic science fiction movie.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The Rolling Stones produced a string of classic singles in the mid 60s including 'Satisfaction' and 'Brown Sugar'.
@@PHRASE3@@work of art
@@DEFINE@@something produced by an artist, especially something that most people agree is of very high quality
@@EXAMPLE0@@Several priceless works of art were badly damaged when the palace was bombed.
@@PHRASE4@@masterpiece
@@DEFINE@@a picture, sculpture etc that is of extremely high quality, especially one that is believed to be the best work of a particular artist
@@EXAMPLE0@@one of the great Italian masterpieces
@@EXAMPLE1@@Many people regard this painting as Raphael's masterpiece.
good weather
@@PHRASE0@@good
@@EXAMPLE0@@Did you have good weather in France?
@@EXAMPLE1@@The weather report says the weather should be good over the weekend.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The weather was a bit better in the second week.
@@PHRASE1@@nice
@@DEFINE@@pleasantly warm and with plenty of sun
@@EXAMPLE0@@Morning, Bill. Nice weather, isn't it?
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's a nice day - why don't we go for a walk?
@@PHRASE2@@beautiful/glorious
@@VARIANT@@lovely
@@DEFINE@@warm and with a lot of sun
@@EXAMPLE0@@a beautiful sunny morning
@@EXAMPLE1@@a glorious summer
@@EXAMPLE2@@What a lovely morning!
@@PHRASE3@@fine
@@DEFINE@@if the weather is fine , it is not raining and the sky is clear
@@EXAMPLE0@@Next week will be fine but a little cooler.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a fine summer evening
how good something is
@@PHRASE0@@quality
@@DEFINE@@the measure of how well something is made or produced, or how good a material is
@@EXAMPLE0@@Supermarket wines tend to vary in price and quality.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We always guarantee the best quality to our customers.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be of good/reasonable/poor etc quality
@@EXAMPLE0@@She always insists that her writing paper is of good quality.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The recording is of very poor quality.
@@PHRASE1@@standard
@@DEFINE@@the measure of how well someone does something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Safety standards are simply not being maintained.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@above/below a standard
@@EXAMPLE0@@In reading tests, 15% of school students were found to be below the standard for their age.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@be of a good/high standard
@@EXAMPLE0@@All his work is of a very high standard.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@be up to standard
@@GLOSS@@be of an acceptable level
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm afraid your driving isn't yet up to standard.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@standard of
@@EXAMPLE0@@The standard of workmanship on this table is extraordinarily high.

@@DEFINE@@something that you are particularly good at in your job, in a sport, or in your life in general
@@EXAMPLE0@@Before choosing a career you should spend time identifying your personal strengths and weaknesses.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His ability to charm people is one of his greatest strengths.
@@PHRASE1@@be somebody's forte
@@DEFINE@@to be the activity that you are best at
@@EXAMPLE0@@Love songs have become Bolton's forte.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She's much better in the longer races. Short distances are not her forte.
ways of saying goodbye
@@PHRASE0@@goodbye/bye
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are leaving or when someone is leaving you. Bye is more informal than goodbye
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Goodbye, Mrs Moore." "Goodbye, Dr Aziz."
@@EXAMPLE1@@Goodbye, Louise. See you soon.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Thank you for calling. Goodbye.
@@EXAMPLE3@@"Bye, Annie." "Bye, Mom," she said, kissing her mother on the cheek.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@bye for now
@@GLOSS@@say this to a friend who you will see again soon
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've got some stuff to do. Maybe we can have a drink or something later tonight. Anyway, bye for now.
@@PHRASE1@@see you
@@VARIANT@@see you later/see you around
@@DEFINE@@use this to say goodbye to a friend you will see again soon
@@EXAMPLE0@@See you, Darren.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Bye, Dad. I'll see you later.
@@EXAMPLE2@@You're still coming to the party tonight, aren't you? Good. See you later then.
@@EXAMPLE3@@She turned at the gate and waved. "See you around, Billy."
@@THESPROPFORM0@@see you tomorrow/in the morning/at the club etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@"See you in the morning," she said as she closed the door.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"We'll be back early next week." "Okay. See you then."
@@THESPROPFORM1@@see you soon
@@EXAMPLE0@@Safe trip back guys and we'll see you soon.
@@PHRASE2@@later/catch you later
@@DEFINE@@use this to say goodbye to a friend you will see again soon. Later and catch you later are used especially by young people
@@EXAMPLE0@@Catch you later, Matt.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Later, Mike." "Later, Steve."
@@PHRASE3@@so long
@@DEFINE@@use this to say goodbye to someone you do not expect to meet again for a long time
@@EXAMPLE0@@"So long," he said. "Don't forget to write."
@@EXAMPLE1@@She grabbed Nick by the shoulders and hugged him affectionately. "So long, Nick."
@@PHRASE4@@have a nice day/good weekend/great time etc
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are saying good bye to someone to wish them a good day, a good weekend, a good holiday etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Have a nice weekend.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Have a great time at the concert, you guys!
@@PHRASE5@@have a good one
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are saying goodbye to someone to wish them a nice day
@@EXAMPLE0@@"I'm off to work." "Alright, have a good one."
@@PHRASE6@@take care
@@DEFINE@@use this to say goodbye to family or friends
@@EXAMPLE0@@"All right, Pat. Take care." "You too, Sally. Bye bye."
@@EXAMPLE1@@Take care and we'll talk to you soon.
@@PHRASE7@@take it easy
@@DEFINE@@use this to say goodbye to a friend or member of your family
@@EXAMPLE0@@"See you next week." "Yeah, take it easy."
@@PHRASE8@@nice to meet you/nice meeting you
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are going to leave someone who you have just met for the first time
@@EXAMPLE0@@Well, it was nice meeting you guys.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"It was nice to meet you, Paul." "Nice to meet you too, Joanne."
ways of saying goodnight
@@PHRASE0@@goodnight/night
@@DEFINE@@say this to say goodbye to someone in the evening. Night is more informal than goodnight
@@EXAMPLE0@@Goodnight. Thanks for having us.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Night, folks." "Goodnight, Don. Careful driving."
@@PHRASE1@@night night
@@DEFINE@@goodbye - use this especially to children
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Night night, Timmy." "Night, Mommy."
to say or wave goodbye to someone
@@PHRASE0@@say goodbye
@@DEFINE@@to say goodbye to someone, or to say the last things that you want to say to them before you leave each other
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've just come to say goodbye.
@@EXAMPLE1@@They left so suddenly, I didn't get a chance to say goodbye.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@say goodbye to
@@EXAMPLE0@@I said goodbye to the kids and got into the car.
@@PHRASE1@@say your goodbyes
@@DEFINE@@if two or more people say their goodbyes , they say the last things they want to say to each other before leaving each other for a long time
@@EXAMPLE0@@We delayed saying our goodbyes until the last possible moment.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Adam went to get the car as Billie and Jenny said their goodbyes.
@@PHRASE2@@wave goodbye
@@DEFINE@@to wave to someone as they go away from you or as you leave them
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Come back soon!" called Mary, waving goodbye from behind the gate.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@wave goodbye to
@@EXAMPLE0@@She waved goodbye to him through the car window.
@@EXAMPLE1@@As we left, I turned to wave goodbye to Helen.
@@PHRASE3@@wave somebody off
@@DEFINE@@to wave to someone as they go away from you
@@EXAMPLE0@@She waved them off, then went slowly back inside.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A crowd of children had gathered on the station platform to wave him off.
@@EXAMPLE2@@She looked back and saw her mother waving her off from the kitchen door.
@@PHRASE4@@see somebody off
@@DEFINE@@to go with someone to the door of your house or to a place such as a station or airport in order to say goodbye to them when they leave
@@EXAMPLE0@@All our friends had come to the airport to see us off.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Mrs Carey went to the door to see him off.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Dee was up the next day at sunrise to see me off.
@@PHRASE5@@bid somebody farewell
@@DEFINE@@to say goodbye to someone, especially when you know you will not meet again for a very long time - used especially in literature
@@EXAMPLE0@@The time has come to bid you all farewell.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Some 400 Pakistani soldiers turned out to bid their comrades farewell.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@bid farewell to somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@Queen Victoria bade farewell to her most trusted servant.
good enough
@@PHRASE0@@good enough
@@EXAMPLE0@@If the weather's good enough next weekend we'll go camping.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@good enough for
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's just a cheap wine but it's good enough for a picnic.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@good enough to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Do you think she's good enough to be in the team?
@@PHRASE1@@satisfactory
@@DEFINE@@something that is satisfactory reaches the expected standard but is not better than it
@@EXAMPLE0@@You won't get paid unless your work is satisfactory.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Lynne got satisfactory grades and was offered a place at university.
@@PHRASE2@@be all right/OK
@@DEFINE@@use this about something that is good enough but not especially good
@@EXAMPLE0@@The children made the cakes. I hope they're all right.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"What did you think of the movie?" "Oh, it was OK - nothing special."
@@EXAMPLE2@@This book is OK for beginners but it's not really suitable for more advanced students.
@@PHRASE3@@not bad
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that something is fairly good, and better than you expected
@@EXAMPLE0@@"What was the food like?" "Oh, not bad - better than last time."
@@EXAMPLE1@@You know, that's not a bad idea.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@not too bad
@@EXAMPLE0@@"How was the exam?" "Oh, not too bad. I think I passed."
@@PHRASE4@@adequate
@@DEFINE@@good enough for a particular purpose, especially by being of a high enough level, amount, or quality
@@EXAMPLE0@@Employers must provide adequate training opportunities.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Now that we have extended the hall, those small electric heaters are no longer adequate.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Make sure that the lighting is adequate so that your guests can see what they are eating.
@@PHRASE5@@acceptable
@@DEFINE@@good enough to be able to be used for a particular purpose
@@EXAMPLE0@@We had a lot of applicants for the job but only a few of them were acceptable.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Some low-fat cheeses have quite an acceptable flavour but some taste like rubber.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@acceptable to
@@EXAMPLE0@@The dispute was settled in a way that was acceptable to both sides.
@@PHRASE6@@passable
@@DEFINE@@good enough, but not very good
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was some bread, a little cheese and a passable French wine.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He gave a passable imitation of Charlie Chaplin.
@@PHRASE7@@reasonable
@@DEFINE@@fairly good, but not very good
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most of her work is of a reasonable standard.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A reasonable number of people turned up for the meeting.
@@EXAMPLE2@@We had an enjoyable weekend and the weather was quite reasonable.
@@PHRASE8@@competent
@@DEFINE@@a piece of work or a performance that is competent is done to a satisfactory standard but does not have any particularly good or skilful features
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most of the essays were competent but one was really outstanding.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Ben took out his pen and produced a quick but very competent sketch of the building.
@@PHRASE9@@decent
@@DEFINE@@of a good enough quality or standard
@@EXAMPLE0@@I want to provide my boys with a decent education.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There isn't one decent restaurant around here.
@@PHRASE10@@will do
@@DEFINE@@to be good enough for a particular purpose
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you don't have any butter, margarine will do.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I want someone to practise first aid on. You'll do, Simon.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@will do somebody
@@GLOSS@@be good enough for someone
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't bother fetching me another chair. This one'll do me fine.
to reach a high enough standard
@@PHRASE0@@make the grade
@@DEFINE@@to succeed in reaching the necessary standard, especially in a difficult job
@@EXAMPLE0@@She would like to become a lawyer but she's not sure whether she'll make the grade.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Only the talented few make the grade in professional golf.
@@PHRASE1@@measure up
@@DEFINE@@use this when you are asking or considering whether someone will be good enough to do a particular job or to reach a particular standard
@@EXAMPLE0@@We'll give you a week's trial in the job so we can see how you measure up.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@measure up to
@@EXAMPLE0@@How will the new General Secretary measure up to his new task?
@@PHRASE2@@come up to somebody's standards/expectations etc
@@DEFINE@@to achieve the level of quality that is necessary or expected
@@EXAMPLE0@@The new design doesn't come up to our usual standards.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The computer system has certainly come up to expectations -- it's great!
@@PHRASE3@@live up to
@@DEFINE@@to be as good as people expect - use this especially about people and their achievements, performances etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was impossible to live up to my parents' expectations of me.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He's been under a lot of pressure to live up to his reputation as the world's best player.
@@PHRASE4@@meet
@@DEFINE@@to be good enough according to a standard that has been officially established
@@EXAMPLE0@@Does the tap water meet government health standards?
@@EXAMPLE1@@The building does not meet the essential safety requirements.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Only one system succeeded in meeting the main performance specifications.
@@PHRASE5@@have what it takes
@@DEFINE@@to be good enough at something, especially something difficult, to be able to do it successfully
@@EXAMPLE0@@Do you have what it takes to run this business, or shall I give someone else the chance?
@@EXAMPLE1@@If you have what it takes and can stand the pace of advertising, you can earn a very good salary.
@@PHRASE6@@pass
@@DEFINE@@to say officially that someone or something has reached the necessary standard
@@EXAMPLE0@@Each car has to be passed by a team of inspectors before it leaves the factory.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His blood pressure was rather high so the doctor couldn't pass him as fit for the job.
something that stops someone or something from being completely bad
@@PHRASE0@@saving grace/redeeming feature
@@DEFINE@@something, often the only thing, that makes someone or something not completely bad
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her only saving grace is her sense of humour.
@@EXAMPLE1@@None of the characters in her novels have any redeeming features.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The accommodation - dirty and freezing cold - had one redeeming feature. It was cheap.
not good enough
@@PHRASE0@@not be good enough
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm afraid I can't translate this letter. My Italian isn't good enough.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@not be good enough for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The soil here isn't good enough for arable farming.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I paid $40 for that champagne, but it wasn't good enough for your snobbish friends.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@not be good enough to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@a good club player, but not good enough to play for his country
@@PHRASE1@@unsatisfactory
@@DEFINE@@not good enough and likely to cause problems or make people unhappy
@@EXAMPLE0@@People should not accept unsatisfactory products. They should complain.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It was a most unsatisfactory meeting - not a single decision was made.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Sharing my office with the two secretaries proved an unsatisfactory arrangement.
@@PHRASE2@@inadequate
@@DEFINE@@not good enough for a particular purpose or for what someone needs
@@EXAMPLE0@@The disease spread quickly because of poor living conditions and inadequate health care.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@hopelessly/woefully inadequate
@@GLOSS@@extremely inadequate
@@EXAMPLE0@@My light clothing was hopelessly inadequate for the cold Japanese winter.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The training that nurses get is woefully inadequate.
@@PHRASE3@@not be up to scratch/not come up to scratch
@@DEFINE@@if someone's performance, work, or products are not up to scratch , they are not of the standard that is necessary or expected
@@EXAMPLE0@@I wonder if Sykes is ill. His work hasn't been up to scratch lately.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Schools are being threatened with closure if exam results are not up to scratch.
@@EXAMPLE2@@If they don't come up to scratch, you can do them all again.
@@PHRASE4@@substandard
@@DEFINE@@generally considered to be below the necessary standard
@@EXAMPLE0@@More money should be spent on the improvement of substandard housing.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Most household goods sold here are substandard, but food is plentiful and cheap.
@@EXAMPLE2@@substandard accommodation
@@PHRASE5@@not come up to/not live up to
@@DEFINE@@to not achieve the level or quality that someone expects
@@EXAMPLE0@@The film didn't live up to our expectations. It was too long and the acting was appalling.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Mark found that he simply could not live up to his teachers' high standards.
@@EXAMPLE2@@So far, she has not lived up to the tremendous promise she displayed earlier.
@@PHRASE6@@won't do
@@DEFINE@@use this about something that is not good enough for a particular purpose
@@EXAMPLE0@@I need strong nylon thread. Cotton won't do.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I can't accept this quality of work. It just won't do.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Handwritten notes won't do for our purposes. You'll have to type them.
@@PHRASE7@@not cut it
@@DEFINE@@to not have the ability, strength etc to succeed in a particular job or activity
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most of the kids who start here are young and haven't worked before. Some just can't cut it.
the people who govern a country
@@PHRASE0@@government
@@DEFINE@@the people who govern a country, state, or local area, and who make all the important decisions about taxes, laws, relationships with other countries etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The government has promised to cut taxes.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Unemployment is a problem that many Western governments continue to face.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@government of
@@EXAMPLE0@@the city government of Los Angeles
@@EXAMPLE1@@The newspaper, La Prensa, was shut down for nearly two years because of its criticism of government policies.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@the French/Japanese/Russian etc government
@@EXAMPLE0@@The French government strongly condemned the killings.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@local/central/federal etc government
@@GLOSS@@the government of a town or city, or a country
@@EXAMPLE0@@The local government has been unable to meet the demand for affordable housing.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It has been difficult for the central government to conduct elections in remote areas.
@@PHRASE1@@administration
@@DEFINE@@the government of a country - use this especially to talk about the national government of the United States
@@THESPROPFORM0@@the administration
@@EXAMPLE0@@The new administration has been strongly criticized for its handling of the affair.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The administration also proposed $600 million in tax breaks for small businesses.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@the Kennedy/Clinton etc administration
@@GLOSS@@the government when this person is president
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Eisenhower administration refused to take military action in Vietnam.
@@PHRASE2@@the authorities
@@DEFINE@@the people or organizations that have the power to decide what people are allowed to do in a country or area
@@EXAMPLE0@@The country is facing famine, and the authorities are doing little to prevent it.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@the South African/Mexican/Swiss etc authorities
@@EXAMPLE0@@The South African authorities arrested Mandela in August 1962.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@local/federal authorities
@@GLOSS@@the authorities in a community, town or city, or in a whole country
@@EXAMPLE0@@On January 12, the local authorities decided that the strike had gone on long enough.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Federal authorities said that no one has claimed responsibility for the bombing as of yet.
@@PHRASE3@@the state
@@DEFINE@@the government, the police, the courts etc, considered as a single group that has the power to control what people do
@@EXAMPLE0@@At that time, the state controlled nearly every aspect of people's lives.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The programs are funded by the state.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@state-run
@@GLOSS@@owned and controlled by the state
@@EXAMPLE0@@CBC, the state-run broadcasting company
@@PHRASE4@@the powers that be
@@DEFINE@@the people in government responsible for making decisions - use this especially if you think that they have too much power or that they use their power badly
@@EXAMPLE0@@The powers that be do not seem interested in solving the city's transportation problems.
@@PHRASE5@@regime
@@DEFINE@@the group of people who are in charge of the government of a country - use this especially about a government you disapprove of because it was not elected to power
@@EXAMPLE0@@The military regime refused to recognize the elections.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The US supported several right-wing regimes in central America.
the most powerful people in a government
@@PHRASE0@@leadership
@@DEFINE@@the leader of a government and the other people in high positions of power
@@THESPROPFORM0@@leadership of
@@EXAMPLE0@@He will challenge Sinclair for the leadership of the Liberal Party.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The collapse of European communism in the late 1980s shocked the Chinese leadership.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@under the leadership of somebody/something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Under the leadership of the Conservative Party, the gap between the rich and the poor widened considerably.
@@PHRASE1@@cabinet
@@DEFINE@@the group of important politicians who run the different departments in a government, for example education, health etc, and advise the leader of the government
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Prime Minister has offered Stroud a position in the cabinet.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@cabinet minister
@@GLOSS@@one of the politicians in the cabinet
@@EXAMPLE0@@The spy scandal involved two cabinet ministers and several civil servants.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@cabinet meeting
@@GLOSS@@a meeting when the cabinet discusses something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The cabinet meeting broke up after four-and-a-half hours.
@@PHRASE2@@executive
@@DEFINE@@the part of a government that approves decisions and laws and is responsible for making them work
@@THESPROPFORM0@@the executive
@@EXAMPLE0@@In theory, the civil service is the non-political arm of the executive.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Power is shared between three main branches of government: the executive, the legislative, and the judiciary.
the people who make the country's laws
@@PHRASE0@@parliament
@@DEFINE@@the group of people who are elected to make a country's laws
@@EXAMPLE0@@During his 28 years in Parliament, the 59-year-old Chuan has been untainted by corruption.
@@EXAMPLE1@@New budget measures were approved Tuesday by the Russian parliament.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Elections for the European parliament are set for late next year.
@@PHRASE1@@Senate
@@DEFINE@@the smaller and more important of the two parts of the parliament of the USA
@@EXAMPLE0@@Bradley was elected to the Senate in 1978.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If approved by the Senate, the bill would make it harder to purchase handguns.
@@PHRASE2@@Congress
@@DEFINE@@the group of people elected to make laws in the US, consisting of the Senate and the House of Representatives
@@EXAMPLE0@@Hirsch doubts Congress will accept the president's proposal.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Congress rejected a measure that would make it easier for low-income workers to get health insurance.
a government that controls people's lives too much
@@PHRASE0@@dictatorship
@@DEFINE@@a government in which one person or group has total power and uses it unfairly and cruelly
@@EXAMPLE0@@In 1971, the country's 10 year military dictatorship came to an end.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Ethiopia's dictatorship was toppled by Eritrean and Ethiopian rebels.
@@EXAMPLE2@@How do we explain the rise in European dictatorship in the 1930s?
@@PHRASE1@@police state
@@DEFINE@@a country where the police and other people who work for the government have too much power and control people's lives too much
@@EXAMPLE0@@The country is a police state and the media is controlled by the government.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Do you want a free society or a police state?" Stark asked the crowd of about 2,000 people.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The Home Secretary denied that the introduction of identity cards would lead to a police state.
@@PHRASE2@@junta
@@DEFINE@@a government run by a small group of army officers who have not been elected but have taken power by force
@@EXAMPLE0@@All the opponents of the junta have been murdered or imprisoned.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@military junta
@@EXAMPLE0@@The country was ruled by a military junta from 1974 until 1982.
@@PHRASE3@@tyranny
@@DEFINE@@a situation in which a government, especially an illegal one, rules unfairly and cruelly
@@EXAMPLE0@@Any political system that refuses to allow people to protest becomes a tyranny.
@@EXAMPLE1@@the extraordinary struggle against tyranny in South Africa
@@PHRASE4@@totalitarian
@@DEFINE@@a totalitarian country or system of government is one in which the government controls every part of people's lives and there is no freedom
@@EXAMPLE0@@A totalitarian state must maintain complete control of the press.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The country held its first elections after 40 years of totalitarian rule.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The minister called the secret police `a product and a tool of the old totalitarian regime'.
@@PHRASE5@@oppressive
@@DEFINE@@an oppressive government treats people in a cruel way, using military force to prevent any opposition
@@EXAMPLE0@@the oppressive rule of Ceaucescu in Romania
@@EXAMPLE1@@A poor, uneducated people does not have the willpower or knowledge to challenge an oppressive government.
different systems of government
@@PHRASE0@@democracy

part of a government that deals with health, education etc

@@EXAMPLE0@@Ellison is now head of the Department of Education.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@the Defense/Justice/Treasury Department

graceful

@@DEFINE@@moving in a smooth, controlled way that is attractive to look at

a letter or number that shows how well a student has done
@@PHRASE0@@grade
@@DEFINE@@a letter that is put on a student's work or on an exam to show how good or bad it is
@@EXAMPLE0@@I wasn't very happy with the grade on my essay.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Class participation is a quarter of your final grade.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@good/bad grade
@@EXAMPLE0@@I need a really good grade on the final exam to pass the class.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@get a grade
@@EXAMPLE0@@If he gets good enough grades, he'll get a scholarship to Michigan State.
@@PHRASE1@@mark
@@DEFINE@@the number or letter that is put on a student's work to show how good or bad it is
@@EXAMPLE0@@His mark on the last test gave him a final average of 88%.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@get a mark
@@EXAMPLE0@@"What mark did you get?" "B."
@@THESPROPFORM1@@good/high mark
@@EXAMPLE0@@She came out with the second highest marks in the class.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@bad/low/poor mark
@@EXAMPLE0@@You have to do the course again if you get low marks.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@get full marks
@@GLOSS@@get the highest possible marks
@@EXAMPLE0@@I got full marks in the history test.
@@PHRASE2@@score
@@DEFINE@@a number which shows how well or badly a student has done in an examination, especially an important exam given to a lot of students
@@THESPROPFORM0@@high/low score
@@EXAMPLE0@@Students at King elementary generally have the highest test scores in the city.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@score on
@@EXAMPLE0@@Scores on standardized tests have been steadily falling over the past ten years.
@@PHRASE3@@results
@@DEFINE@@all the marks that a student gets in a set of tests or examinations, that show whether he or she has been successful or not
@@EXAMPLE0@@The school's "GCSE" results had been much better the previous year.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@get good results
@@EXAMPLE0@@Ceri got better results than she expected.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@exam results
@@EXAMPLE0@@David had appaling exam results at school despite his obvious intelligence.
@@PHRASE4@@grade point average/GPA
@@DEFINE@@the average score that a student earns based on all their grades. Usually an A is 4 points, a B is 3 , a C is 2, and a D is 1, and an F is 0
@@EXAMPLE0@@To be on the honor roll, students must have a GPA of at least 3.5.
to decide how well a student has done
@@PHRASE0@@mark
@@VARIANT@@grade

@@EXAMPLE2@@The examiners who marked her A-level paper were very lenient and gave her a pass.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@mark/grade somebody/something on something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The rough draft is graded on content, not on grammar.

to feel guilty
@@PHRASE0@@feel guilty
@@DEFINE@@to feel worried and unhappy because you have done something wrong or because you have upset someone
@@EXAMPLE0@@I felt really guilty after spending all that money.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Are you feeling guilty because you didn't help her?
@@THESPROPFORM0@@feel guilty about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Ed felt guilty about leaving work so early.
@@PHRASE1@@be/feel ashamed
@@DEFINE@@to feel very guilty and disappointed with yourself because you have done something wrong or behaved in an unpleasant or embarrassing way
@@EXAMPLE0@@She felt thoroughly ashamed when she remembered how drunk she'd been.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be/feel ashamed of
@@EXAMPLE0@@I feel ashamed of what I did.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@be/feel ashamed to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm ashamed to admit it, but I wasn't really sorry when he died.
@@PHRASE2@@feel bad
@@DEFINE@@to feel very sorry because you have upset someone or done something that you should not have done
@@EXAMPLE0@@We had a long talk about it afterwards and I know she felt bad.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@feel bad that
@@EXAMPLE0@@I should have told Helen I was sorry. I feel really bad that I didn't.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@feel bad about
@@EXAMPLE0@@I feel bad about what I said. Things haven't been easy for either of us.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@feel bad about doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I feel bad about not going to Debbie's party, but I've just got too much to do.
@@PHRASE3@@blame yourself
@@DEFINE@@to feel that it was your fault that something bad happened
@@EXAMPLE0@@You mustn't blame yourself. It was an accident. There was nothing you could have done.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@blame yourself for
@@EXAMPLE0@@Assistant coach Rex Hughes blamed himself for the team's poor performance.
@@PHRASE4@@feel responsible
@@DEFINE@@to feel guilty about something bad that has happened even though you did not cause it, especially when you feel you could have prevented it
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm sorry it didn't work out. I feel responsible.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@feel responsible for
@@EXAMPLE0@@For a long time afterwards I felt responsible for his death.
@@PHRASE5@@have a guilty conscience
@@DEFINE@@to feel guilty for a long time and keep thinking about something bad that you have done
@@EXAMPLE0@@I suppose I did have a guilty conscience for a while, but not any more.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@have a guilty conscience about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Why is she being so nice to everyone all of a sudden? She's obviously got a guilty conscience about something.
@@PHRASE6@@be on somebody's conscience
@@DEFINE@@if something bad that you have done is on your conscience , you cannot stop feeling guilty and thinking about it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Even if you didn't get caught, the murder would be on your conscience for the rest of your life.
@@EXAMPLE1@@In the end Martin told his wife about his affair - he just couldn't live with it on his conscience.
a guilty feeling
@@PHRASE0@@guilt
@@DEFINE@@the feeling you have when you have done something that you know is wrong
@@EXAMPLE0@@Guilt can be a very destructive emotion.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@feeling of guilt
@@EXAMPLE0@@People often have feelings of guilt after a divorce.
@@PHRASE1@@shame
@@DEFINE@@the guilty feeling that you have when you know that you have behaved badly and lost people's respect
@@EXAMPLE0@@Voting through cuts in benefits to the poorest people is a matter of shame for all of us.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@shame about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Too many women are taught to feel guilt or shame about sex.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@shame at
@@EXAMPLE0@@As he left the house, Mungo felt a pang of shame at telling Alice a lie.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@almost die of shame
@@GLOSS@@be very ashamed
@@EXAMPLE0@@The next day I remembered how drunk I'd been , and almost died of shame.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@bring shame on somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some girls feel that refusing their parents' choice of husband will bring shame on their family.
@@PHRASE2@@remorse
@@DEFINE@@a feeling of being very sorry for something bad that you have done, so that you wish you had not done it
@@EXAMPLE0@@He admitted killing the man but showed no sign of remorse.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@remorse for
@@EXAMPLE0@@She was full of remorse for hurting her family.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@remorse at
@@EXAMPLE0@@Many men are afflicted with guilt and remorse at leaving their wives.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@twinge/pang of remorse
@@GLOSS@@a small feeling of remorse
@@EXAMPLE0@@The woman sounded so nice, McKee felt a twinge of remorse at what he had done to her family.
@@PHRASE3@@conscience
@@DEFINE@@a set of feelings that stop you from doing something wrong or that make you feel guilty when you have done something wrong
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her murderer was a psychopath with a total lack of conscience.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@twinge/pang of conscience
@@GLOSS@@a sudden feeling of guilt
@@EXAMPLE0@@He was capable of making the most ruthless decisions with no apparent pangs of conscience.
to not feel guilty about something
@@PHRASE0@@not feel guilty
@@EXAMPLE0@@I made her cry but I don't feel guilty -- she deserved it.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@not feel guilty about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Working mothers shouldn't feel guilty about wanting a career.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I don't understand how on earth he can go on lying like that and not feel guilty about it.
@@PHRASE1@@a clear conscience
@@DEFINE@@if you have a clear conscience , you feel that you have not done anything wrong, so that you do not feel guilty about anything you have done
@@THESPROPFORM0@@with a clear conscience
@@EXAMPLE0@@You can face Lionel with a clear conscience -- you've done nothing to harm him.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@have a clear conscience
@@EXAMPLE0@@Let them say whatever they like. I have a clear conscience.
@@PHRASE2@@have no qualms
@@DEFINE@@if you have no qualms about doing something, you have no worries or doubts about whether what you are doing is right, even though other people may think it is wrong
@@THESPROPFORM0@@have no qualms about
@@EXAMPLE0@@She had no qualms about sending her young children to boarding school.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Donald had been stealing stationery from work for years and had no qualms about it at all.
@@PHRASE3@@have/feel no compunction
@@DEFINE@@to not feel guilty about doing something, even though other people may think it is wrong
@@EXAMPLE0@@I warn you. These people have no compunction whatsoever and cannot be trusted.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@have/feel no compunction about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Eliot felt no compunction about living at the expense of his friends.
to stop yourself feeling guilty
@@PHRASE0@@salve your conscience
@@DEFINE@@to try to stop yourself feeling guilty by doing something good or kind
@@EXAMPLE0@@She felt guilty and tried to salve her conscience by inviting him out for a meal.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Don't think you can salve your consciences by giving us money. We won't forgive you that easily.
@@PHRASE1@@clear your conscience
@@DEFINE@@to stop yourself feeling guilty by telling someone about something bad that you have done
@@EXAMPLE0@@She decided to clear her conscience and confess everything.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He knew he might get into trouble if he went to the police but he had to do it to clear his conscience.
something that you do very often without thinking
@@PHRASE0@@habit
@@DEFINE@@something that you do very often and without thinking about it, because you have done it so many times before
@@EXAMPLE0@@Peter had some pretty odd habits.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Patterns of behaviour develop gradually until they become unconscious habits.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@bad habit
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't start smoking - it's a very bad habit.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@have a habit of doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@He has a really annoying habit of leaving his clothes all over the floor.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@become a habit
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you have one or two drinks each day, it soon becomes a habit.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@be/get into the habit of doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@You ought to get into the habit of planning your work at the beginning of each week.
@@THESPROPFORM4@@eating/dating/viewing etc habits
@@EXAMPLE0@@People need to change their eating habits and include more fruit and vegetables in their diet.
@@PHRASE1@@mannerism
@@DEFINE@@a way of speaking, or a small movement of your face or body, that is part of your usual behaviour, and that other people think is strange or funny
@@EXAMPLE0@@All the kids imitated Mr Pearce's mannerisms.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Before you go to an interview, ask yourself whether you have any irritating mannerisms such as saying 'you know' all the time.
@@PHRASE2@@ways
@@DEFINE@@someone's ways are their habits and their usual behaviour - use this especially when you think someone's usual behaviour is slightly strange
@@EXAMPLE0@@Rosy had a warm easy-going personality, so she was good at tolerating other people's ways and opinions.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It was a small rural community, and its people felt deeply suspicious of foreigners and their strange ways.
when someone does something because it is a habit
@@PHRASE0@@from habit/out of habit
@@DEFINE@@if you do something from habit , you do it just because it is your habit to do it, not because you have deliberately decided to do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some people drink alcohol from habit, as much as from desire.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Out of habit he continued to get up at six o'clock, even after he'd retired.
@@PHRASE1@@force of habit
@@DEFINE@@if you do something from force of habit , you do it because you had often done the same thing in the past and not for any other reason
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Why did you call her 'Miss'? She's `Mrs' now, you know." "Sorry, force of habit."
@@THESPROPFORM0@@by/from/through/out of force of habit
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most women apply the same old make-up year after year through force of habit.
@@PHRASE2@@compulsive
@@DEFINE@@a compulsive activity or way of behaving is one that someone cannot stop himself or herself doing repeatedly, especially because they have a mental problem
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her problem is compulsive over-eating.
@@EXAMPLE1@@compulsive hand-washing
@@THESPROPFORM0@@compulsive liar/eater/gambler etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Compulsive shoppers often never even open the goods they buy.
to happen
@@PHRASE0@@happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@The accident happened at two o'clock this afternoon.
@@EXAMPLE1@@What's happened? Why are you crying?
@@EXAMPLE2@@The strangest thing happened when I was in Singapore.
@@EXAMPLE3@@Before I realised what was happening, the man had grabbed my bag and run off with it.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@anything can/could/might happen
@@GLOSS@@used to say that it is uncertain what will happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@You mustn't go there alone at night. Anything might happen!
@@PHRASE1@@take place
@@DEFINE@@to happen - use this about events, performances, ceremonies and other things that have been planned to happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@The wedding will take place at St Andrew's church.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Police are trying to prevent the demonstration from taking place.
@@PHRASE2@@there is
@@DEFINE@@if there is an event, accident, change etc, it happens
@@EXAMPLE0@@There's a concert at the school next Saturday.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There has been a major accident on the Santa Monica Freeway.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I'll let you know if there's any change in our plans.
@@PHRASE3@@be
@@DEFINE@@if a planned event is at a particular time or place, it happens or is arranged to happen at that time or place
@@EXAMPLE0@@Dinner is at eight, so come at about half past seven.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Christmas will be on a Saturday next year.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Last year's degree ceremony was in the main university building.
@@PHRASE4@@occur
@@DEFINE@@to happen - use this especially about things that have not been planned or that people do not expect
@@EXAMPLE0@@Major earthquakes like this occur very rarely.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The court will have to decide exactly what occurred on the night Mellor died.
@@PHRASE5@@come about
@@DEFINE@@to happen, especially as a result of earlier events or decisions
@@EXAMPLE0@@Our problems came about because we ignored the advice of experts.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A number of educational reforms have come about as a result of the report.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@come about through
@@EXAMPLE0@@The decrease in the number of salmon has come about through commercial overfishing.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@how did it come about that
@@EXAMPLE0@@How did it come about that she married an awful man like that?
@@PHRASE6@@crop up
@@DEFINE@@if something such as a problem crops up , it happens suddenly and unexpectedly
@@EXAMPLE0@@A couple of problems cropped up while you were away.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If anything crops up, give me a call.
@@EXAMPLE2@@You have to learn to deal with difficult situations when they crop up.
@@PHRASE7@@come up
@@DEFINE@@if something, especially a problem or a chance to do something comes up , it happens unexpectedly
@@EXAMPLE0@@He rang to say he would be late home -- something had come up at the office.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There are job vacancies from time to time. I'll let you know if anything comes up.
@@EXAMPLE2@@When the opportunity to go to the States came up, Dora took it at once.
@@PHRASE8@@be coming up
@@DEFINE@@if a planned event is coming up , it will happen soon
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't forget you've got exams coming up in a couple of weeks' time.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Our 12th annual Folk Festival is coming up again soon.
@@PHRASE9@@turn up
@@DEFINE@@if something such as a job or a chance to do something turns up , it happens or becomes available, especially through good luck
@@EXAMPLE0@@Ben's been looking for a job for two months, but nothing good's turned up.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'd almost given up hope of finding a house I liked, and then suddenly this one turned up.
@@PHRASE10@@arise
@@DEFINE@@if a problem or difficult situation arises , it happens and comes to your attention
@@EXAMPLE0@@It would be best to deal with these issues at once, before a crisis arises.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@arise over
@@EXAMPLE0@@Several problems have arisen recently over questions of pay.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@arise from
@@GLOSS@@as a result of something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The conflict arose from tensions between the different ethnic groups.
@@PHRASE11@@strike
@@DEFINE@@if something unpleasant strikes , it suddenly happens
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is always devastating when this illness strikes.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Most people were fast asleep when the hurricane struck at 4.05 pm.
when what you want or expect happens
@@PHRASE0@@happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@We'd always feared that this might happen.
@@EXAMPLE1@@For some time there had been predictions of a major earthquake, and then on April 19, 1906, it happened.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I want to make things up with her, but I don't think it's going to happen.
@@PHRASE1@@come true
@@DEFINE@@if your wishes, dreams etc come true , what you have wished for or dreamed about actually happens
@@EXAMPLE0@@Patterson's dream came true when he won the Boston marathon on his first attempt.
@@EXAMPLE1@@People say that if you make a wish at the top of the hill, it always comes true.
@@PHRASE2@@be realized
@@VARIANT@@be realised
@@DEFINE@@if your expectations, hopes, fears etc are realized , what you expected or hoped for actually happens
@@EXAMPLE0@@At thirty-five her ambition of running her own business was finally realized.
@@EXAMPLE1@@My worst fears were realised when I saw what was on the exam paper.
@@PHRASE3@@be fulfilled
@@DEFINE@@if a wish or promise is fulfilled , what someone wished for or was promised actually happens
@@EXAMPLE0@@Tom decided to run the farm himself, so that his father's wish might be fulfilled.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We knew that the 'democratic elections' were a promise which would not be fulfilled.
@@PHRASE4@@materialize
@@VARIANT@@materialise
@@DEFINE@@if an event which has been planned, expected, or promised materializes , it actually happens
@@EXAMPLE0@@Even if the salary rise materialises, it won't be worth much.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It was rumoured that Apple would be sold to Sun Microsystems, but that deal never materialized.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fail to materialize
@@GLOSS@@not happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@The promised recovery failed to materialize and unemployment kept on rising.
ways of saying something happens to someone or something
@@PHRASE0@@happen to
@@DEFINE@@if something happens to someone or something, it happens and has an effect on them, usually a bad effect
@@EXAMPLE0@@I wonder what's happened to Dave. He should have been here by now.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A lot of people don't seem to care about what is happening to the environment.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it can happen to anyone
@@GLOSS@@use this to emphasize that something is not someone's fault
@@EXAMPLE0@@The crash wasn't her fault, it could have happened to anyone.
@@PHRASE1@@experience
@@DEFINE@@if someone experiences something such as a problem, a difficult situation etc, it happens to them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Many local companies have recently been experiencing financial difficulties.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@experience difficulties/problems etc with
@@EXAMPLE0@@They've experienced a lot of problems with their eldest son.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@experience something at first hand
@@GLOSS@@experience something personally
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is shocking to think of boys as young as sixteen experiencing at first hand the horrors of war.
@@PHRASE2@@undergo
@@DEFINE@@if someone or something undergoes a change or an unpleasant event, it happens to them or it is done to them
@@EXAMPLE0@@He has undergone tremendous emotional problems following the breakdown of his marriage.
@@EXAMPLE1@@In the last few years the museum has undergone extensive renovation.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Part of Mrs Galley's right arm was shattered and she underwent a five-hour emergency operation.
@@PHRASE3@@meet with
@@DEFINE@@to get a particular reaction, especially an unpleasant one, from other people
@@EXAMPLE0@@The initial plan to sell off part of the company met with intense criticism.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@meet with something from somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@Many working women still meet with prejudice from men.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Rebel forces entered the town and met with no resistance from government troops.
to happen with a good or bad result
@@PHRASE0@@turn out
@@DEFINE@@to happen so that the final result is good, bad, unexpected etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@We were worried when only twenty people came to the party but it turned out very well.
@@EXAMPLE1@@How did things turn out in the end?
@@THESPROPFORM0@@turn out to be something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I was a bit doubtful at first, but it turned out to be a really good idea.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@not turn out as planned/expected
@@EXAMPLE0@@We wanted the baby to be born at home, but it didn't quite turn out as planned.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@as it turned out
@@GLOSS@@used to say that this is what happened in the end
@@EXAMPLE0@@As it turned out, James was delayed and didn't arrive until three.
@@PHRASE1@@work out/pan out
@@DEFINE@@to happen with a particular result, especially a successful or unsuccessful one
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some election campaigns work out better than others.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We had a few problems when Jake first gave up work, but things are panning out very well now.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I'm not sure if we'll decide to get married or not - we'll wait and see how things work out.
@@PHRASE2@@go
@@THESPROPFORM0@@go well/badly/smoothly etc
@@DEFINE@@if something such as an arranged event or someone's work goes well, badly etc, it happens in a way that is successful, unsuccessful etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Did the party go well?
@@EXAMPLE1@@Things went badly for the company last year. Their profits are down by 50%.
@@EXAMPLE2@@How's the job going these days?
@@PHRASE3@@go off
@@THESPROPFORM0@@go off well/successfully/smoothly etc
@@DEFINE@@if an arranged event goes off well, successfully etc, it happens and is completed without any problems
@@EXAMPLE0@@Thanks to the helpful staff at the hotel, the conference went off very well.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'm sure that everything will go off smoothly on the day.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@go off without a hitch
@@GLOSS@@happen without any problems
@@EXAMPLE0@@Everyone was relieved when the ceremony at the Ambassador's residence went off without a hitch.
ways of saying that something is happening
@@PHRASE0@@be happening
@@EXAMPLE0@@She looked out of the window to see what was happening.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Property prices continue to rise and we still don't understand exactly why it's happening.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@what's happening?
@@EXAMPLE0@@The room began to shake and we stared at each other in terror. "What's happening?" asked Robert.
@@PHRASE1@@be going on
@@DEFINE@@if something is going on it is happening, especially if it makes you feel worried or annoyed
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was obvious from the way they kept looking at each other that there was something going on.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@what's going on?
@@EXAMPLE0@@"What's going on at the town hall?" asked my mother. "There's a huge crowd of people there."
@@PHRASE2@@be in progress
@@DEFINE@@if an arranged event, game, or operation is in progress , it has started and has not finished yet
@@EXAMPLE0@@By the time we got to the stadium, the match was already in progress.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There must be no noise in the school while examinations are in progress.
@@EXAMPLE2@@An emergency relief operation is already in progress in Southern Sudan.
@@PHRASE3@@be on
@@DEFINE@@to be happening now or to be going to happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@The summer sales are on next week.
@@EXAMPLE1@@People have to learn to economize when there is a war on.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The presidential election was on when we arrived in the States.
@@PHRASE4@@be in full swing
@@DEFINE@@if an organized activity or an event such as a party is in full swing , it has already been happening for some time and people are taking part in a very active way
@@EXAMPLE0@@By 10 o'clock the party was in full swing and everyone was dancing.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Barcelona was full of visitors, and preparations for the Olympic Games were in full swing.
@@PHRASE5@@be in operation
@@DEFINE@@if a plan or a system is in operation , it is being used and is working
@@EXAMPLE0@@Over 20 training programmes are in operation, with almost 2000 trainees.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Pushing kids so hard from such an early age is likely to have some harmful results.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Scientists tend to agree that most diets don't work and can be harmful.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The destruction of the ozone layer will have a very harmful effect on the environment.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@harmful to
@@EXAMPLE0@@80% of Americans think that television is harmful to society and especially to children.
@@PHRASE1@@damaging
@@DEFINE@@harmful and usually having a permanent effect
@@EXAMPLE0@@Up to 1500 patients suffered damaging side-effects after taking the drug.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The publicity that followed the scandal has been extremely damaging.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@damaging to
@@EXAMPLE0@@The British beef crisis was damaging to the livelihoods of thousands of people in the industry.
@@PHRASE2@@negative
@@DEFINE@@likely to harm someone or something, especially in a way that is not too serious - use this especially about something that could also have a good effect if the situation was different
@@EXAMPLE0@@Doctors have a duty to inform patients of the possible negative side-effects of the drug.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The school environment can be a negative force as well as a positive one.
@@PHRASE3@@be bad for
@@DEFINE@@to have a harmful effect on something such as an activity, organization, or type of work
@@EXAMPLE0@@When companies close down, it's bad for the town and bad for the local economy.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A bad marriage is bad for the kids.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Reading without good lighting is bad for your eyes.
likely to harm people's health or the environment
@@PHRASE0@@harmful
@@EXAMPLE0@@Scientists have recommended that new technology be used to target harmful bacteria.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Many of the products that we have around our homes are harmful if swallowed.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The protests were aimed at ending the dumping of harmful industrial waste at sea.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@harmful to
@@EXAMPLE0@@The sun's rays can be very harmful to the skin.
@@PHRASE1@@poisonous
@@DEFINE@@something that is poisonous contains a chemical that makes people, animals, or plants etc very ill or could kill them if they breathe it, swallow it, or touch it etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't drink that -- it's poisonous!
@@EXAMPLE1@@The adder is the only poisonous snake in Britain.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@highly poisonous
@@EXAMPLE0@@Carbon monoxide is a highly poisonous gas, mostly produced by cars.
@@PHRASE2@@hazardous
@@THESPROPFORM0@@hazardous chemicals/waste/substances etc
@@DEFINE@@substances that are poisonous and will harm people, animals, or the environment if they are not dealt with or got rid of carefully
@@EXAMPLE0@@Lead is one of the most hazardous substances known, causing cancer and nerve damage.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The building is now unoccupied, and all radioactive or hazardous materials have been removed.
@@EXAMPLE2@@We need better regulations regarding the transportation of hazardous waste along public roads.
@@PHRASE3@@toxic
@@DEFINE@@chemicals, gases, or waste products that are poisonous and harmful to people, animals, or the environment - used especially in technical or scientific contexts
@@EXAMPLE0@@Research has found that the drug contains a toxic chemical that can cause respiratory problems.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@toxic waste
@@GLOSS@@from factories etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@We need more installations for the disposal of toxic waste.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@highly toxic
@@EXAMPLE0@@highly toxic radioactive waste products
@@THESPROPFORM2@@toxic to
@@EXAMPLE0@@Carbon dioxide is not highly toxic to animals or humans in small amounts.
@@PHRASE4@@noxious
@@DEFINE@@a noxious chemical or gas harms your health and is very unpleasant
@@EXAMPLE0@@Residents have to put up with noxious fumes from the nearby factory.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Increasing tax on petrol would encourage people to drive smaller cars with fewer noxious emissions.
not harming anything or anyone
@@PHRASE0@@harmless
@@EXAMPLE0@@I don't know why you're so upset -- it was only a harmless bit of fun.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Radioactive waste needs to be stored for 25,000 years before it is harmless.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@harmless enough
@@GLOSS@@used to say that someone or something that may seem harmful, is in fact not harmful
@@EXAMPLE0@@He's a little crazy, I know, but he's harmless enough.
@@PHRASE1@@innocuous
@@DEFINE@@not harmful - use this especially when people have said or believe that something or someone is harmful
@@EXAMPLE0@@The producer dismissed the comment as quite innocuous.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The murder suspect was an innocuous-looking man with wire-framed glasses.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@seemingly/apparently innocuous
@@GLOSS@@seeming harmless, but actually intended to be harmful
@@EXAMPLE0@@Someone stood up and asked the professor an apparently innocuous question about his laboratory work.
@@PHRASE2@@do no harm/not do any harm
@@DEFINE@@if an action, activity, experience etc does no harm , it does not harm someone or something and may even help
@@EXAMPLE0@@Learning how to live on your own for a while will do you no harm at all.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it would do no harm to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I expect they've sold all the tickets, but it won't do any harm to ask.
@@PHRASE3@@friendly
@@THESPROPFORM0@@environment-friendly/ozone-friendly etc
@@DEFINE@@used especially about products in shops, meaning that they do not harm the environment etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Look for aerosols which say 'ozone-friendly' on the can.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Tighter laws are needed to prevent manufacturers from falsely claiming their products are environment friendly.
to feel strong dislike and anger towards someone or something
@@PHRASE0@@hate
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Go away!" Jackie screamed. "I hate you!"
@@EXAMPLE1@@I hated my first husband. He used to hit me and the children.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Turner was a rebel from the start. He hated authority and he hated the law.
@@EXAMPLE3@@He was an evil dictator who was universally hated.
@@EXAMPLE4@@It takes many years for kids who have suffered so much to learn to love and not to hate.
@@PHRASE1@@hate somebody's guts
@@DEFINE@@to hate someone very much
@@EXAMPLE0@@I wish she'd die tomorrow. I hate her guts.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The sergeant knew the men all hated his guts for the way he treated them.
@@PHRASE2@@can't stand
@@DEFINE@@to have a very strong feeling of dislike for a person or for their behaviour because they make you feel very angry or uncomfortable when you are with them
@@EXAMPLE0@@We used to be quite good friends but now I can't stand her.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I can't stand the way he's always telling people what they should do.
@@EXAMPLE2@@If there's one thing I can't stand, it's hypocrisy.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@can't stand the sight of somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't invite Alice. Mum can't stand the sight of her.
@@PHRASE3@@detest
@@DEFINE@@to have a strong feeling of hatred, especially for a particular kind of person, or a particular type of behaviour
@@EXAMPLE0@@He was exactly the kind of arrogant, self-satisfied man I detest.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I detest any form of cruelty toward animals.
@@EXAMPLE2@@According to Hollywood gossip, both the leading actors were detested by the rest of the cast.
@@PHRASE4@@loathe
@@DEFINE@@to have a very strong feeling of hatred for someone or for a type of behaviour, because you think that they are the very worst kind of person or behaviour that there is
@@EXAMPLE0@@Mrs Morel loathed her husband when he was drunk and violent.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Kemp was loathed by all the other prisoners, who regarded him as a traitor.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I really loathe it when people make promises and then don't keep them.
@@PHRASE5@@despise
@@DEFINE@@to hate someone or something and think they have no importance or value
@@EXAMPLE0@@We were brought up to despise the people from the poor side of town. They seemed so dirty and ignorant.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Otis despised inherited wealth and social class.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@despise somebody for (doing) something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I felt that the other kids despised me for having the wrong accent and the wrong colour skin.
@@PHRASE6@@abhor
@@DEFINE@@to hate a particular kind of behaviour or attitude, especially because you think it is morally wrong
@@EXAMPLE0@@The great majority of the Irish people have always abhorred violence.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The president abhorred all forms of racism.

@@PHRASE0@@hate
@@EXAMPLE0@@I hate it when you speak to me like that.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Tony hated science when he was at school because he wasn't any good at it.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Don't go in now - she hates being interrupted.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@hate to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Hurry up - I hate to be late!
@@PHRASE1@@can't stand/can't bear
