@@EXAMPLE0@@She stopped working in the factory because she couldn't stand the smell.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Turn the radio off. I can't bear that noise.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@can't stand/can't bear doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@He couldn't bear seeing her in so much pain.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@can't stand/bear somebody doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I can't stand people smoking around me when I'm eating.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@can't stand/can't bear to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I can't bear to think about the day she actually leaves home.
@@PHRASE2@@detest
@@DEFINE@@to hate something very much, especially a particular activity, taste, or smell
@@EXAMPLE0@@When he was at school he detested football.
@@EXAMPLE1@@You don't understand. It's not just that I don't like cabbage -- I absolutely detest it!
@@THESPROPFORM0@@detest doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I detested spending two hours every day travelling to work and back.
@@PHRASE3@@loathe
@@DEFINE@@to dislike something very much, especially because it makes you feel sick or nervous
@@EXAMPLE0@@She loathes spiders.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If there's one thing I really loathe, it's long car journeys.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@loathe doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Even after years of practice, he still loathed making public speeches.
a feeling of hating someone or something
@@PHRASE0@@hatred
@@DEFINE@@an angry feeling of deep dislike for someone or something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I could see the jealousy and hatred in Jeff's eyes.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@hatred of
@@EXAMPLE0@@The long cold winter had only increased his hatred of the place.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@have a hatred of something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Tom had a hatred of any kind of authority.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@hatred for/towards
@@GLOSS@@use this about a feeling of hate for people, not things
@@EXAMPLE0@@In her autobiography, she describes her hatred for her stepfather.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@deep hatred
@@EXAMPLE0@@The experience left him with a deep hatred of politicians.
@@PHRASE1@@hate
@@DEFINE@@the angry feeling that someone has when they hate someone and want to harm them
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was anger and hate in her voice, and I felt afraid.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be filled with hate
@@EXAMPLE0@@His mind was filled with hate and the desire for revenge.
@@PHRASE2@@loathing

@@THESPROPFORM0@@loathing for/of

@@THESPROPFORM1@@fear and loathing

@@PHRASE3@@animosity

@@GLOSS@@for personal, not political reasons

@@PHRASE4@@abhorrence
@@DEFINE@@a deep feeling of hatred towards something that you think is morally wrong or unpleasant
@@EXAMPLE0@@The thought of marrying him filled her with abhorrence.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@abhorrence of

@@PHRASE5@@contempt

@@EXAMPLE0@@I feel nothing but contempt for people who are obsessed with fast cars and designer clothes.

@@EXAMPLE0@@The teachers were very old-fashioned, treating any new ideas with contempt and scorn.

@@PHRASE0@@but for somebody/something
@@DEFINE@@use this when a situation would be different if something was not happening now or had not happened in the past
@@EXAMPLE0@@I would have walked out of the job earlier but for the fact that I desperately needed the money.
@@EXAMPLE1@@But for the actions of a brave fireman, I wouldn't be alive now.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Whole industries would have collapsed but for a massive injection of public funds.
@@PHRASE1@@if it had not been for
@@DEFINE@@use this when a situation would have been different if something had not happened or someone had not done something in the past
@@EXAMPLE0@@If it hadn't been for the war, Larry would have stayed on the farm.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If it hadn't been for Christine, I would never have met Michael.
@@PHRASE2@@if it wasn't/weren't for
@@DEFINE@@use this when you would do something different if a particular situation did not exist now
@@EXAMPLE0@@He'd be playing in this afternoon's game if it wasn't for his injury.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If it weren't for the children, I'm sure she would leave her husband.

@@PHRASE0@@sickly
@@DEFINE@@a sickly child is often ill
@@EXAMPLE0@@He was a sickly child with a bad chest and a permanent cough.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Louise, who was often sickly, couldn't join in the other children's games.
@@PHRASE1@@delicate
@@DEFINE@@unhealthy and weak and likely to become ill easily
@@EXAMPLE0@@Clare was more active than her brother, who had always been a delicate child.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Mr Humphreys' wife was delicate - the doctor was called in once or twice a week.
@@PHRASE2@@in poor health
@@DEFINE@@fairly ill all the time or over a long period of time, and generally not strong and healthy
@@EXAMPLE0@@When he left Trinidad he was already over 60, frail, and in poor health.
@@PHRASE3@@infirm
@@DEFINE@@not healthy or strong, especially because of old age
@@EXAMPLE0@@She lives with her grandmother who is elderly and infirm.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@the infirm
@@GLOSS@@people who are infirm
@@EXAMPLE0@@The "Meals on Wheels' service delivers food to the old and infirm.
@@PHRASE4@@prone to something
@@DEFINE@@likely to become ill or to get a particular illness
@@EXAMPLE0@@As a child she had always been prone to allergies.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The disease had left her weak and prone to all kinds of infections.
someone who imagines they are ill
@@PHRASE0@@hypochondriac
@@DEFINE@@someone who often thinks that they are ill when they are not and worries too much about their health
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't be such a hypochondriac - it's only a cold!
@@EXAMPLE1@@She's a bit of a hypochondriac - always looking up her minor illnesses in a medical book.
to feel ill
@@PHRASE0@@feel ill
@@VARIANT@@feel sick
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Do you feel ill, darling?" asked Rosie anxiously.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I was feeling ill, so I went home.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Mark said he felt sick, so I've made an appointment with the doctor.
@@PHRASE1@@not feel (very) well
@@VARIANT@@not feel too good
@@VARIANT@@not feel good
@@DEFINE@@to feel slightly ill
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you don't feel well the best thing to do is to stay in bed.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"I don't feel very well," said Jamie, suddenly going very pale.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Ben's not feeling good this morning. I think it's something he ate.
@@EXAMPLE3@@No, I don't think I'll be coming out tonight. I'm not feeling too good.
@@PHRASE2@@feel funny
@@DEFINE@@to feel slightly ill - use this especially when you do not know what is wrong with you
@@EXAMPLE0@@I felt a bit funny and dizzy, and then the next thing I knew I was lying on the floor.
@@PHRASE3@@feel rough
@@DEFINE@@to feel ill
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't get up if you're feeling rough - I'll bring you some breakfast in bed.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Liz said she was feeling pretty rough yesterday -- I don't think she'll come to work today.
@@PHRASE4@@feel sick
@@VARIANT@@feel sick to your stomach
@@DEFINE@@to feel as if you are going to vomit (=bring food up from your stomach )
@@EXAMPLE0@@We'd only been in the car two minutes when David said he felt sick.
@@EXAMPLE1@@When I was pregnant, the smell of coffee made me feel sick to my stomach.
@@PHRASE5@@groggy
@@DEFINE@@feeling weak and tired as a result of illness or drugs
@@EXAMPLE0@@You shouldn't drive after taking these pills. They're likely to make you feel groggy.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@groggy from
@@EXAMPLE0@@I went to see Sally in hospital, but she was still groggy from the anaesthetic.
@@PHRASE6@@feel faint
@@DEFINE@@to feel very weak and as if you are going to become unconscious
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was a very hot day, and I suddenly felt faint and sick.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If at any time you feel faint or nauseous, stop taking the tablets.
to become ill
@@PHRASE0@@get/become ill
@@VARIANT@@get/become sick
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's horrible when you get ill on holiday.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If you take vitamin C every day, it helps to stop you getting sick.
@@EXAMPLE2@@My father first became ill when I was 12, and died a few months later.
@@EXAMPLE3@@People were scared of becoming sick because they couldn't pay the doctor's bills.
@@PHRASE1@@fall ill
@@VARIANT@@fall sick
@@DEFINE@@to become ill, especially with a long or serious illness
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you live alone, you often wonder who would look after you if you fell ill.
@@EXAMPLE1@@New Year's Eve revellers fell sick after drinking an orange liquid at a downtown 'rave' party.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fall ill with
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was the first time the president had been back to his office since falling ill with pneumonia in January.
@@PHRASE2@@be taken ill
@@DEFINE@@to suddenly or unexpectedly become ill
@@EXAMPLE0@@I heard that her sister had been taken ill and rushed to hospital.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be taken ill with
@@EXAMPLE0@@The band cut short their tour after singer Robert Smith was taken ill with severe stomach pains.
someone who is ill
@@PHRASE0@@patient
@@DEFINE@@someone who is ill and is being looked after by a doctor, nurse etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@St Dominic's Hospital treats about 10,000 patients a year.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@cancer/leukemia/AIDS etc patients
@@EXAMPLE0@@He gave a half million pound donation towards the care of AIDs patients.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@patients with cancer/aids/leukemia etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Clinical trials show that some patients with breast cancer do better if they take the drug for five years after surgery.

@@DEFINE@@someone who has a particular illness or who often has a particular illness
@@EXAMPLE0@@Lupus is a disease of the immune system and nine out of ten sufferers are women.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@hay fever/asthma/cancer etc sufferer
@@EXAMPLE0@@The health centre runs a support group for Parkinson's disease sufferers.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Summer can be a nightmare for hay fever sufferers.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@sufferer from hay fever/asthma/cancer etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Many sufferers from depression struggle on for years before seeking help.
@@PHRASE2@@invalid
@@DEFINE@@someone who is permanently ill and needs to be looked after, especially if they have to stay in bed
@@EXAMPLE0@@My father's an invalid, and needs constant care.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@somebody's invalid wife/son etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Barbara decided to move her invalid mother to Mississippi, so that she could look after her herself.
@@PHRASE3@@the sick
@@DEFINE@@people who are ill and need to be helped or treated
@@EXAMPLE0@@At that time there were no state benefits for the old and the sick.
@@EXAMPLE1@@terrible wartime photographs of the sick and the dying

@@EXAMPLE1@@We're in love and we want to get married right away.
@@EXAMPLE2@@You said it was important so I came straight away.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Few observers expect the jury to acquit Mr Hoskins.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His lawyer thought he had a good chance of being acquitted at the trial, if no further evidence was found.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@acquit somebody of something
@@EXAMPLE0@@To her relief she was acquitted of all the charges laid against her.
@@PHRASE2@@clear
@@DEFINE@@if you are cleared of a crime, a court of law says that you are innocent, because it is impossible to legally prove that you are guilty
@@EXAMPLE0@@After Pagones was cleared in court, he sued his accusers.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@clear somebody of something
@@EXAMPLE0@@A jury cleared the company of all criminal charges in connection with the accident.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Marshall was given his job back after being cleared of accusations that he abused drugs.
in order to get something, achieve something, or make something happen
@@PHRASE0@@to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@She went to the bank to get some money.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Salt is spread on roads in cold weather to prevent the formation of ice.
@@EXAMPLE2@@To lose weight, you must eat sensibly.
@@EXAMPLE3@@You didn't come all that way just to see me, did you?
@@THESPROPFORM0@@so as not to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@When I get home late I sleep in the spare room, so as not to disturb my wife.
@@PHRASE1@@in order to do something
@@DEFINE@@done so that something else happens as a result, or necessary if something else is to be possible
@@EXAMPLE0@@Many drug users get involved in crime simply in order to pay for their supplies of cocaine and heroin.
@@EXAMPLE1@@In order to be a doctor, you have to study for six years.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@in order not to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@In order not to offend anyone, I did not tell them the real reason for my visit.
@@PHRASE2@@so (that)
@@DEFINE@@if you do something so that you or another person can do something else, you do it in order to make the other thing possible
@@EXAMPLE0@@She's studying English at night school so that she can go to university.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'll move my car so you can get into the garage.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Steps must be taken so that this kind of disaster never happens again.
@@PHRASE3@@for
@@DEFINE@@if you do something for something, you do it for a particular purpose
@@EXAMPLE0@@She's gone into hospital for a check-up.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I went into the store for some tomatoes and came out with two bags of groceries.
@@EXAMPLE2@@We climbed up here for the view, and also because we wanted to get some exercise.
@@PHRASE4@@with the aim of doing something
@@DEFINE@@if you do something with the aim of doing something else, you do it in order to try and achieve this
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Green Party was started with the aim of protecting the environment.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I originally went out to the Far East with the aim of setting up my own import-export business.
@@PHRASE5@@with a view to doing something
@@DEFINE@@if you do something with a view to doing something else, you do it because you are planning to do something else later and this will help you to achieve it
@@EXAMPLE0@@We bought the cottage with a view to settling down there after retirement.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The idea was to pool resources with a view to lowering operating costs.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Children often choose high-fat fast foods in preference to fresh, healthy ones.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Occasionally, he makes his staff work overtime and gives them time off in lieu.

@@EXAMPLE0@@They used to give the landlord poultry and eggs in lieu of rent.

@@DEFINE@@not being serious about something that should be taken seriously, so that people think you do not care
@@EXAMPLE0@@People ask me if I'm related to him, and my answer is usually a flippant "No, but I wish I were."
@@EXAMPLE1@@When asked what is wrong with the economy, analysts reply "Not enough money." This answer is not as flippant as it sounds.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Sorry if that sounded flippant or heartless - it wasn't meant to be.
@@PHRASE1@@playful
@@DEFINE@@actions or behaviour that are playful are not serious, but they are fun and friendly
@@EXAMPLE0@@He gave me a playful slap on the shoulder.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She tried to sound playful but somehow the words came out the wrong way.
@@PHRASE2@@facetious
@@DEFINE@@making jokes or trying to be funny in a clever or unkind way that people think is annoying
@@EXAMPLE0@@At the risk of sounding facetious, who really cares about what happens?
@@EXAMPLE1@@The speech saying drug users should be shot was clearly facetious, but it contained a serious point.
@@PHRASE3@@tongue-in-cheek
@@DEFINE@@a remark, statement etc that is tongue-in-cheek is intended as a joke but is said or written in a serious or sincere way
@@EXAMPLE0@@His tongue-in-cheek articles are brilliantly funny and very political.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"This just shows you what a great coach I am," said Braden, tongue-in-cheek.
to decide how good, bad etc someone or something is
@@PHRASE0@@judge
@@DEFINE@@to form an opinion about a person or situation, using your knowledge, experience, and intelligence
@@EXAMPLE0@@The changes should be judged by their results.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@judge when/whether/what etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@How do you judge when a house needs a new roof?
@@EXAMPLE1@@2,000 foreign and local monitors were watching to judge whether the elections were free and fair.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@judge somebody/something to be something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Women judged to be at high risk for breast cancer should be examined every year.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@judging from/by something
@@GLOSS@@when you form an opinion based on a particular fact
@@EXAMPLE0@@Judging from Monday night's game, the team still has a lot of work to do.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@judge (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some students may judge that the benefits they receive from further education are less than the costs of that education.
@@THESPROPFORM4@@judge it wise/proper/dangerous etc to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Dwight judged it dangerous to navigate in darkness in these waters.
@@PHRASE1@@assess
@@DEFINE@@to consider someone's work, ideas, or products, or to consider a situation or event, in order to judge how good they are, what standard they have reached, or how useful they might be to you
@@EXAMPLE0@@This test provides an excellent way of assessing students' progress.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He has written a guidebook that assesses the quality of Californian hotels.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The booklet aims to help parents assess recent educational changes.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@assess how/whether/what etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The committee will continue to assess how we can improve.
@@PHRASE2@@evaluate
@@DEFINE@@to carefully consider how useful or valuable an activity, plan, or suggestion is, especially in order to decide whether or not to start doing it or continue doing it
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was not enough time to evaluate the information before the meeting.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The new drug is being evaluated in clinical trials.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The police force should not evaluate officers' performance in terms of the number of arrests they make.
@@PHRASE3@@critique
@@DEFINE@@an article, book, speech etc that carefully examines a subject and says what is good or bad about it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The speech was a devastating critique of Reagan's economic policy.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Marx's critique of capitalism in the 19th century

@@EXAMPLE0@@He suffered a fatal injury to the neck.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fatal to
@@EXAMPLE0@@A sudden shock could be fatal to anyone with a weak heart.
@@PHRASE1@@lethal
@@DEFINE@@something that is lethal can cause death - use this especially about weapons or substances
@@EXAMPLE0@@The poison produced by the frog's skin is so lethal that it can paralyze a bird or a monkey immediately.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A lethal cocktail of pollutants is being poured into Scotland's coastal waters, according to Greenpeace.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@lethal weapon
@@EXAMPLE0@@Almost any sharp or pointed object can potentially be a lethal weapon.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@lethal to
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most pesticides are lethal to earthworms on or near the surface.
@@PHRASE2@@deadly
@@DEFINE@@something such as a disease or poison that is deadly can cause death
@@EXAMPLE0@@In the First World War pneumonia was as deadly as bullets and shells.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Some mushrooms are edible while others, which look almost identical, contain deadly poisons.
@@PHRASE3@@killer
@@DEFINE@@a killer disease or thing could kill or has killed a lot of people - used especially in newspapers
@@EXAMPLE0@@A swarm of killer bees has attacked 70 children in a village in northern Mexico.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Killer floods and hurricanes in Asia have destroyed whole towns.
@@PHRASE4@@mortal
@@DEFINE@@a mortal injury, wound, or disease is one that causes death - used especially in literature
@@EXAMPLE0@@He killed Leonardo and received a mortal wound himself.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He gathered all his strength to deliver his opponent the final mortal blow.
to kill an animal
@@PHRASE0@@kill
@@EXAMPLE0@@Is it morally acceptable to kill animals for food?
@@EXAMPLE1@@You shouldn't really kill spiders, even if you're frightened of them.
@@EXAMPLE2@@They were so hungry they killed the rest of their livestock that winter.
@@PHRASE1@@slaughter
@@DEFINE@@to kill farm animals, either for their meat or skins, or because they are ill
@@EXAMPLE0@@The only way to stop the virus spreading is by slaughtering all infected animals.
@@EXAMPLE1@@As part of the ceremony a cow was slaughtered and placed on the stone altar.
@@PHRASE2@@destroy
@@DEFINE@@to kill an animal in a painless way, especially using drugs, because it is dangerous or in pain
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Animal Disease Authority decided to destroy the cattle that were infected with the disease.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@have something destroyed
@@EXAMPLE0@@The court ordered the owner of the rottweilers to have the dogs destroyed.
@@PHRASE3@@put down/put to sleep
@@DEFINE@@to kill an animal, especially a pet, in a painless way, because it is very old or very ill, or is not wanted
@@EXAMPLE0@@When our old cat became very sick we had to ask the vet to put her down.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She rescued Sandy from the Animal Shelter the day before he was due to be put to sleep.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@have something put down/put to sleep
@@EXAMPLE0@@A blind dog is no use to a shepherd. I'm afraid I'm going to have to have him put down.
@@PHRASE4@@cull
@@DEFINE@@to kill a large number of animals, for example in order to stop a disease spreading or to keep the numbers of a particular animal population down
@@EXAMPLE0@@Over two million sheep have been culled to prevent the spread of foot and mouth disease.

@@EXAMPLE1@@The American legal system says that you are innocent until proven guilty.
part of a law or legal agreement
@@PHRASE0@@article
@@DEFINE@@one of the parts, usually numbered, of a written law or legal agreement
@@EXAMPLE0@@Article 1 of the constitution guarantees freedom of religion.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The country signed the treaty but then violated each of its 143 articles.
@@PHRASE1@@clause
@@DEFINE@@a part of a written law or legal document, concerning a particular point or idea
@@EXAMPLE0@@I was told that this clause would be removed from the contract.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Courts ruled that prayer in school violates a clause of the First Amendment.
@@PHRASE2@@loophole
@@DEFINE@@a detail that is missing from a law or legal document that makes it possible to avoid something in that law
@@EXAMPLE0@@He pays very little tax because of some loophole in income tax legislation.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@close a loophole
@@GLOSS@@to add details to a law so that there is no way for people to avoid following it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The new rules will close loopholes in British immigration law.
to make a new law
@@PHRASE0@@pass
@@DEFINE@@to accept a new law in a government or parliament, so that it officially becomes a law
@@EXAMPLE0@@Congress has passed an education-reform law.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The law was passed with only a few MPs voting against.
@@PHRASE1@@legislate
@@DEFINE@@to officially make laws that are intended to control a particular activity or situation
@@THESPROPFORM0@@legislate against
@@EXAMPLE0@@Should parliament legislate against experiments on animals?
@@THESPROPFORM1@@legislate on
@@EXAMPLE0@@The government was under a lot of public pressure to legislate on equal pay.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@legislate for
@@EXAMPLE0@@Thomas Jefferson said that Britain had no right to legislate for its American colonies.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@legislate something
@@EXAMPLE0@@States are legislating stricter automobile safety measures for young children.
ways of saying that a law is officially accepted
@@PHRASE0@@become law
@@DEFINE@@if a new or suggested law becomes law , it is officially accepted and starts to exist
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Education Bill finally became law last month.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Until the Food Protection Bill became law, the ministry had no power to ban dangerous pesticides.
@@PHRASE1@@get onto/reach the statute book
@@VARIANT@@be on the books
@@DEFINE@@if a law gets onto the statute book , it officially becomes a law
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Employment Bill was passed in 1982 but did not reach the statute book until 1984.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The laws have been on the books for decades, but city officials failed to enforce them.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Rita dropped a blob of paint on the new carpet.

@@EXAMPLE2@@Put a blob of glue on each surface and carefully press together.

@@PHRASE0@@thin
@@DEFINE@@a thin liquid flows very easily - use this about liquids that are often thick
@@EXAMPLE0@@The paint was too thin, and was dripping everywhere.
@@EXAMPLE1@@For these crepes you will need a fairly thin batter, so do not add too much flour.
@@PHRASE1@@runny
@@DEFINE@@food that is runny is liquid but should be thicker than it is
@@EXAMPLE0@@a boiled egg with a runny yolk
@@EXAMPLE1@@runny custard
@@PHRASE2@@watery
@@DEFINE@@food or drink that is watery contains too much water, so that it does not taste or look good
@@EXAMPLE0@@The coffee is horrible - really weak and watery.
@@EXAMPLE1@@All they had to eat for weeks was bread and watery cabbage soup.

@@EXAMPLE0@@If you want to make the sauce thicker, add flour.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Add the chocolate to the butter and eggs, stirring the mixture until it is thick and creamy.
@@PHRASE3@@smooth
@@DEFINE@@if a liquid is smooth , it is thick and has no lumps in it, especially because it has been mixed very well
@@EXAMPLE0@@Beat the eggs and flour until they are smooth.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Blend the strawberries with a little icing sugar in a food processor until it forms a smooth purée.

@@DEFINE@@if something solid melts or if heat melts it, it becomes liquid

@@EXAMPLE1@@Melt the butter in a saucepan and stir in the sugar.
@@PHRASE1@@dissolve

@@EXAMPLE0@@The crystals dissolve in water to create a purple liquid.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Dissolve the salt in 125 ml of hot water.

someone or something that you cannot find
@@PHRASE0@@missing
@@DEFINE@@a missing object is lost and may have been stolen; a missing person cannot be found and may be in danger
@@EXAMPLE0@@She's been missing for three days now, and we're very worried.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The painting, which has been missing for almost half a century, only turned up when the owner of the house died.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@missing from
@@EXAMPLE0@@Police are 'very concerned' for the safety of a teenager who's been missing from home for three days.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Two pages were missing from my copy of the report.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@go missing (from)
@@GLOSS@@become lost or be stolen
@@EXAMPLE0@@A small sum of money went missing from the office last night.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@report somebody/something missing (from)
@@GLOSS@@tell someone in authority that someone or something is lost or stolen
@@EXAMPLE0@@The man had reported his girlfriend missing three days after she disappeared.
@@PHRASE1@@lost
@@DEFINE@@if something is lost , no-one knows where it is
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've looked everywhere for the car keys. I think they must be lost.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Divers are searching for the plane's lost flight recorder.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@get lost
@@EXAMPLE0@@You haven't gotten my letter yet? It must have gotten lost in the mail.
@@PHRASE2@@disappear
@@DEFINE@@if something or someone disappears , they cannot be found and you think they may have been stolen or may be in danger
@@EXAMPLE0@@I thought I had a copy of the notes, but they seem to have disappeared somewhere.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The parents of an art student who disappeared in the middle of his exams have made an emotional plea for him to come home.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@disappear from
@@EXAMPLE0@@The letter had mysteriously disappeared from the file overnight.
@@PHRASE3@@be nowhere to be seen/found
@@DEFINE@@if someone or something is nowhere to be seen or nowhere to be found , you have looked everywhere for them but still cannot find them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Our tour guide was nowhere to be seen, so we set off to explore the city alone.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She'd looked everywhere for her glasses, but they were nowhere to be found.

@@PHRASE0@@maybe/perhaps
@@DEFINE@@use this when you think that something may happen or may be true, but you are not sure. Perhaps is more formal than maybe .
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Will you be there tomorrow?" "I don't know, maybe."

@@EXAMPLE1@@Housing prices will continue to rise, though perhaps not as much as was predicted last year.
@@PHRASE1@@may/might/could
@@DEFINE@@use this with other verbs, to show that something is possible, or likely, but you are not sure about it. May and might are more formal than could
@@EXAMPLE0@@Take your umbrella -- it might rain.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Hundreds of workers may lose their jobs if the strike continues.
@@EXAMPLE2@@We could be home before midnight if the traffic isn't too bad.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@may/might/could have done something
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Bruce isn't here yet." "He may have decided not to come."
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's a good thing we got her to the hospital right away -- the doctor said she could have died if we'd waited.
@@PHRASE2@@it is possible (that)/there's a chance (that)
@@DEFINE@@use this when you think that something may happen or may be done, but that it is not very likely
@@EXAMPLE0@@I might have to work on Saturday, so it's possible I won't be able to come to your party.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There's a chance that I'll be in California in October, so I might be able to visit you for a few days.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it is just possible (that)/there is just a chance (that)
@@GLOSS@@when something is possible, but very unlikely
@@EXAMPLE0@@Tomorrow should be sunny but there's just a chance of showers in the afternoon.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's just possible we'll finish the job by tonight, but it'll probably be tomorrow.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@outside chance/possibility
@@EXAMPLE0@@Martinez will need surgery, but there's an outside chance he'll be playing again before the end of the season.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@slim chance/possibility
@@EXAMPLE0@@Sims has some numbness and weakness in her legs, and surgeons say there is a slim possibility of paralysis.
@@PHRASE3@@possibly
@@DEFINE@@use this when you think that something may be true, but you do not have enough information to be sure
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Do you think she was murdered, inspector?" "Possibly."
@@EXAMPLE1@@He's playing in the US Open Golf Championships - possibly for the last time.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Stone is possibly America's finest film director.
@@EXAMPLE3@@The cancer was possibly caused by exposure to asbestos.
@@EXAMPLE4@@Trade between the two countries began in the 11th century, possibly even earlier.
@@EXAMPLE5@@Many analysts believe interest rates will rise, possibly as early as next spring.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@quite possibly
@@GLOSS@@very possibly
@@EXAMPLE0@@The examination hall was vast, with at least 700 or 800 students and quite possibly as many as 1000.
@@PHRASE4@@conceivably
@@DEFINE@@if you think something may conceivably happen or be true, it seems unlikely but you can imagine that it is possible
@@EXAMPLE0@@Reservations are advised but you might conceivably find a hotel the day you arrive.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It is still unlikely, but unemployment could conceivably begin to fall by the end of the year.

@@DEFINE@@if something is unnecessary or not necessary , you do not need to have it or do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't fill your report with unnecessary information.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A lot of the expenses that he's claiming seem totally unnecessary.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it is unnecessary/not necessary to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's not necessary to spend a lot of money on clothes to look good.
@@PHRASE1@@hardly necessary
@@DEFINE@@not necessary at all - use this when you are surprised that someone thinks something is necessary
@@EXAMPLE0@@They asked to see my passport, my driver's license, and my bank card, which was hardly necessary.
@@EXAMPLE1@@At first glance, it seems hardly necessary to make another film about Van Gogh.
@@PHRASE2@@needless
@@DEFINE@@use this to describe bad things that are unnecessary because they could easily have been prevented or avoided
@@EXAMPLE0@@"I am very saddened by this needless loss of life," the President said at a news conference Tuesday.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He accused the local council of allowing a needless tragedy, through a policy of not fitting smoke detectors to council houses.
@@PHRASE3@@gratuitous
@@DEFINE@@done for no reason, and seeming shocking or offensive
@@THESPROPFORM0@@gratuitous violence/insults/cruelty etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The network refused to televise the film because it contained too much gratuitous violence.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It was a completely gratuitous insult -- I hadn't said anything to offend her.
nervous
@@PHRASE0@@nervous
@@EXAMPLE0@@Bill looked nervous, and I could see his hands were shaking.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@nervous about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Kelli was so nervous about her exam that she couldn't sleep.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'm a little nervous about leaving the kids at home all alone.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Many investors are nervous about their investments after the recent drop in the stock market.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@make somebody nervous
@@EXAMPLE0@@It makes me nervous when you drive that fast.
@@PHRASE1@@tense
@@DEFINE@@so worried about something that you cannot relax, and you easily get angry or upset
@@EXAMPLE0@@I always feel tense after driving all day.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Mary's problems at work were making her tense and irritable.
@@EXAMPLE2@@You seem awfully tense - why don't you have a drink and try to relax?
@@PHRASE2@@jumpy/jittery
@@DEFINE@@very nervous so that you are unable to relax and are easily surprised by sudden sounds or movements
@@EXAMPLE0@@The dogs are jumpy tonight - I wonder if there's something outside.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She was getting jumpy thinking about the trip.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I was feeling extremely jittery - all I wanted was to leave the bar as quickly as possible.
@@EXAMPLE3@@Investors are jittery due to uncertainty about interest rates.
@@PHRASE3@@on edge
@@DEFINE@@if someone is on edge or if their nerves are on edge , they are nervous and likely to become angry or upset very easily
@@EXAMPLE0@@Jerry had had a hard day and his nerves were on edge.
@@EXAMPLE1@@As reports of robberies continued to appear in the press, the whole community was increasingly on edge.
@@PHRASE4@@uneasy
@@DEFINE@@nervous that something bad might happen, so that you feel anxious and unable to relax until the danger has passed
@@EXAMPLE0@@There's something I don't trust about him. He makes me feel very uneasy.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It was the same uneasy feeling he'd experienced that morning when he saw the police car outside.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@uneasy about
@@EXAMPLE0@@Rebecca was already beginning to feel uneasy about accepting the stranger's offer of a ride.
@@PHRASE5@@panicky
@@DEFINE@@very nervous and anxious about something, especially when you are in a dangerous situation that you cannot control or change
@@EXAMPLE0@@I began to feel panicky, sure that I was going to miss the train.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Is he really dead?" Abe asked in a panicky voice.
@@EXAMPLE2@@After waiting for him for two hours, Lorna got panicky and called the police.
to be nervous
@@PHRASE0@@have butterflies
@@DEFINE@@to feel nervous about doing something that you are going to do very soon because it is important and you want to do it well
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some actors never have butterflies before going on stage.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@have butterflies in your stomach
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was the morning of the World Cup Final and most of the players had butterflies in their stomachs.
@@PHRASE1@@be a nervous wreck
@@DEFINE@@if someone is a nervous wreck , they have been made so nervous that they have completely lost all their confidence and their ability to remain calm or think sensibly
@@EXAMPLE0@@Before the plane took off she was a nervous wreck - she had to be strapped into her seat.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Even though I'd been practicing for months, by the day of the competition I was a nervous wreck.
@@PHRASE2@@be a bundle of nerves
@@DEFINE@@to be so nervous that you are shaking and you find it impossible to behave calmly, especially for a long time
@@EXAMPLE0@@Since she lost her job Rosie's been a bundle of nerves.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Harry was a bundle of nerves the whole time his wife was in the hospital.
someone who is often or always nervous
@@PHRASE0@@nervous
@@DEFINE@@someone who is often or always worried and frightened that something unpleasant may happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@She's such a nervous child we don't like to leave her on her own.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Mr Darby was a mild, nervous man who seemed to expect people to ignore him.
@@PHRASE1@@highly-strung
@@VARIANT@@high-strung
@@DEFINE@@always nervous and unable to relax, especially so that you react in a very extreme way to ordinary situations
@@EXAMPLE0@@Mark's a little high-strung, so go easy on him.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Her main problem is that she is very highly-strung which tends to make other people feel nervous too.
@@PHRASE2@@uptight
@@DEFINE@@unable to be relaxed about life in general, so that this makes you seem unfriendly and unhappy
@@EXAMPLE0@@He tries to be kind, but he always seems a little uptight.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She's one of those narrow-minded, uptight people who think that for a work of art to be great it can't be pleasurable.
a feeling of being nervous
@@PHRASE0@@nerves
@@DEFINE@@the feeling of being nervous because you are worried or a little frightened about something, especially if this feeling is likely to affect your behaviour or performance
@@EXAMPLE0@@Normally she's very relaxed and amusing. It must be nerves.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@a case/attack of nerves
@@EXAMPLE0@@She had a sudden attack of nerves and refused to go to see the dentist.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@calm/steady etc your nerves
@@GLOSS@@try to relax
@@EXAMPLE0@@Arnie had a drink before the meeting to steady his nerves.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@suffer from nerves
@@EXAMPLE0@@Although a competent teacher, he suffers from nerves when the students behave badly.
@@PHRASE1@@tension
@@DEFINE@@a feeling of being nervous and unable to relax, especially before something is about to happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her voice trembled with tension.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@tension is high
@@GLOSS@@people feel very nervous
@@EXAMPLE0@@The tension was high in Mexico as the day of the decision approached.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@tension mounts
@@GLOSS@@people feel more and more nervous
@@EXAMPLE0@@A crowd gathered and tension mounted till the riot broke out.
a situation in which people feel nervous
@@PHRASE0@@tense
@@DEFINE@@a tense situation makes people feel nervous and anxious, especially because they are worried about what might happen next or what someone might do
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was a tense silence, and then everyone began to laugh.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The negotiations became increasingly tense as the weeks went by.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The journey through the mountains went well even though there were a few tense moments when the car skidded.
@@EXAMPLE3@@When someone mentioned Andy's time in prison, the atmosphere grew tense.
@@PHRASE1@@strained
@@DEFINE@@a situation that is strained makes people feel nervous, embarrassed, and uncomfortable, and unable to behave naturally
@@EXAMPLE0@@After the argument there was a strained silence.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Since my father's affair things have been very strained between him and my mother.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The strained atmosphere at the dinner made it difficult to chat with people.
@@PHRASE2@@uneasy
@@DEFINE@@a situation that is uneasy makes people feel a little nervous because they are uncertain about what will happen next or what someone might do
@@EXAMPLE0@@After the speech there was an uneasy silence and nobody clapped.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Since the two sides declared a ceasefire, there has been an uneasy calm throughout the region.
@@PHRASE3@@unsettling
@@DEFINE@@an unsettling situation makes you feel slightly nervous and unable to relax or concentrate completely
@@EXAMPLE0@@The weather forecast was unsettling - we had nowhere to go if a really big storm hit.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Greenspan delivered more unsettling news about the economy the next day.
@@PHRASE4@@nailbiting
@@DEFINE@@a nailbiting situation is so exciting that it makes you nervous, especially because you are waiting for a result or decision
@@EXAMPLE0@@Waiting to become a father is one of the most nailbiting situations a man can face.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@nailbiting finish
@@EXAMPLE0@@With three minutes left, the World Cup Final is set for a nailbiting finish.
@@PHRASE5@@nerve-wracking
@@DEFINE@@a nerve-wracking situation makes you feel very nervous because it is difficult or frightening
@@EXAMPLE0@@Your first appearance on stage is always a nerve-wracking experience
@@EXAMPLE1@@Trying to keep track of all those little kids at the same time must be pretty nerve-wracking.
@@PHRASE6@@charged
@@DEFINE@@a charged situation or subject makes people feel very nervous and is likely to cause arguments or violence
@@EXAMPLE0@@Abortion is still a very emotionally charged issue in the U.S.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@highly charged
@@EXAMPLE0@@In a highly charged press conference, Armstrong defended his attack on the children.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@charged atmosphere
@@EXAMPLE0@@The already charged atmosphere erupted into violence when police told the crowd to disperse.
to make someone feel nervous
@@PHRASE0@@make somebody nervous
@@EXAMPLE0@@Have you seen the way he looks at people? He makes me nervous.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Don't watch me while I'm typing - it makes me really nervous.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Thunder and lightning always make the horses nervous.
@@PHRASE1@@unsettle
@@DEFINE@@if something unsettles you, it makes you feel slightly nervous and unable to relax or concentrate completely
@@EXAMPLE0@@Ted's angry outbursts unsettled the whole family.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The threat of war has been enough to unsettle international oil traders.
@@EXAMPLE2@@She was still recovering from the accident so he avoided any subjects which might unsettle her.
@@PHRASE2@@unnerve
@@DEFINE@@to make someone very nervous, especially by shocking or surprising them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Moore had been extremely unnerved by the FBI's visit.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The daily news stories of the worsening economy unnerved the nation.
@@PHRASE3@@psych out
@@DEFINE@@to try to make someone, especially someone you are competing against in a game, lose their confidence and their ability to remain calm
@@THESPROPFORM0@@psych out somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@McEnroe often used his bad behaviour in difficult tennis matches to psych out his opponent.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@psych somebody out
@@EXAMPLE0@@Whenever we play chess Bill tries to psych me out by smirking every time I make a move.
@@PHRASE4@@put somebody on edge
@@DEFINE@@to make someone feel very nervous so that they cannot relax
@@EXAMPLE0@@Trying to keep the plan a secret put us all on edge.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Layoffs and work upheavals have put many employees on edge, both at work and at home.
never
@@PHRASE0@@never
@@DEFINE@@not once, or not at any time
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Have you ever been to Paris?" "No, never."
@@EXAMPLE1@@Ali had never seen snow before.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The view was spectacular - I'll never forget it.
@@EXAMPLE3@@He walks right past me and never even says "hello".
@@THESPROPFORM0@@never do/say etc something
@@EXAMPLE0@@(=used to tell someone not to do something ) Never go there alone at night.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@never have I/did he etc
@@GLOSS@@used for emphasis
@@EXAMPLE0@@Never in my whole life have I felt so angry.
@@PHRASE1@@not ever
@@DEFINE@@not at any time
@@EXAMPLE0@@I haven't ever had champagne before.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Don't ever do that again.
@@EXAMPLE2@@"I won't leave you," she said, "not ever."
@@PHRASE2@@never ever/never, never
@@DEFINE@@say this when you want to emphasize strongly that something has never happened or will never happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@You must never ever tell anyone what you heard tonight.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'll never, never stop loving you.
@@PHRASE3@@never/not in a million years
@@DEFINE@@say this when you think it is completely impossible that something could ever happen
@@EXAMPLE0@@You won't get Kieran to agree - not in a million years!
@@PHRASE4@@not once
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are surprised or annoyed because someone never did something, although they often had the opportunity to do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@After all the help I've given her, she's never said thank you - not once!
@@EXAMPLE1@@My father hasn't once come here to see us, even though he lives quite nearby.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@not once have I/did they etc
@@GLOSS@@used for emphasis
@@EXAMPLE0@@Not once did she think of giving up, despite all the problems involved.
@@PHRASE5@@never for a moment/not for a moment
@@DEFINE@@if you say you never for a moment thought something, you are emphasizing that this idea never came into your mind
@@EXAMPLE0@@I always knew that I would be famous one day. I never for a moment doubted it at all.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Did you ever suspect that he was cheating on you?" "No, not for one moment."
@@THESPROPFORM0@@never for a moment have I/did they etc
@@GLOSS@@used for emphasis
@@EXAMPLE0@@Never for a moment did it enter my mind that something was wrong.
@@PHRASE6@@at no time
@@DEFINE@@never in the past
@@THESPROPFORM0@@at no time have I/did they etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@At no time did anyone suggest that the drug was dangerous.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Despite what I'd been told about the local people's attitude to strangers, at no time did I encounter any rudeness.
@@PHRASE7@@have never been known to do something
@@DEFINE@@you say that someone or something has never been known to do something when you mean that this has never happened before, so it is strange if it happens now
@@EXAMPLE0@@We were very worried -- Peter had never been known to disappear from home before.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Killer whales have never been known to attack humans without the provocation of a bullet or harpoon.

ways of saying no to a question, request, or suggestion
@@PHRASE0@@no
@@DEFINE@@use this when someone asks you a question or makes a request or suggestion
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Are you Italian?" "No, I'm Spanish."
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Shall I help you?" "No, no -- I can do it on my own, thanks."
@@THESPROPFORM0@@the answer's no
@@EXAMPLE0@@If she asks to borrow any more money, the answer's no!
@@PHRASE1@@not at all
@@DEFINE@@use this when what someone has suggested is not at all true, or when saying you do not mind at all if someone does something
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Your boys are keen on sport, aren't they?" "Not at all - just the opposite in fact."
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Is my radio bothering you?" "Not at all -- I'm quite enjoying it."
@@EXAMPLE2@@"I'd like to be on my own for a while. Do you mind?" "Not at all," she said kindly.
@@PHRASE2@@I'm afraid not
@@DEFINE@@use this when saying that you are sorry that you cannot do something that someone has asked you to do, do not have something someone has asked you for etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Are you coming to the barbecue tomorrow?" "No, I'm afraid not. I've promised to go and see my Mum."
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Have you got change for £20?" "No, I'm afraid not."
@@PHRASE3@@of course not
@@DEFINE@@use this to say no very strongly, when you think what someone has suggested or asked is clearly unlikely or stupid
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Are you serious about Sam?" "Of course not, we're just good friends."
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Don't tell anyone else, will you?" "Of course not."
@@PHRASE4@@not really
@@DEFINE@@use this when someone asks if you want to do something, if you like something etc, and although you say no you do not have very strong feelings about it
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Do you want to come to the movie with us?" "Not really. I think I'll just stay in and read."
@@EXAMPLE1@@"But you quite enjoy your job, don't you?" "Not really, no. I feel I could do with a change."
@@PHRASE5@@certainly not
@@DEFINE@@use this especially when forbidding someone to do something or when you are annoyed or shocked that they have suggested something
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Can I have some wine?" "Certainly not -- you're far too young!"
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Are you thinking of resigning?" "Certainly not."
@@PHRASE6@@no way
@@DEFINE@@use this when you are saying very strongly that you refuse to do something or when you are sure that something cannot possibly be true
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm not going to work late on Friday night! No way!
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Do you think we can make the trip in two hours?" "No way! It'll take more like four."
@@EXAMPLE2@@I don't believe he stole the money -- no way!
@@PHRASE7@@you must be joking/kidding
@@DEFINE@@use this when you think that what someone has asked or suggested seems stupid or dangerous and you would definitely not consider doing it
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Want a ride on the back of my motorcycle?" "You must be kidding."
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Are you going out with Jake?" "You must be joking! I wouldn't go out with him if he was the last person on earth."

@@THESPROPFORM0@@debt of
@@EXAMPLE0@@The government now has debts of $2.5 billion.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@pay off/repay a debt
@@GLOSS@@pay all the money that you owe
@@EXAMPLE0@@It took us three years to pay off all our debts.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@write off a debt
@@GLOSS@@agree that it will not and does not need to be repaid
@@EXAMPLE0@@He protected less profitable state farms by writing off their debts.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@foreign debt
@@GLOSS@@money owed by foreign countries
@@EXAMPLE0@@To pay the interest on our foreign debt, we will have to import less.
@@THESPROPFORM4@@a bad debt
@@GLOSS@@a debt that will never be repaid
@@EXAMPLE0@@Lenders must try and protect themselves against bad debts.
@@PHRASE1@@overdraft
@@DEFINE@@an amount of money that you owe to your bank when you have spent more money that you had in your bank account
@@EXAMPLE0@@I've already got an enormous overdraft.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@a £100/$1500 etc overdraft
@@EXAMPLE0@@When he left college, he had a $3000 overdraft.
@@PHRASE2@@liabilities
@@DEFINE@@the debts that a company, government etc is legally responsible to pay - used especially in legal and business contexts
@@EXAMPLE0@@The chart shows the movements in the company's liabilities and assets during a particular trading period.
@@EXAMPLE1@@US external net liabilities rose throughout the 1980s.
@@PHRASE3@@borrowings
@@DEFINE@@the total amount of money that a company has borrowed and owes - used in business contexts
@@EXAMPLE0@@Borrowings at the end of the year amounted to nearly $27 million.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The company was now so large it could increase its borrowings to almost any figure it chose.
@@PHRASE4@@IOU
@@DEFINE@@a note that you write saying that you owe someone money or that you will pay for something later - often used by journalists as an informal word for a legal agreement in which one business or organization owes another money
@@EXAMPLE0@@Essentially, a bond is an IOU.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@give somebody an IOU
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was anger among farmers, who were being given IOUs instead of cash for their crops.

@@PHRASE0@@dilemma
@@DEFINE@@a situation in which it is very difficult to decide what to do, because all the choices seem equally good or equally bad

@@PHRASE1@@catch-22
@@DEFINE@@a situation in which you cannot do one thing until you do another thing, but you cannot do that thing until you do the first thing, with the result that you can do neither
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's catch-22 -- she can't get a job unless she has experience, and she can't get experience unless she has a job.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@a catch-22 situation
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's a catch-22 situation: The project won't receive government money until it is shown to be successful, but it cannot be successful without adequate funds.
@@PHRASE2@@no-win situation

@@EXAMPLE0@@It's a no-win situation -- if I tell him, he'll be upset, but if I don't he'll be mad at me for not telling him.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Hospitals are in a no-win situation, since protecting patients' privacy may conflict with protecting the health of doctors, nurses, and other hospital workers.
@@PHRASE3@@a chicken-and-egg problem/situation/dilemma
@@DEFINE@@a difficult situation in which you do not know which of two things was the cause of the other and which was the result, because neither could exist if the other did not
@@EXAMPLE0@@We all hate lawyers, but they're in business because so many people sue each other: it's a classic chicken-and-egg situation.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The airport faces a chicken-and-egg dilemma: Airlines won't add more flights unless there is more demand, and there won't be more demand until there are more flights.
@@PHRASE4@@vicious circle

@@EXAMPLE0@@Many people who diet put on even more weight when they stop, creating a vicious circle.
@@EXAMPLE1@@More and more teenagers are caught in a vicious circle of drug addiction and crime.

@@EXAMPLE0@@The contract contains a guarantee that the building will be finished within 6 months.
@@EXAMPLE1@@After the Second World War, Belgium wanted a guarantee that it would not be invaded again.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@under guarantee
@@GLOSS@@within the period when a company promises to repair a product free of charge if something goes wrong
@@EXAMPLE0@@Is the camera still under guarantee?

@@PHRASE0@@I promise

@@EXAMPLE0@@I won't go. I promise I won't go.
@@PHRASE1@@I give you my word/you have my word
@@DEFINE@@say this when you want to make a very serious and sincere promise
@@EXAMPLE0@@You won't regret this - I give you my word.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@I give you my word/you have my word (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@I give you my word that I'll do everything I can.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Do I have your word, Mr Bigelow, that this problem will be corrected?
@@PHRASE2@@cross my heart
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are making a promise to someone you know well - used especially by children
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Do you promise?" "Cross my heart."
@@PHRASE3@@I swear
@@DEFINE@@say this when you are making a very firm promise, that you will never break. I swear is used in court
@@EXAMPLE0@@I swear that the evidence I give will be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

to show that something is correct or true
@@PHRASE0@@prove
@@DEFINE@@to show that something is definitely true, by providing facts or information
@@EXAMPLE0@@We're sure Jason took the money, but we can't prove it.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Until there is evidence to prove any of these claims, we cannot pass judgement.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@prove that
@@EXAMPLE0@@Can you prove that you were at home at the time of the attack?
@@EXAMPLE1@@He wanted to prove that he was just as clever as his sister.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@prove somebody wrong/innocent/guilty
@@EXAMPLE0@@I would love to prove him wrong.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@prove something to somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm telling the truth, and I can prove it to you.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@prove where/how etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't trust anyone who turns up at your door, unless they can prove who they are.
@@THESPROPFORM4@@prove something conclusively/beyond doubt
@@EXAMPLE0@@His guilt has never been conclusively proven.
@@PHRASE1@@show
@@DEFINE@@if facts or actions show that something is true, they prove that it is true
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Prime Minister's comments show his ignorance of people's feelings.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@show (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Research shows that smiling increases the levels of hormones that promote good health.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@show where/how etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@These figures show how serious the company's problems are.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@show something/somebody to be something
@@EXAMPLE0@@A scientific theory is only 'true' until someone shows it to be false or inaccurate.
@@PHRASE2@@demonstrate
@@DEFINE@@to do something or provide information which makes it very clear to people that something is true
@@EXAMPLE0@@The studies demonstrate a clear link between smoking and heart disease.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@demonstrate (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@The President is anxious to demonstrate that he has a strong foreign policy.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@demonstrate where/how etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Try to round off your answer by demonstrating how your old job has prepared you to do the job you are applying for.
@@PHRASE3@@confirm
@@DEFINE@@if a piece of new information confirms an idea or belief that people already have, it shows that it is definitely true
@@EXAMPLE0@@Police have found new evidence that confirms his story.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@confirm that
@@EXAMPLE0@@The discovery seems to confirm that people lived here over 10,000 years ago.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@confirm somebody's worst fears
@@GLOSS@@prove that something is as bad as someone thought it was
@@EXAMPLE0@@In July his worst fears were confirmed: he had cancer.
@@PHRASE4@@support
@@THESPROPFORM0@@support a theory/claim/notion/ view etc
@@DEFINE@@to help to prove that a belief, idea etc is probably true
@@EXAMPLE0@@Do you have any evidence to support these claims?
@@EXAMPLE1@@The notion that women are worse drivers than men is simply not supported by the facts.
@@EXAMPLE2@@For twenty-five years he painstakingly amassed evidence to support his hypothesis.
@@PHRASE5@@back up
@@DEFINE@@to provide additional information to help prove that a statement, belief, or explanation is correct
@@THESPROPFORM0@@back up something
@@EXAMPLE0@@When you write a history essay, you should back up all your points with facts.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@back something/it/them up
@@EXAMPLE0@@They claim they can give us the best deal, but can they back this up with guarantees?
@@EXAMPLE1@@Wright was accused of pretending to be injured, and this was backed up by video evidence.
@@PHRASE6@@bear out
@@DEFINE@@if facts or information bear out a claim or opinion, they support it and help to prove that it is probably true
@@THESPROPFORM0@@bear out something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most of the available evidence bears out the view that students learn better in small classes than in large classes.
@@EXAMPLE1@@My warnings about Jean-Paul were later borne out by his dishonesty.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@bear somebody out
@@GLOSS@@prove what someone has said is true
@@EXAMPLE0@@Last summer I predicted an increase in terrorist violence, and recent events have borne me out.
@@PHRASE7@@substantiate
@@DEFINE@@to provide additional information that helps to prove that a statement is correct, especially if the statement is difficult to believe
@@THESPROPFORM0@@substantiate a claim/an allegation
@@EXAMPLE0@@The authorities claimed they were conspiring to overthrow the government, but offered no evidence to substantiate these claims.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Allegations made by prisoners are usually only considered when substantiated by the evidence of a prison officer.
@@PHRASE8@@validate
@@DEFINE@@to prove that information or results are correct by using scientific tests or very careful checking - used in scientific or technical contexts
@@EXAMPLE0@@All the information used in this report has been validated by an independent panel of experts.
@@EXAMPLE1@@This is an interesting hypothesis, but all attempts to validate it have so far failed.
@@PHRASE9@@corroborate
@@DEFINE@@to provide additional information which supports or agrees with something that most people already accept as true - used in scientific and legal contexts
@@EXAMPLE0@@Levine claims that a third car was involved in the accident and witnesses have corroborated this.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Professor Carling's findings have been corroborated by more recent research.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@corroborate a story
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was no one to corroborate her story about the disturbance in the lounge.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@corroborating evidence
@@EXAMPLE0@@No doctor would order surgery on the basis of a single test result, without corroborating clinical evidence.
to prove that something is wrong, untrue, or does not exist
@@PHRASE0@@disprove

@@EXAMPLE1@@The existence of God is a question of faith, and therefore impossible to prove or disprove.

@@DEFINE@@something that is pointless has no purpose and makes you angry or sad
@@EXAMPLE0@@a film full of pointless violence
@@EXAMPLE1@@Never give your students pointless exercises to do -- always provide interesting, meaningful tasks.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be pointless to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is pointless to argue about who is more to blame.
@@PHRASE1@@aimless
@@DEFINE@@not having any purpose or plan and therefore boring or sad
@@EXAMPLE0@@The novel seems aimless, and the characters are stereotypes.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She changed from an aimless, pregnant teenager into a purposeful young woman.
@@PHRASE2@@senseless
@@DEFINE@@a crime or something bad that is senseless seems to have no meaning or purpose and you cannot understand why someone would do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was a senseless and cruel murder.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Smashing up trains is such a senseless form of vandalism.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The suicide was described as a senseless waste of a young woman's life.
@@PHRASE3@@meaningless
@@DEFINE@@without any meaning or purpose and therefore boring, sad, or having no effect
@@EXAMPLE0@@a meaningless campaign pledge
@@EXAMPLE1@@So many of us spend our lives doing meaningless work in huge faceless companies.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Several companies dismissed the ruling as "meaningless," saying it would have no effect on their operations.
@@PHRASE4@@lack direction
@@VARIANT@@lack of direction
@@DEFINE@@if something lacks direction or has a lack of direction , it does not have a clear purpose and is not well organized
@@EXAMPLE0@@It could have been a good film, but I felt it lacked direction.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He quit over the company's lack of direction.

when you are ready to do something
@@PHRASE0@@ready
@@DEFINE@@if you are ready for something, you have done everything that needs to be done in order to prepare for it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Are you ready? The taxi's here.
@@EXAMPLE1@@When everyone is ready, I'll give the signal to start.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@ready for
@@EXAMPLE0@@I don't feel that I'm ready for the test yet.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@ready to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Everything is packed and we're ready to leave.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@get ready
@@GLOSS@@prepare yourself to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@That's settled then. I'll go and get ready.
@@EXAMPLE1@@My sister always spends hours getting ready to go out.
@@EXAMPLE2@@It was soon time for the actors to get ready for the evening performance.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@ready and waiting
@@EXAMPLE0@@The wedding guests were all ready and waiting long before the bride arrived.
@@THESPROPFORM4@@ready when you are
@@GLOSS@@I am ready to do something as soon as you are
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Shall we go then?" "Yes, ready when you are."
@@PHRASE1@@prepared
@@DEFINE@@ready to deal with a situation, because you were expecting it or because you have made careful preparations
@@THESPROPFORM0@@prepared for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The police were prepared for trouble.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I was not prepared for all the questions they asked.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@well prepared
@@EXAMPLE0@@The team was well prepared and focussed on the issues.
@@PHRASE2@@be ready to go
@@DEFINE@@to be ready and eager to start doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@On Christmas Day, the kids are always up and ready to go at 6 o'clock.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If everyone's ready to go, let's get started.
@@PHRASE3@@be all set
@@DEFINE@@to be ready to start doing something that you have planned to do and want to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@Dad got on his bike. "Are you all set?" he called.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be all set for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The team are all set for another comfortable victory.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@be all set to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@We were all set to start the barbecue when it started to rain.
@@PHRASE4@@be geared up
@@DEFINE@@if an organization or group of people are geared up for something that is going to happen, they have made careful plans so that they can deal with it as soon as it happens
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be geared up for
@@EXAMPLE0@@There are clear signs that the governor is geared up for a second attempt at the White House.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@be geared up to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Companies that survive are the ones that are geared up to meet the demands of the future.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@get geared up
@@EXAMPLE0@@The airport was getting geared up to deal with a heavier schedule of flights.
@@PHRASE5@@in readiness
@@DEFINE@@if you do something in readiness for something that you expect will happen, you do it so that you will be ready
@@EXAMPLE0@@As the conflict grew worse, troops waited in readiness at the borders.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@in readiness for
@@EXAMPLE0@@A new stage and seating area has been built in readiness for tonight's sell-out performance.
@@PHRASE6@@do something when you are good and ready
@@DEFINE@@used to tell someone who is impatient for you to do something that you will not do it until your are ready
@@EXAMPLE0@@Dad says he'll come when he's good and ready.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Leave me alone! I'll tell her when I'm good and ready.
@@PHRASE7@@be good to go
@@DEFINE@@to have completed all the necessary preparations and be ready to start doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@We just need to get you a pair of skis and you're good to go.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Do you have all the hiking gear?" "Yeah, I'm good to go."
@@PHRASE8@@be ripe for
@@DEFINE@@to be in a suitable condition to be ready for something, especially a positive change
@@EXAMPLE0@@Economists regard the region as being ripe for development.
@@EXAMPLE1@@After the divorce I was thoroughly fed up and ripe for a new start, so I agreed to take the job.
ready to be used or eaten
@@PHRASE0@@ready
@@DEFINE@@if something is ready , you can use it or eat it immediately
@@EXAMPLE0@@Lunch is ready!
@@EXAMPLE1@@When the pasta's ready, add the sauce.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I'm sorry, your car isn't ready yet, sir.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@ready to eat/collect/use etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Your suit will be ready to pick up on Wednesday.
@@EXAMPLE1@@In a year's time, the wine will be ready to drink.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I tend to buy a lot of meals that are ready to eat (=they have already been cooked ).
@@THESPROPFORM1@@ready for
@@EXAMPLE0@@Is everything ready for the party?
@@THESPROPFORM2@@get something ready
@@GLOSS@@prepare it
@@EXAMPLE0@@It took several months to get the boat ready for the voyage.
@@PHRASE1@@be in place
@@DEFINE@@if equipment, a system, a rule, or a plan is in place , it is ready to start being used
@@EXAMPLE0@@A new PA system should be in place in the next three to six months.
@@EXAMPLE1@@When everything is in place, the building work begins, even if it means running two massive projects at the same time.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The uncertain economy is forcing us to accelerate cost-cutting plans that are already in place.
@@PHRASE2@@ripe
@@DEFINE@@ripe fruit is soft, sweet, and ready to eat
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't pick the apples until they're really ripe.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Is this melon ripe enough to eat?
@@PHRASE3@@at the ready
@@DEFINE@@if something is at the ready , it is nearby or in your hands, so that you can use it immediately if something happens and you need it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Several reporters were outside, microphones at the ready.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@have/keep something at the ready
@@EXAMPLE0@@I kept my camera at the ready in case the bird reappeared.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@with something at the ready
@@EXAMPLE0@@Two police officers advanced, with guns at the ready.
@@PHRASE4@@in readiness
@@DEFINE@@ready to be used when something that you are expecting happens
@@EXAMPLE0@@The table was carefully laid in readiness.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@in readiness for
@@EXAMPLE0@@Everything was laid out on the bed, in readiness for the new baby.
ready to take action if it is needed
@@PHRASE0@@be standing by
@@DEFINE@@to be ready to take action or provide something when it is needed
@@EXAMPLE0@@Officers in full riot gear were standing by outside the police station.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A plane was standing by to take the hostages from the airport.
@@PHRASE1@@be on standby
@@DEFINE@@if a group of people, especially soldiers or police are on standby , they are waiting, ready to go somewhere if they are needed when something happens that is expected to happen soon
@@EXAMPLE0@@Extra troops have been brought in, and riot police are on standby.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Bomb squads are on 24-hour standby because of the threats.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be on standby to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@RAF medical crews are on standby to fly out to the war zone.
@@PHRASE2@@be on call
@@DEFINE@@if someone such as a doctor or engineer is on call , they are ready to give advice on the phone or go and help where they are needed, as part of their job
@@EXAMPLE0@@As a doctor, you will be on call regularly at weekends.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There are four physiotherapists on call at the sports injury clinic.
@@PHRASE3@@be on full alert
@@DEFINE@@if soldiers, police officers etc are on full alert , they are completely ready to deal with a dangerous situation
@@EXAMPLE0@@All ships were on full alert.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@put/place something on full alert
@@EXAMPLE0@@By 7 pm the President had placed American military forces on full alert.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@be on full alert for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The police were on full alert for further riots.
when you are not ready to do something
@@PHRASE0@@not ready
@@DEFINE@@if you are not ready for something, you have not done everything that needs to be done in order to prepare for it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Wait a minute! I'm not ready yet.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@not ready for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The coaches felt Stark wasn't ready for major league baseball yet.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@not ready to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I felt that I wasn't ready to make a final decision.
@@PHRASE1@@unprepared
@@DEFINE@@not ready to deal with something because you were not expecting it, and have not thought about it or made plans
@@THESPROPFORM0@@unprepared for
@@EXAMPLE0@@Mexico was unprepared for war.
@@EXAMPLE1@@When I told her the news, I was totally unprepared for her reaction.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@unprepared to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The study showed that 50% of the students were unprepared for work or college.
not ready to eat or use
@@PHRASE0@@not ready
@@DEFINE@@if something is not ready , you cannot use it or eat it immediately
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm afraid dinner's not ready yet.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The blackberries won't be ready for another week or two.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@not ready for
@@EXAMPLE0@@The zero-emission care is not ready for mass production.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@not ready to eat/drink/use etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The paint's not ready to use when you buy it. You have to mix it with water.
@@PHRASE1@@unripe
@@DEFINE@@fruit that is unripe is not soft, sweet, or ready to eat
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't use unripe apples for making cider.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The cherries on the tree were still unripe.
to do something or to happen when someone is not ready
@@PHRASE0@@be caught napping
@@DEFINE@@if you are caught napping by something that happens, you are not expecting it and are not ready to deal with it, although you should expect it and be ready for it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Stock traders who ignore these signs are in danger of being caught napping when a recession hits.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be caught napping by
@@EXAMPLE0@@Nowadays, no company can afford to be caught napping by a technological development.
@@PHRASE1@@catch somebody off guard
@@DEFINE@@to say or do something when someone is not expecting it so that they cannot deal with it as well as they would like to
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Are you married?" Vick asked, catching her off guard.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The Prime Minister admitted to being caught off guard by news of the attack.
@@PHRASE2@@catch somebody with their pants down
@@DEFINE@@to arrive or to do something when someone is not ready, and make them feel stupid or embarrassed
@@EXAMPLE0@@The city got caught with its financial pants down, and the scandal has led to 12 high-level officials losing their jobs.
@@PHRASE3@@catch somebody on the hop
@@DEFINE@@to do something, or to happen, when someone is not expecting it and is not ready to deal with it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The dramatic fall in share prices caught even the experts on the hop.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Many politicians have been caught on the hop by a good interviewer.
@@PHRASE4@@wing it
@@DEFINE@@to try to do something even though you are not ready, especially when you have to pretend you know more about something that you do
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you are asked a question that you're not ready for, it's better to say "I hadn't considered that" than to wing it and get it wrong.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We have to wing it in the first game, but we'll be more prepared for the next one.
not false or artificial
@@PHRASE0@@real
@@DEFINE@@not false or artificial
@@EXAMPLE0@@Is that a real diamond?
@@EXAMPLE1@@Are those flowers real or artificial?
@@EXAMPLE2@@People call him Baz, but his real name is Reginald.
@@PHRASE1@@genuine
@@DEFINE@@real, not just seeming to be real or pretending to be real
@@EXAMPLE0@@For years people thought the picture was a genuine Van Gogh, but in fact it's a fake.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We need a much faster system for dealing with genuine refugees.
@@EXAMPLE2@@If a student has genuine religious objections to a school activity, they do not have to participate.
@@PHRASE2@@authentic
@@DEFINE@@authentic food, music, clothes etc are correct for the place or the period in history that they are supposed to be from
@@EXAMPLE0@@a friendly restaurant offering authentic Greek food
@@EXAMPLE1@@They play music on authentic medieval instruments.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The dancers wore authentic Native American designs.
@@PHRASE3@@bona fide
@@DEFINE@@people or things that are bona fide are really what they say they are, especially when this can be checked by looking at official records, personal papers etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@This club is only open to bona fide members.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We have to check that he holds a bona fide qualification.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The company can only reimburse bona fide business-related expenses.
@@PHRASE4@@natural
@@DEFINE@@not artificial and no made by people
@@EXAMPLE0@@I prefer natural fibres such as wool and cotton.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His natural hair color is brown.
@@EXAMPLE2@@We only use natural products.
@@PHRASE5@@the real thing
@@DEFINE@@something that is the thing it is meant to be, and not a cheaper or lower quality thing
@@EXAMPLE0@@Recorded music will never be as good as listening to the real thing.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'd seen pictures of the painting, but it was very different seeing the real thing.
@@PHRASE6@@the genuine article
@@DEFINE@@something such as a car, painting, or piece of furniture or clothing, that really is made, produced, or designed by a famous and admired person or company
@@EXAMPLE0@@He owns a 1947 Ferrari -- the genuine article.
@@EXAMPLE1@@With paintings it is sometimes difficult to distinguish the genuine article from a good reproduction.
@@PHRASE7@@the real McCoy
@@DEFINE@@something that is real, and not a cheaper, lower quality product
@@EXAMPLE0@@The moment I smelled the cigar, I knew it was the real McCoy.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The dress had a designer label, but I couldn't tell if it was the real McCoy or a cheap imitation.

@@PHRASE0@@real

@@EXAMPLE0@@Jane's been a real friend to me over the years.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She's a real tomboy!
@@EXAMPLE2@@What the country needs now is a real leader.

@@DEFINE@@someone who is a true friend, believer etc is not just pretending to be one and has all of the qualities that a friend, believer etc is supposed to have

@@EXAMPLE1@@Being a true Red Sox fan, he never missed a game.

@@DEFINE@@real and not something similar which is not as good
