@@EXAMPLE1@@"Where's Pam going?" "I don't know. She didn't say."
@@EXAMPLE2@@It says in today's paper that gas prices are going up again.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@say (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@James wrote to the bank and said we needed a loan.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Did Peter say that he would be late?
@@THESPROPFORM1@@say what/where/why etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Did they say how long the operation would take?
@@THESPROPFORM2@@say hello/sorry/no etc (to somebody)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Lauren came over to say goodbye to us.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I asked Dad if he'd lend me some money, but he said no.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@say something to somebody
@@EXAMPLE0@@What did you say to her?
@@THESPROPFORM4@@something/anything to say
@@EXAMPLE0@@I couldn't think of anything to say.
@@THESPROPFORM5@@say so
@@EXAMPLE0@@If there's anything you're not happy about, please say so.
@@PHRASE1@@pronounce
@@DEFINE@@to make the sound of a word or a part of a word in a particular way - use this also to ask or say what is the correct way to say something
@@EXAMPLE0@@How do you pronounce your name?
@@EXAMPLE1@@Some students find it difficult to pronounce the word "the".
@@EXAMPLE2@@Words like 'chicken' and 'cheese' were once pronounced with a 'k'.
@@PHRASE2@@mention
@@DEFINE@@to talk about someone or something, but without giving details or saying very much about them
@@EXAMPLE0@@He mentioned something about a party, but he didn't say when it was.
@@EXAMPLE1@@When I mentioned her name, he looked embarrassed.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@mention (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@I forgot to mention that I won't be in tomorrow.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@mention where/when/who etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Did he mention where he went to school?
@@THESPROPFORM2@@it is worth mentioning that
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is worth mentioning that young children are particularly vulnerable to accidents in the home.
@@PHRASE3@@point out
@@DEFINE@@to tell someone something that they had not noticed or had not thought about
@@EXAMPLE0@@As Sharon pointed out, the story was rather hard to believe.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@point out something
@@EXAMPLE0@@He pointed out the dangers of setting off without the right equipment.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@point out (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's worth pointing out that very few people ever die of this disease.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@point something out
@@EXAMPLE0@@He never used to notice when people took advantage of him, so I started pointing it out.
@@PHRASE4@@express
@@DEFINE@@to let someone know your feelings, by putting them into words
@@EXAMPLE0@@Ollie found it hard to express his feelings about the war.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Parents have expressed concern about the amount of violence in some children's shows.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@express yourself
@@GLOSS@@make people understand what you are thinking or feeling
@@EXAMPLE0@@Young children often find it difficult to express themselves in words.
@@PHRASE5@@put it
@@DEFINE@@to express an idea in a particular way, choosing your words carefully to explain what you mean simply or clearly
@@THESPROPFORM0@@put it another way
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you don't understand, I'll try and put it another way.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@to put it bluntly/briefly/simply etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Their performance was, to put it bluntly, atrocious.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@put it this way
@@GLOSS@@use this when you are trying to say something in the clearest possible way
@@EXAMPLE0@@Put it this way: if we don't make a profit, we're out of a job.
@@PHRASE6@@comment
@@DEFINE@@to say what your opinion is about someone or something that you have seen, heard, or read about
@@EXAMPLE0@@"He only wears those clothes to prove that he's rich," commented Harold.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Journalists asked General Curran how the campaign was going, but he refused to comment.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@comment on/upon
@@EXAMPLE0@@The prime minister was asked to comment on the crisis.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@comment that
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some critics have commented that the film lacks originality.
@@PHRASE7@@remark
@@DEFINE@@to say what you have noticed about a particular person, situation etc or to express an opinion about them
@@EXAMPLE0@@"There's a strange smell in here," she remarked.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@remark that
@@EXAMPLE0@@Kate remarked that it was amazing how much her kids knew about science.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@remark on
@@GLOSS@@notice something and then say something about it
@@EXAMPLE0@@A lot of our customers remark on the quality of our workmanship.
@@PHRASE8@@add
@@DEFINE@@to say something more, after what has already been said or written
@@EXAMPLE0@@Is there anything you'd like to add, Peter?
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Finally", she added, "I would like to thank my family for their support".
@@THESPROPFORM0@@add that
@@EXAMPLE0@@I should add that I do not agree with Doctor Mitchell.
to say something publicly or officially
@@PHRASE0@@say
@@DEFINE@@to say something publicly or officially, using spoken or written words
@@THESPROPFORM0@@say (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@The President said he had no intention of resigning.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The rules say that sports shoes must be worn in the gym at all times.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@say what/how/who etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The police are refusing to say where Davies is being held.
@@PHRASE1@@announce
@@DEFINE@@to officially tell people what has happened or what will happen, in a written or spoken public statement
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Company announced profits of about $400 million.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@announce (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Prime Minister has just announced there is to be a General Election next month.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@announce your engagement
@@GLOSS@@to officially tell people that you are going to get married
@@EXAMPLE0@@They announced their engagement last year, but have still not set a date for their wedding.
@@PHRASE2@@state
@@DEFINE@@to say something publicly or officially, especially in clear, definite language
@@EXAMPLE0@@The government needs to clearly state its policy on possible military action.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@state that
@@EXAMPLE0@@The law states that you are innocent until proved guilty.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Justice Cohen stated clearly that no further action would be taken.
@@PHRASE3@@declare
@@DEFINE@@to officially state that a particular situation exists or a person or thing is in a particular condition
@@THESPROPFORM0@@declare somebody insane/unfit/a traitor etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@In the last century, mothers of illegitimate babies could be declared insane.
@@EXAMPLE1@@After nearly forty years' membership, the Communist party declared him a traitor.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@declare (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Finally, the doctor declared that the man was dead.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@declare war/an amnesty/a state of emergency
@@EXAMPLE0@@In 1941 the US declared war on the Axis powers.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A state of emergency has been declared in Bangladesh.
@@PHRASE4@@make/issue a statement
@@DEFINE@@to say or write something publicly in order to tell people what you intend to do, what your opinion is etc - use this especially about politicians, business leaders, and other people in authority
@@EXAMPLE0@@The party's environment spokesman intends to make a statement either today or tomorrow.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The president's press corps issued this statement today.
@@PHRASE5@@lay down
@@DEFINE@@to officially state the rules that say what is allowed in a particular situation
@@THESPROPFORM0@@lay down something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The new law lays down strict rules about the way guns may be bought and sold.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@lay down that
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is laid down in the club rules that guests are not allowed in unless they are accompanied by a club member.
@@PHRASE6@@be worded
@@DEFINE@@if something such as an official statement or document is worded in a particular way, the speaker or writer has deliberately chosen their words in that way to get a particular effect
@@EXAMPLE0@@His speech to the police officers about racial violence had to be very carefully worded.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The Defence Secretary made a public statement about the crisis, but it was worded in such a way as to give very little information.
to say that something is definitely true
@@PHRASE0@@claim
@@DEFINE@@to say that something is true, even though it has not been proved and people may not believe it
@@THESPROPFORM0@@claim (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Martin claimed that he was with friends at the time of his wife's murder.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She claimed she was fired from her job for being pregnant.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@claim to be something
@@EXAMPLE0@@She claims to be a descendent of Charles Dickens.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@claim to have done something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Doctors claim to have discovered a cure for the disease.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@claim responsibility/credit etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@No one has yet claimed responsibility for planting the bomb.
@@PHRASE1@@maintain
@@DEFINE@@to repeatedly say that something is true, especially when other people do not believe you
@@THESPROPFORM0@@maintain (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@My mother always maintains that I learned to talk at six months.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The authors of "Superdiet' maintain you can lose pounds without eating less.
@@PHRASE2@@assert
@@DEFINE@@to state very firmly that something is true
@@THESPROPFORM0@@assert (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Professor Sykes has asserted that the skeleton, which was said to be man's first ancestor, is in fact a fake.
@@EXAMPLE1@@After 1947, Nehru began to assert his supremacy and sack party chiefs who opposed him.
@@EXAMPLE2@@If women are to have equal opportunity, they must loudly assert their ability to do all traditional "male' jobs.
@@PHRASE3@@confirm
@@DEFINE@@if you confirm something that other people have already said is true, you say publicly that it is definitely true
@@EXAMPLE0@@Mr Eastwood refused to confirm or deny the rumour.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@confirm (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Police have confirmed that they are questioning a woman about the disappearance of baby Kelly Truman.
@@PHRASE4@@testify
@@DEFINE@@to make a formal statement of what is true, especially in a court of law
@@EXAMPLE0@@Police had to guard him in hospital until he was well enough to testify.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@testify that
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm prepared to testify in court that I was in Carolyn's apartment that night.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@testify against somebody
@@GLOSS@@say something intended to prove someone is guilty
@@EXAMPLE0@@The witness who had testified against him withdrew her allegation.
@@PHRASE5@@swear
@@DEFINE@@to say very firmly that what you have said is the truth
@@THESPROPFORM0@@swear (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was a mistake -- she swears that she didn't mean to do it.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The plane flew so low that Geoff swears he saw one wing touch the top of a tree.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@swear blind (that)
@@GLOSS@@used for emphasizing that someone is telling the truth
@@EXAMPLE0@@She swears blind that she never met the man.
@@PHRASE6@@certify
@@DEFINE@@if someone such as a doctor or another professional person certifies something, they officially say that it is true
@@THESPROPFORM0@@certify (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Doctors have certified that the suspect was in a lot of pain at the time of the incident.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@certify somebody fit/dead/insane etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The doctor certified me unfit to go to work for the next month.
@@PHRASE7@@insist
@@DEFINE@@to say and repeat that something is true, especially when a lot of people think that it might not be true
@@THESPROPFORM0@@insist (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Though there are no other witnesses, she insists she saw a man in the yard that night.
@@EXAMPLE1@@UFO spotters will always insist that their data is correct.
@@PHRASE8@@protest
@@DEFINE@@to firmly and repeatedly state that you have not done something wrong
@@THESPROPFORM0@@protest (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Marge protested that she had never had any kind of affair with Lawrence.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@protest your innocence
@@GLOSS@@say repeatedly that you did not commit a crime
@@EXAMPLE0@@Throughout the trial Reilly protested his innocence.
@@PHRASE9@@deny
@@DEFINE@@to say that you have not done something bad that people say you have done
@@EXAMPLE0@@Bowlam denied all charges of selling drugs to children.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@deny (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@The singer denies that he copied the tune from an old Beatles song.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@deny doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Did he actually deny meeting Jenny that night?
@@THESPROPFORM2@@flatly/categorically deny
@@GLOSS@@deny very strongly
@@EXAMPLE0@@The foreman had not informed us that the paraffin might explode. In fact he had categorically denied there was any danger.
to say clearly what your opinion is
@@PHRASE0@@say what you think
@@EXAMPLE0@@She usually says what she thinks even if it offends her political colleagues.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@say what you think about/of
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'll make a few suggestions, and the rest of you can say what you think about them.

to say that something you previously said was true is not true

@@DEFINE@@if you say something in a roundabout way , you say it in an indirect way, especially to avoid offending or embarrassing someone

@@EXAMPLE1@@She adjusted the mirror to avoid being blinded by the glare.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The floodlight had blinded him and he couldn't see to reload his gun.
@@PHRASE1@@dazzle
@@DEFINE@@if a very bright light dazzles you, it is so strong that you cannot see anything else, especially when this may have dangerous results
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you are dazzled by oncoming traffic, slow down and look for a place to stop.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She slowly opened her eyes, only to be dazzled by a strong shaft of sunlight.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I moved aside so that the light no longer dazzled me.
unable to see
@@PHRASE0@@blind
@@DEFINE@@someone who is blind cannot see at all

@@EXAMPLE2@@There's a blind man who sells popcorn on the corner.

@@GLOSS@@become blind
@@EXAMPLE0@@Without treatment, the patient will go blind.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@the blind
@@GLOSS@@people who are blind
@@EXAMPLE0@@a radio programme specially for the blind
@@PHRASE1@@can't see
@@DEFINE@@if you can't see , you are unable to see things, either because there is something wrong with your sight, or because something is preventing you seeing clearly
@@EXAMPLE0@@He makes fun of me because I can't see that well.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It was pitch black and I couldn't see.
@@EXAMPLE2@@You can't see from here, but they're out there.
@@EXAMPLE3@@That was the morning I got up, and I couldn't see.

@@DEFINE@@if something is short , there is only a small length or distance from one end of it to the other
@@EXAMPLE0@@These curtains are much too short.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She has short curly hair and wears glasses.
@@EXAMPLE2@@a short-sleeved T-shirt
@@EXAMPLE3@@You look different - your hair's shorter.
@@EXAMPLE4@@The hotel is just a short distance from the station.
@@EXAMPLE5@@Chris went for a short walk to clear his head.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@short cut
@@GLOSS@@a shorter, and therefore quicker, way of getting to a place
@@EXAMPLE0@@Sandy took a short cut home.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Do you know any short cuts to the hospital?
@@PHRASE1@@stubby/stumpy
@@DEFINE@@body parts that are stubby or stumpy are short and thick
@@EXAMPLE0@@Pheasants have short stubby wings which enable them to fly very fast and low.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a fat little boy with stumpy legs
when something you say or write is short
@@PHRASE0@@short
@@DEFINE@@a short piece of writing or speech does not have many pages or words
@@EXAMPLE0@@Graham made a short speech of thanks after the ceremony.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a book of short stories
@@EXAMPLE2@@The chapters are really short, so I read a couple every night.
@@EXAMPLE3@@We had a short pep talk from the coach before the game.
@@EXAMPLE4@@Please write a short paragraph explaining your reasons for applying to this college.
@@PHRASE1@@brief
@@DEFINE@@a brief note, description, remark etc uses very few words and gives very few details
@@EXAMPLE0@@The book begins with a brief outline of the history of modern China.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We just have to write a very brief piece on what we did in the vacation.
@@EXAMPLE2@@There was a brief note with the flowers.
@@PHRASE2@@concise
@@DEFINE@@short and clear, and with no unnecessary words
@@EXAMPLE0@@Saussure expressed his arguments in a concise and logical way.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Sergeant Hanks gave us concise, sensible instructions.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@clear and concise
@@EXAMPLE0@@Make sure that your answers are as clear and concise as possible.
@@PHRASE3@@succinct
@@DEFINE@@expressing something well but with very few words
@@EXAMPLE0@@The new labelling is more succinct and advises consumers simply that oat bran may help prevent heart disease.
to make something shorter
@@PHRASE0@@shorten
@@DEFINE@@to make something shorter, especially by removing part of it
@@EXAMPLE0@@I heard she had an operation to shorten her nose.
@@EXAMPLE1@@You can improve your writing just by shortening some of these long sentences.
@@EXAMPLE2@@It costs £12 to get trousers shortened.
@@EXAMPLE3@@This essay's still too long, I'll have to shorten it by a couple of thousand words.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@shorten something to something
@@EXAMPLE0@@His name's Lawrence, but it's usually shortened to Larry.
@@PHRASE1@@make something shorter
@@DEFINE@@to make something shorter, especially by removing part of it
@@EXAMPLE0@@You could make your speech shorter by taking out all the quotations.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@make something one metre/two centimetres etc shorter
@@EXAMPLE0@@Engineers have removed a section of the pipeline, making it about a hundred metres shorter.
@@PHRASE2@@cut
@@DEFINE@@to make a film or piece of writing shorter by removing parts from it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Even after it had been cut, the film was still over three hours long.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I had to cut huge chunks out to get this essay to the right length.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@cut something from something
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's so difficult to cut even a couple of scenes from a play without losing some of the story.
@@PHRASE3@@cut down
@@DEFINE@@to make a piece of writing shorter by removing parts of it completely
@@THESPROPFORM0@@cut something down
@@EXAMPLE0@@The introduction's too long. Can you try and cut it down?
@@EXAMPLE1@@Did you have to cut your dissertation down?
@@THESPROPFORM1@@cut down something
@@EXAMPLE0@@They want me to cut down my article so that it'll all fit onto one page.
@@PHRASE4@@condense
@@DEFINE@@to shorten something spoken or written, by not giving as much detail, or by using fewer words to give the same information
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'd like to condense that statement still further.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@condense something into something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Hawkins condensed all his writings into one volume for publication.
@@EXAMPLE1@@How could he condense all he had lived through into a sixty-minute speech?

@@PHRASE0@@shortened
@@THESPROPFORM0@@shortened version (of something)

@@EXAMPLE0@@The following article is an abridged version of a speech given by Porter in May 2000.

when a name or word is a shorter way of saying something
@@PHRASE0@@be short for
@@EXAMPLE0@@VHF is short for Very High Frequency.
@@EXAMPLE1@@'Is "Shelley" short for anything?' 'Yes, my real name's Michelle.'
@@EXAMPLE2@@What's 'ISP' short for?
@@PHRASE1@@stand for
@@DEFINE@@if a letter stands for a name or word, it is the first letter of that name or word
@@EXAMPLE0@@'What does "NAC" stand for?' 'National Aerobics Championships'.
@@EXAMPLE1@@On a US ship, you see 'USS', standing for 'United States Ship'.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The 'F' in 'John F Kennedy' stood for 'Fitzgerald'.
@@PHRASE2@@for short
@@DEFINE@@if you call someone or something a particular name for short , you call them by a name that is a shorter way of saying their real name
@@EXAMPLE0@@Hi, my name's Moses -- Mo for short.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He's actually called Jeremy, but everyone who knows him calls him Jem for short.
@@PHRASE3@@abbreviate
@@DEFINE@@to make a long name or word shorter so that it is easier to say or write
@@EXAMPLE0@@Is it correct to abbreviate 'Avenue', 'Street' and so on when writing an address on an envelope?
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be abbreviated to something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The word "kilogram' is usually abbreviated to "kg'.
@@PHRASE4@@abbreviation
@@DEFINE@@a shorter way of saying a word or the name of something such as an organization or someone's job, especially by using the first letters of words instead of the whole words
@@EXAMPLE0@@Disk Operating Systems are usually known by the abbreviation DOS.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a Dictionary of Acronyms and Abbreviations
@@EXAMPLE2@@I never knew the abbreviation 'GI' stood for 'Government Issue'.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@abbreviation for
@@EXAMPLE0@@BBC is an abbreviation for British Broadcasting Corporation.

when you should do something because it is your duty or is right
@@PHRASE0@@should
@@DEFINE@@if you should do something, it is your duty to do it, or it is the best thing to do because it is right, fair, or honest
@@EXAMPLE0@@I don't feel like working late tonight but I suppose I should.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@should do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I think you should tell her the truth.
@@EXAMPLE1@@You really should go see him while he's in the hospital.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Should we contact Joe's parents and tell them what's happened?
@@THESPROPFORM1@@should not/shouldn't do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@You shouldn't talk to your father like that.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@should have done something
@@GLOSS@@it was the right thing to do, but someone did not do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@They should have given you your money back.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@shouldn't have done something
@@GLOSS@@it was the wrong thing to do, but someone did it
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm sorry. I shouldn't have shouted at you.
@@PHRASE1@@ought to
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that someone should do something because you think that it is right or that it is the best thing to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Do you think we should tell him?" "Well, we ought to really."
@@THESPROPFORM0@@ought to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@You ought to go to church more often.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Do you think we ought to call the police?
@@EXAMPLE2@@The Government ought to spend more on education.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@ought not to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I think animals have rights, and we ought not to use them for experiments.
@@PHRASE2@@had better (do something)
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that you think someone should do something because it would be the correct, polite, or fair thing to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@I had better phone Alan and tell him I'm going to be late.
@@EXAMPLE1@@You'd better apologize to your mother for forgetting her birthday.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@had better not do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@We'd better not tell anyone about this just yet.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@had better
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Do you think we ought to tell Jane about the money?" "Yes, I think we'd better."
@@PHRASE3@@be supposed to (do something)
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that someone should do something because there is a rule that says they should, because they have been told to do it, or because it is part of their job
@@EXAMPLE0@@You're supposed to knock before you come in.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Put that cigarette out! You're not supposed to smoke in here.
@@EXAMPLE2@@What time are we supposed to meet?
@@EXAMPLE3@@I don't know why they're blaming him -- he only did what he was supposed to.
@@PHRASE4@@be expected to do something
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that people think someone should do something because of their position, age etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@In many societies women are expected to stay at home.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The employees are well-paid but they're also expected to work long hours.
@@PHRASE5@@it is somebody's job (to do something)
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that someone is responsible for doing something, because it is officially part of their job, or because they have agreed to do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's my job to check that the equipment is in good working order.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I thought we'd agreed it was Mike's job to send out all the invitations.
@@PHRASE6@@it's up to somebody (to do something)
@@DEFINE@@say this to emphasize that a particular person is responsible for doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's up to parents to teach their children the difference between right and wrong.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it's up to somebody
@@GLOSS@@a particular person is responsible for making a decision
@@EXAMPLE0@@I really don't think we should have to work on Saturday but it's not up to me.
@@PHRASE7@@be somebody's duty (to do something)/have a duty (to do something)
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that someone should do something because it is their legal or moral duty
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is the judge's duty to give a fair summary of both sides of the case.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The government has a duty to provide education for every child.

@@DEFINE@@to make your mouth curve upwards, as a sign that you are happy or amused or that you want to be friendly
@@EXAMPLE0@@She smiled and said, "Good morning."
@@EXAMPLE1@@Kathy couldn't help smiling as the children came back into the room.
@@EXAMPLE2@@'Stop worrying, you look very nice,' she smiled reassuringly. (=said with a smile )
@@EXAMPLE3@@My father rarely smiled.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@smile at
@@EXAMPLE0@@The twins turned and smiled at each other, sharing a private joke.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He winked, and she smiled back at him.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@smile broadly
@@GLOSS@@smile with your mouth very wide
@@EXAMPLE0@@She smiled broadly when her name was called.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@make somebody smile
@@EXAMPLE0@@He can make people smile just by walking into a room.
@@PHRASE1@@grin
@@DEFINE@@to give a big happy smile
@@EXAMPLE0@@Grinning shyly, he offered her a drink.
@@EXAMPLE1@@'I've been a complete idiot', grinned Ian. (=said with a grin )
@@THESPROPFORM0@@grin broadly
@@GLOSS@@grin with your mouth very wide
@@EXAMPLE0@@She sat back down again, grinning broadly.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@grin at
@@EXAMPLE0@@She kept grinning at me as if we were old friends.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@grin from ear to ear
@@GLOSS@@to grin a lot because you are very happy
@@EXAMPLE0@@She was holding the baby, and grinning from ear to ear.
@@PHRASE2@@beam
@@DEFINE@@to smile for a long time, especially because you are very pleased about or proud of something or someone
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her parents stood there beaming as she went up to receive the prize.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@beam at
@@EXAMPLE0@@After the song was over, Miss Timms beamed at the class.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@beam with pleasure/pride etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Daddy sat in the first pew, beaming with pride.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Just a short time before, they had been beaming with optimism.
@@PHRASE3@@somebody's face lights up
@@DEFINE@@if someone's face lights up , they suddenly look happy, for example because they have received some good news
@@EXAMPLE0@@He gave her the letter and watched as her face lit up.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The moment she walked into the room, Bob's face lit up.
@@PHRASE4@@break into a smile/grin
@@DEFINE@@to suddenly start smiling
@@EXAMPLE0@@All at once she broke into a smile as she remembered what had happened.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She broke into a grin, and started to run towards me.
@@EXAMPLE2@@"We're going to have a visitor," said her mother, and Anna's face broke into a smile at the thought.
@@PHRASE5@@be all smiles
@@DEFINE@@to be very happy, smile a lot, and be friendly toward other people, especially because a situation is the way you want it
@@EXAMPLE0@@I don't understand it -- he was all smiles this morning and now he won't talk to me.
@@PHRASE6@@force a smile
@@DEFINE@@to try hard to smile when you do not feel happy
@@EXAMPLE0@@"I'm getting married," he said. Somehow I managed to force a smile.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Alice forced a smile, hoping it looked natural.
to smile in an unpleasant way
@@PHRASE0@@smirk
@@DEFINE@@to smile in an unpleasant way, for example because you are pleased about someone else's bad luck or because you know something that they do not know
@@EXAMPLE0@@She sits there smirking as if she's the only one who knows the answer.
@@EXAMPLE1@@'You realise you'll be stuck out here on your own, don't you?' he smirked. (=said with a smirk )
@@THESPROPFORM0@@smirk at
@@EXAMPLE0@@What are you smirking at?
@@PHRASE1@@leer
@@DEFINE@@to smile in a way that is unpleasant or threatening and that shows unwelcome sexual interest in someone
@@EXAMPLE0@@The man with the gold tooth leered and slapped his hand on her knee.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@leer at
@@EXAMPLE0@@My boss was a disgusting man who used to leer at me whenever he passed by my desk.
@@PHRASE2@@sneer
@@DEFINE@@to smile in an unpleasant and offensive way that shows you think someone is stupid or less good than you
@@EXAMPLE0@@As she read the letter, she started to sneer.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Some clients would sneer or smile sarcastically when I showed them my old laptop -- until they saw what it could do.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@sneer at
@@EXAMPLE0@@She'd not forgotten how Gareth had laughed and sneered at them when they'd first tried to be friendly.

@@PHRASE0@@smile
@@DEFINE@@the look on your face when you make your mouth curve upwards to show that you are happy, friendly, amused etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Helga has a lovely smile.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Johnny's broad smile changed slowly to a frown.
@@EXAMPLE2@@'Hi,' said Sophie, with the most radiant smile I have ever seen.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@break into a smile
@@GLOSS@@to suddenly start smiling
@@EXAMPLE0@@She clapped her hands and broke into one of her huge smiles.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@give somebody a smile
@@GLOSS@@smile at them
@@EXAMPLE0@@Barry gave the old lady a warm smile.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@with a smile on your face
@@EXAMPLE0@@He fell asleep with a contented smile on his face.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@have a smile on your face
@@EXAMPLE0@@She's really happy for me; she has a big smile on her face.
@@PHRASE1@@grin
@@DEFINE@@a big happy smile
@@EXAMPLE0@@Her face broke into a delighted grin.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Joel gave her a wicked grin.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The television camera captured his sheepish grin as he stepped from the train.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@give somebody a grin
@@GLOSS@@grin at them
@@EXAMPLE0@@William gave her a friendly grin as he walked past.
@@PHRASE2@@smirk
@@DEFINE@@an unpleasant, satisfied smile, for example when you are pleased about someone else's bad luck or when you think you know something that they do not know
@@EXAMPLE0@@Penny's lips curved in a superior smirk as he rushed from the room.
@@PHRASE3@@leer
@@DEFINE@@an unpleasant or threatening smile, showing an unwelcome sexual interest in someone
@@EXAMPLE0@@He leaned over the girl with a leer and she could smell the whisky on his breath.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The look on my cousin's face changed from its usual cocky leer to one of complete bewilderment.
@@PHRASE4@@sneer
@@DEFINE@@an unpleasant, offensive smile, that shows that you think that someone is stupid or that you are better than them
@@EXAMPLE0@@"And what's your name?" he demanded, his lip curling into a sneer.
to smoke a cigarette, pipe etc
@@PHRASE0@@smoke
@@DEFINE@@to breathe in smoke from a cigarette, pipe etc, either from one cigarette etc or regularly
@@EXAMPLE0@@How old were you when you started smoking?
@@EXAMPLE1@@Do you mind if I smoke?
@@EXAMPLE2@@He sat behind his desk, smoking a fat cigar.
@@EXAMPLE3@@Sue never smoked a cigarette in her life, yet she still got lung cancer.
@@EXAMPLE4@@Anyone who smokes 40 a day can expect to have a lot of health problems.
@@PHRASE1@@smoking
@@DEFINE@@the habit or act of smoking
@@EXAMPLE0@@Some teenage girls think that smoking helps keep their weight down.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Smoking is not allowed in any part of the building.
@@EXAMPLE2@@These days smoking is seen as an anti-social habit.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@passive smoking
@@GLOSS@@when you breathe in the smoke from other people's cigarettes
@@EXAMPLE0@@Roy believed his illness was caused by passive smoking.
@@PHRASE2@@puff on
@@DEFINE@@to take small amounts of smoke into your mouth from a cigarette, cigar, or pipe
@@EXAMPLE0@@He lit a cigar and puffed on it thoughtfully.
@@EXAMPLE1@@They drove in silence, Charlie contentedly puffing on his pipe.
@@PHRASE3@@draw on
@@DEFINE@@to breathe in a lot of smoke from a cigarette, pipe etc in one long breath
@@EXAMPLE0@@She lit her last cigarette, and drew on it slowly.
to smoke a lot
@@PHRASE0@@smoke a lot/smoke heavily
@@EXAMPLE0@@When we were students, we all used to smoke a lot.
@@EXAMPLE1@@This disease is more common in people who smoke heavily.
@@PHRASE1@@smoke like a chimney
@@DEFINE@@to smoke a lot, especially too much
@@EXAMPLE0@@She's only thirteen and she already smokes like a chimney.
@@PHRASE2@@chain-smoke
@@DEFINE@@to smoke one cigarette after another, without a break
@@EXAMPLE0@@James sat silently through her speech, chain-smoking.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Although he chain-smoked cigarettes, his hands were unstained.

@@PHRASE0@@smoker
@@DEFINE@@someone who smokes regularly
@@EXAMPLE0@@The survey shows that most smokers would like to stop smoking.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The average smoker spends about £35 a week on cigarettes.
@@PHRASE1@@heavy smoker
@@DEFINE@@someone who regularly smokes a lot
@@EXAMPLE0@@He had been a heavy smoker all his life and only stopped when his doctor told him to.
@@PHRASE2@@chain-smoker
@@DEFINE@@someone who smokes a lot of cigarettes, and who lights another cigarette immediately after finishing one
@@EXAMPLE0@@I noticed that the thin, nervous man was a chain-smoker.

@@PHRASE0@@don't smoke
@@DEFINE@@if you don't smoke , you never smoke cigarettes, pipes etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@He doesn't smoke or drink.
@@EXAMPLE1@@"Cigarette?" "No thanks, I don't smoke."
@@PHRASE1@@stop smoking
@@VARIANT@@give up smoking
@@VARIANT@@quit smoking
@@VARIANT@@quit
@@DEFINE@@to stop smoking, especially when you make a firm decision that you will not smoke again
@@EXAMPLE0@@Make a list of all the benefits of stopping smoking, for example better health, fresher breath, and more money.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'm trying to give up smoking, but it isn't easy.
@@EXAMPLE2@@I didn't gain any weight when I quit smoking.
@@PHRASE2@@non-smoker
@@VARIANT@@nonsmoker
@@DEFINE@@someone who never smokes
@@EXAMPLE0@@This part of the restaurant is reserved for non-smokers.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Non-smokers get cheaper health insurance.
@@PHRASE3@@no-smoking
@@DEFINE@@use this about rules or signs that say people must not smoke in a particular area
@@EXAMPLE0@@There were big no-smoking signs on all the walls.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The company has a no-smoking policy in all its offices.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Most restaurants and cafes have set aside small no-smoking areas.
@@PHRASE4@@non-smoking
@@DEFINE@@use this about places where you are not allowed to smoke
@@EXAMPLE0@@I asked for a seat in the non-smoking section of the plane.
@@PHRASE5@@smoke-free
@@DEFINE@@a restaurant, room etc that is smoke-free does not have any areas where people can smoke
@@EXAMPLE0@@Most workers prefer a smoke-free environment at the office.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We are calling for all airlines to be smoke-free.

@@EXAMPLE1@@We have received a number of complaints about last night's programme.
@@EXAMPLE2@@A number of her ideas were very good indeed.
@@PHRASE4@@a couple of
@@DEFINE@@a very small number but at least two
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'd just like to ask you a couple of questions before you go.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Those baskets are nice, and they only cost a couple of quid.
@@EXAMPLE2@@There wasn't much mail this morning - just a couple of bills.

@@PHRASE0@@some

@@EXAMPLE0@@Would you like some more wine?

@@GLOSS@@fairly rarely
@@EXAMPLE0@@Every once in a while he disappears for days on end.

@@DEFINE@@if something happens at times , it happens on particular occasions but it is not normal or typical of what usually happens

ways of saying what the result of something is
@@PHRASE0@@so
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that someone does something or something happens as a result of something else
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was nothing on TV, so I decided to go to bed.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The rest of the week I'm busy, I'm afraid, so it'll have to be Monday.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The shop doesn't open until 11am and so it loses a lot of business.
@@PHRASE1@@therefore
@@DEFINE@@so - use this in formal speech and writing
@@EXAMPLE0@@The building work is taking quite a long time, and therefore costing us money.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Jewish weddings are both religious and civil. Therefore two official applications for marriage are necessary.
@@PHRASE2@@so big/tall/old etc (that)
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that because someone or something is very big, tall etc, something happens as a result
@@EXAMPLE0@@I was so busy today that I didn't have time for lunch.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He always thought he was so good looking that no woman would turn him down.
@@PHRASE3@@such a bad day/an old car/a tall man etc (that)
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that because it is a very bad day, a very old car etc something happens or someone does something as a result
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was such a nice day that we decided to go for a picnic.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The dress was such a bargain, I had to buy it.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Paul remained silent for such a long time that we were beginning to wonder if he'd fallen asleep.
@@PHRASE4@@so that/with the result that
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that because of a particular situation, another situation exists or happens. With the result that is more formal than so that
@@EXAMPLE0@@His hair was very long and covered his eyes, so that you could hardly see his face.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A car pulled out right in front of me, so that I had to slam on the brakes.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The company paid excellent salaries and provided good working conditions, with the result that its employees were of a very high standard.
@@PHRASE5@@as a result/consequently
@@DEFINE@@use this to say that because of a particular situation, something else happens or is true. Consequently is more formal than as a result
@@EXAMPLE0@@I had made a lot of contacts, and had good job opportunities as a result.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The virus attacks the plant, the flower does not open, and consequently no seeds are produced.
@@PHRASE6@@then
@@DEFINE@@use this to say what you would expect the result of an action or situation to be
@@EXAMPLE0@@"My father's quite laid back." "Then he won't mind if you borrow his car, will he?"
@@EXAMPLE1@@"I'm full up." "Does that mean you don't want any dessert then?"

@@THESPROPFORM0@@fall/drop etc something with a clatter
@@EXAMPLE0@@Bert put down his tools with a clatter, and looked round the room.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@the clatter of something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Just then there was the clatter of hooves on the road outside.
@@PHRASE5@@bump
@@DEFINE@@the dull, fairly quiet sound produced when something such as part of your body hits something or falls against a surface
@@EXAMPLE0@@At night, the old house seemed to be full of strange creaks and bumps.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fall/sit down/hit etc something with a bump
@@EXAMPLE0@@Martin sat down suddenly with a bump.
@@PHRASE6@@thump
@@DEFINE@@the dull, fairly loud sound produced when something heavy suddenly hits something else or falls hard on a surface
@@EXAMPLE0@@There was a loud thump as Eddie threw Luther back against the wall.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@hit something/fall etc with a thump
@@EXAMPLE0@@A suitcase toppled off the top of the wardrobe and landed on the floor with a thump.

@@PHRASE0@@knocking

@@EXAMPLE1@@The builders' knocking and hammering made it difficult for me to concentrate on my work.

@@GLOSS@@move around with a pattering sound

@@PHRASE3@@rattle

@@THESPROPFORM1@@rattle along/past etc

@@EXAMPLE1@@It sounded as though something outside was tapping against the window.

@@EXAMPLE1@@The left side of the brain controls speech.
not able to speak
@@PHRASE0@@can't speak
@@DEFINE@@to be unable to speak because you are too ill, weak, frightened etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@I was so terrified, I couldn't speak.
@@EXAMPLE1@@A lump welled up in his throat and he could not speak.
@@PHRASE1@@lose your voice
@@DEFINE@@to become unable to speak because of illness, or because you have been using your voice too much
@@EXAMPLE0@@On the first night of the show, the star of the play lost his voice and couldn't perform.
@@PHRASE2@@mute
@@DEFINE@@unable to speak, especially permanently - use this especially in medical contexts
@@EXAMPLE0@@A stroke left her mute and unable to use her legs.
@@PHRASE3@@dumb
@@DEFINE@@permanently unable to speak because of a physical condition - many people now consider this word to be offensive
@@EXAMPLE0@@According to the story, he was struck dumb (=made dumb ) by the gods.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She was born deaf and dumb.
@@PHRASE4@@be at a loss for words/be lost for words
@@DEFINE@@to be unable to say anything because you are very surprised, upset etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Rimes, who is rarely at a loss for words, was overcome with emotion as she received her award.
special
@@PHRASE0@@special
@@DEFINE@@something that is special is different from other things, for example because it is better, more important, or intended for a particular purpose
@@EXAMPLE0@@United Airlines is offering a special deal on flights to London.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Let us know if you have any special dietary needs in advance.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Today is a very special day for us - it was 50 years ago that we first met.
@@EXAMPLE3@@Did you do anything special at the weekend?
@@EXAMPLE4@@I made a special effort to be nice to him.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@special occasion
@@GLOSS@@a wedding, birthday, or other time when people celebrate something
@@EXAMPLE0@@He has a dark suit, which he only wears on special occasions.
@@PHRASE1@@specially
@@THESPROPFORM0@@specially designed/made/chosen etc
@@DEFINE@@designed, made, built etc for a special purpose
@@EXAMPLE0@@a new range of beauty products specially designed for teenagers
@@EXAMPLE1@@Customs officers use specially trained dogs for drug searches.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Did you get your ring specially made?
@@PHRASE2@@particular
@@DEFINE@@use this to emphasize that something is different or separate from other things of the same kind, or that something is more important than other things
@@EXAMPLE0@@Is there any particular reason why you want to go back to Japan?
@@EXAMPLE1@@Each class will focus on one particular aspect of American culture.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@be of particular interest/importance (to somebody)
@@EXAMPLE0@@This discovery is of particular interest to scientists studying the origins of the universe.
@@PHRASE3@@unique
@@DEFINE@@someone or something that is unique is so special and unusual that it is the only one of its kind - use this especially about things or people that you think are extremely good
@@EXAMPLE0@@It was a unique achievement - no-one has ever won the championship five times before.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The exhibition provided a unique opportunity to see all of the artist's work.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Every child is unique, with their own needs, preferences and talents.

@@GLOSS@@move slower

@@EXAMPLE1@@What you need for Africa is a simple, durable and inexpensive vehicle.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The roofs are constructed from heavy and durable timbers, usually teak or mahogany.
@@PHRASE4@@heavy-duty
@@DEFINE@@heavy-duty materials, tools, machines etc are specially made to be stronger than usual, often because they are going to be used a lot or used in difficult conditions
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you are going to put an electric cable underground, you must use the special heavy-duty type.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The emergency equipment includes food, a first-aid kit, and a heavy-duty flashlight.
@@PHRASE5@@hardwearing
@@DEFINE@@a hardwearing cloth or material is strong and will last a long time, even if it is used a lot
@@EXAMPLE0@@Polyester is not particularly hardwearing but it is cheap.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It's best to lay a good quality, hardwearing carpet.
@@PHRASE6@@reinforced
@@DEFINE@@a reinforced material or part has had other materials or parts added to make it stronger
@@EXAMPLE0@@A reinforced concrete dome, two metres thick, protects the radioactive core of the nuclear reactor.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Like all the clothes in the range it has specially reinforced seams.
@@PHRASE7@@unbreakable
@@DEFINE@@something that is unbreakable is difficult or impossible to break because it is made of a very strong substance
@@EXAMPLE0@@Make sure your patio doors are made of unbreakable glass.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a virtually unbreakable vacuum flask
@@PHRASE8@@indestructible
@@DEFINE@@impossible to break, damage or destroy
@@EXAMPLE0@@Until the accident, the ship was considered indestructible.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There is little point putting an indestructible door in a frame that will rot in 10 years.

@@EXAMPLE0@@You can use this herb to flavour almost any savoury dish.
@@EXAMPLE1@@As a child I didn't like sweets, but I loved crisps, nuts, and anything savoury.
@@PHRASE2@@bitter
@@DEFINE@@bitter foods, such as coffee without sugar or very dark chocolate, have a strong, sometimes unpleasant taste
@@EXAMPLE0@@Try not to burn the oil, it will make the sauce taste bitter.
@@EXAMPLE1@@strong, bitter coffee
@@EXAMPLE2@@The herb rue has a bitter taste, which makes it unpopular for cooking.
@@PHRASE3@@dry
@@DEFINE@@a dry wine is not sweet at all
@@EXAMPLE0@@We drank a dry white wine with our fish.
@@EXAMPLE1@@dry sherry
with a sour taste
@@PHRASE0@@sour
@@DEFINE@@food that is sour , especially fruit, has a taste that stings your tongue slightly, like a lemon does
@@EXAMPLE0@@The strawberries are a little sour - you may need to put sugar on them.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Kvass is a mild beer that is sometimes used in Russian cooking for its sour flavor.
@@PHRASE1@@tart
@@DEFINE@@fruits that are tart , especially apples, sting your tongue and make water come into your mouth
@@EXAMPLE0@@This tart citrus dressing is great on salads.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Red currants are quite tart and usually need sugar or honey.
@@PHRASE2@@sharp
@@DEFINE@@having a strong but pleasant taste that stings your tongue
@@EXAMPLE0@@The drink had a very sharp lemony taste.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I like this marmalade. It's very sharp.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The lemon juice gives the dressing its sharp flavour.
@@PHRASE3@@tangy
@@DEFINE@@having a fresh, pleasant taste that stings your tongue slightly
@@EXAMPLE0@@The orange juice had a delicious tangy taste.
@@EXAMPLE1@@We made a tangy mayonnaise from yoghurt and honey.
with a hot taste
@@PHRASE0@@hot
@@DEFINE@@food that has a hot taste seems to burn your mouth, and makes you want to drink a lot of water
@@EXAMPLE0@@The curry was so hot I couldn't finish it.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The sauce had a hot, peppery taste.
@@PHRASE1@@spicy
@@DEFINE@@spicy food tastes pleasantly hot and often seems to have a mix of different tastes
@@EXAMPLE0@@Tina loves hot spicy food.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I added ginger and cumin to give the rice a spicy flavour.
@@PHRASE2@@fiery
@@DEFINE@@food or drink that is fiery has an extremely hot taste that burns your throat
@@EXAMPLE0@@Peter always makes really fiery chilli con carne.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Discard all the chilli seeds, unless you want an extremely fiery soup.
with a strong taste
@@PHRASE0@@strong
@@DEFINE@@food or drinks that are strong have a very noticeable and particular taste
@@EXAMPLE0@@"How do you like your tea?" "Strong please, with no sugar."
@@EXAMPLE1@@I left the restaurant with rather a strong taste of onions in my mouth.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Stilton is a very strong English cheese, which has blue-green veins running through it.
@@PHRASE1@@rich
@@DEFINE@@food that is rich contains a lot of cheese, cream, butter, or chocolate, and makes you feel full very quickly
@@EXAMPLE0@@You mustn't eat too much rich food -- it's bad for you.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The meat was browned to perfection and topped with a rich sauce.
@@PHRASE2@@full-flavoured
@@VARIANT@@full-flavored
@@DEFINE@@something such as cheese or coffee that is full- flavoured has a strong pleasant taste
@@EXAMPLE0@@This coffee is strong and full-flavoured, excellent for after dinner.
@@PHRASE3@@full-bodied
@@DEFINE@@a full-bodied wine has a strong pleasant taste
@@EXAMPLE0@@The beautiful color and full-bodied taste of these Australian wines make them an excellent accompaniment to meat dishes.
with little or no taste
@@PHRASE0@@tasteless
@@DEFINE@@food that is tasteless has little or no taste and is rather unpleasant
@@EXAMPLE0@@Why is airplane food always so tasteless?
@@EXAMPLE1@@a plate of tasteless, overcooked vegetables
@@PHRASE1@@bland
@@DEFINE@@food or drink that is bland has very little taste and is not interesting to eat or drink
@@EXAMPLE0@@If the sauce is bland, add a little more vinegar.
@@EXAMPLE1@@At first, give the baby tiny portions of any bland food that has been sieved or pureed.
@@PHRASE2@@have no taste/not have any taste
@@DEFINE@@to have very little taste - use this especially when you think something should have more taste
@@EXAMPLE0@@The most disappointing dish was the chicken-filled tortellini with a pesto sauce that had almost no taste.
@@EXAMPLE1@@You need to add salt or something - this doesn't have any taste at all.
@@PHRASE3@@not taste of anything
@@VARIANT@@not taste like anything
@@DEFINE@@to have no particular taste
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm not sure what kind of soup this is supposed to be. It doesn't taste of anything to me.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The dessert wasn't awful, but it didn't taste like anything.
@@PHRASE4@@mild
@@DEFINE@@something such as cheese or coffee that is mild has a pleasant taste but is not hot or strong
@@EXAMPLE0@@It's a smooth, mild coffee, excellent for finishing off a meal.
@@EXAMPLE1@@a mild cigar
@@EXAMPLE2@@a mild English cheese
@@PHRASE5@@delicate
@@DEFINE@@a delicate taste or flavour is pleasant and not very strong
@@EXAMPLE0@@The fish was served with a delicate mushroom sauce.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Salmon has quite a delicate flavour, and it should not be over-cooked.

@@DEFINE@@to make someone seriously promise that they will not tell anyone about something you have told them or something that they know about
@@EXAMPLE0@@"What's she doing here?" "I'd better not say. She swore me to secrecy."
@@EXAMPLE1@@Nobody knows much about the organization because its members are all sworn to secrecy.
@@PHRASE1@@between you and me
@@DEFINE@@used when you are telling someone that what you are saying is a secret, and you do not want them to tell anyone else about it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Between you and me, I think Elizabeth is a bit of a nightmare.
to tell someone to do something
@@PHRASE0@@tell
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Wait here!" he told the children.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@tell somebody to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The teacher told us to be quiet.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I thought I told you to be in bed by 10 o'clock!
@@THESPROPFORM1@@tell somebody not to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@She told him not to phone her again.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@tell somebody (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@The doctors have told me that I should give up smoking.
@@THESPROPFORM3@@tell somebody how/what/where etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Don't tell me how to behave in public!
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'm in charge here, and I'm not going to have anyone telling me what to do.
@@THESPROPFORM4@@do as you are told
@@GLOSS@@used to tell children to obey
@@EXAMPLE0@@Do as you're told and go and wash your hands.
@@PHRASE1@@order
@@DEFINE@@to tell someone to do something in a threatening way
@@EXAMPLE0@@"Don't move", he ordered.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@order somebody to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@A man with a gun ordered the woman to give him all her money.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He was ordered to pay £4000 towards the court costs of £10,000.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@order somebody out of/into/back etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@She pointed her gun at him, ordering him out of the room.
@@PHRASE2@@ask somebody to do something
@@DEFINE@@to tell someone politely but firmly to do something or to stop doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Mr Evans, I must ask you to come with me to the police station.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@ask somebody not to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Would you ask visitors not to park their cars in front of the entrance.
@@PHRASE3@@demand
@@DEFINE@@to tell someone that they must do something, especially when you are angry or impatient and want them to do it immediately
@@THESPROPFORM0@@demand (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@You should demand that they finish the job now, not some time in August.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Realizing that her husband had deceived her, she demanded that he tell her the whole truth.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@demand an apology/a refund etc
@@GLOSS@@tell someone that they must say they are sorry, give money back etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@How dare you say that! I demand an apology.
@@PHRASE4@@insist
@@DEFINE@@to tell someone firmly and repeatedly that they must do something, especially something that they do not want to do
@@EXAMPLE0@@I didn't want to tell dad about the fight, but he insisted.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@insist (that)
@@EXAMPLE0@@I wanted to pay by cheque but the landlord insisted that I pay him in cash.
@@EXAMPLE1@@They're insisting we report the matter to the police right away.
@@PHRASE5@@dictate
@@DEFINE@@to tell someone exactly what they must do or how they must behave, as if you had power to make them obey you
@@THESPROPFORM0@@dictate to
@@EXAMPLE0@@She refused to be dictated to by some stupid official in Washington.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@dictate how/what/where etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Your parents have no right to dictate how you should spend your money.
to officially tell someone to do something
@@PHRASE0@@order

@@EXAMPLE0@@The court ordered that Gilmore should be executed.

@@EXAMPLE0@@It wasn't until 1973 that Nixon finally ordered US troops out of Vietnam.

@@GLOSS@@in the way that you have been instructed
@@EXAMPLE0@@She took the tablets three times every day, as instructed by her doctor.

@@DEFINE@@if someone such as a leader or officer gives orders or gives instructions , they tell other people exactly what they must do

@@EXAMPLE0@@It was the police chief who had given orders to shoot.

@@PHRASE3@@issue orders/instructions
@@DEFINE@@if someone such as a leader or officer issues orders or issues instructions , they tell people exactly what they should do, especially by sending a written statement
@@EXAMPLE0@@The EC plans to issue orders banning the sale of the drug.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@issue orders/instructions that
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Department of Defense has issued instructions that no one should enter the area without permission.
@@PHRASE4@@decree
@@DEFINE@@if a government, parliament, or court decrees that something should happen, they officially order it by making a law or by changing the existing law

@@PHRASE5@@command
@@DEFINE@@if someone such as a king or a military officer commands someone to do something, they tell them officially that they must do it
@@THESPROPFORM0@@command somebody to do something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Admiral Boyle commanded the entire crew to assemble on deck.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@command that
@@EXAMPLE0@@The King had the power to command that parliament be dissolved.
@@PHRASE6@@direct somebody to do something
@@DEFINE@@if someone in a position of legal authority such as a judge directs someone to do something, they order them to do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The judge directed the jury to find her not guilty.
@@EXAMPLE1@@He was jailed for refusing to answer questions when directed to do so in court.
@@PHRASE7@@subpoena
@@DEFINE@@to officially order someone to appear in a court of law in order to answer questions - used in legal contexts
@@EXAMPLE0@@If you refuse to attend the trial we can always get you subpoenaed.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Another three of the president's advisors were subpoenaed.

a test on something to check it or find out about it
@@PHRASE0@@test

@@EXAMPLE1@@The elderly people were taught meditation in the 12-week experiment.

@@GLOSS@@an experiment using something
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Institute plans to conduct no further experiments on monkeys.
@@PHRASE2@@trial
@@DEFINE@@a test in which a new product, such as a drug, a weapon, or a vehicle, is used by a small number of people in order to find out if it is safe and effective
@@EXAMPLE0@@Results of the drug trial will be available soon.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@trial of
@@EXAMPLE0@@Probert is overseeing the trials of the new explosives.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@clinical trial
@@GLOSS@@a trial of a drug or treatment that is done carefully by doctors on humans
@@EXAMPLE0@@Until now, the drug was only available to people taking part in clinical trials.
@@PHRASE3@@testing
@@DEFINE@@when something such as a process, system, substance etc is being examined, in order to see whether it exists, is safe, or is working properly
@@EXAMPLE0@@The U.S. conducted atomic weapons testing in Nevada during the 1950s.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The aircraft is still in the early stages of testing and production.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@drug/genetic/AIDS etc testing
@@EXAMPLE0@@Athletes will be subject to random drug testing.
@@PHRASE4@@trial run
@@DEFINE@@an occasion when you test a new method or system to see if it works well
@@EXAMPLE0@@The national railroad is doing a few trial runs to test new equipment.
@@PHRASE5@@pilot
@@DEFINE@@a test in which a new idea or plan is used in a limited number of places or situations, in order to see if it is worth continuing or doing in a more general way
@@EXAMPLE0@@The results of the pilot have been encouraging.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@pilot study/project/program etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@The government sponsored a pilot project to find out how the education reforms would work in schools.

@@DEFINE@@a process in which a new system or product is tested using different groups of people in order to see how effective and popular it will be
@@EXAMPLE0@@Extensive piloting has shown us our study book will be a useful aid to students.

@@EXAMPLE1@@The company's gross earnings were up $12 million over last year.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The gross weight of the package is 10 kilos, including the packaging.
when several numbers produce another number as a total
@@PHRASE0@@come to
@@DEFINE@@to be the total amount when everything is counted
@@EXAMPLE0@@Including wine, the bill came to $70.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Total profits from all sources for the year came to about $15 million.
@@PHRASE1@@reach
@@DEFINE@@if a total reaches 10, 50, 100 etc, it increases until it is equal to that number
@@EXAMPLE0@@Hurricane damage could reach billions of dollars.
@@EXAMPLE1@@China's economic output is likely to reach $13 trillion within the next few years.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The city's population is expected to reach 12 million by the year 2010.
@@PHRASE2@@make
@@DEFINE@@if numbers added together make 10, 50, 100 etc, that is the answer or the total
@@EXAMPLE0@@Two plus two makes four.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If Jane comes, that will make six of us.
@@EXAMPLE2@@There are eight submarines as well as the ships, making a total fleet of 34.
@@PHRASE3@@add up to
@@DEFINE@@if a set of several figures adds up to 10, 50 etc, that is the total when you add them all together
@@EXAMPLE0@@The three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If you follow the diet exactly, it adds up to about 1,200 calories per day.
@@EXAMPLE2@@With the hotel, the flights, and the food, it all added up to much more than I had expected.
@@PHRASE4@@amount to
@@DEFINE@@to reach a total, especially a large total
@@EXAMPLE0@@Credit card fraud amounts to about $17 million a year.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Nationally, deaths from smoking-related illnesses amount to about 30 people each day.
@@EXAMPLE2@@A thousand-word essay might amount to roughly 6,000 bytes on a computer disk.
@@PHRASE5@@total
@@DEFINE@@to reach a particular total - used especially in official contexts
@@EXAMPLE0@@The company was forced to pay fines and penalties totalling $24.8.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The number of people included in the study totalled 170.
@@PHRASE6@@number
@@DEFINE@@if a group of people or things numbers a particular figure, especially a large figure, that is the total when they are all included
@@EXAMPLE0@@The crowd of students numbered at least 2000.
@@EXAMPLE1@@In the capital, unemployed workers now number 12% of the workforce.

a special event that is part of a tradition
@@PHRASE0@@ceremony
@@DEFINE@@a special formal event which is part of the religious or social tradition of a place, and in which there is a fixed set of words and actions
@@THESPROPFORM0@@wedding/funeral etc ceremony
@@EXAMPLE0@@After the wedding ceremony we went to a reception at the bride's parents' house.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@hold a ceremony
@@GLOSS@@have a ceremony
@@EXAMPLE0@@A ceremony is held every year to remember those who died in the war.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@attend a ceremony
@@EXAMPLE0@@Over 2,000 people attended the official opening ceremony of the Olympic Games.
@@PHRASE1@@ceremonial
@@DEFINE@@ceremonial clothes, objects, and activities are used in important religious or social ceremonies
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Queen was in full ceremonial dress for the state opening of Parliament.
@@EXAMPLE1@@His right hand rested on his ceremonial sword.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The full costume is only worn on important ceremonial occasions.
@@PHRASE2@@ritual
@@DEFINE@@a set of words and actions that are always done in the same way, for example as part of a religious ceremony
@@EXAMPLE0@@The book examines rituals for childbirth from different parts of the world.
@@EXAMPLE1@@After an elaborate ritual, the boys are formally accepted into the tribe.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@perform a ritual
@@EXAMPLE0@@The ritual is performed in order to thank the Sun Goddess for the rice harvest.
@@PHRASE3@@rite
@@DEFINE@@a special action that is done as part of an important religious or social ceremony, especially one that only particular people, for example priests, are allowed to perform
@@EXAMPLE0@@Buddhist rites
@@THESPROPFORM0@@perform a rite
@@EXAMPLE0@@The Batak chieftains perform the traditional initiation rite.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@last rites
@@GLOSS@@final prayers and ceremonies for someone who is dying
@@EXAMPLE0@@A priest was called to perform last rites for the dying woman.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@funeral rites
@@EXAMPLE0@@The body cannot be buried until the funeral rites have been performed.

@@EXAMPLE0@@The conclusions of the survey are questionable because the research was based on a very small sample of people.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it is questionable whether
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is questionable whether the advertisements will increase sales.
@@PHRASE2@@open to question/debate
@@DEFINE@@something that is open to question or open to debate seems doubtful and needs to be checked or discussed
@@EXAMPLE0@@Many people feel that the safety of the drug is now open to question.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Just why the guerrillas decided to shoot down the unarmed plane remains open to debate.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@it is open to question/debate whether
@@EXAMPLE0@@It is open to debate whether the new government is any better than the old one.
@@PHRASE3@@moot point
@@DEFINE@@something that different people have different opinions about
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'm not sure that bringing in computers has made our job easier. It's a moot point.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Whether or not increasing taxes will result in a fairer society remains a moot point.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Jo Columbo lay in a coma, paralyzed by bullet wounds.

what you say when something is not important
@@PHRASE0@@it doesn't matter
@@DEFINE@@say this to tell someone that something is not important and will not cause any serious problems

@@DEFINE@@say this when you think something is not important enough to affect what happens or change what someone decides

@@EXAMPLE1@@Even if she had known he was lying it would have made no difference.
@@EXAMPLE2@@It doesn't make any difference whether you use fresh berries or frozen ones.

@@EXAMPLE0@@You can have a single room or a double -- it makes no difference to the price.
@@PHRASE2@@it's no big deal/it's not a big deal
@@DEFINE@@say this when you do not think something is important or worrying, even though other people may think it is
@@EXAMPLE0@@My leg's a little sore, but it's no big deal.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Just copy your work onto a disk - it's no big deal.
@@EXAMPLE2@@She assumed he'd be furious, but the whole incident just wasn't a big deal to him.

@@EXAMPLE0@@We decided to use the second bedroom as a junk room.

@@DEFINE@@if you do something with a tool, piece of equipment etc you use a tool, piece of equipment etc to do it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Beat the egg with a fork.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Do you have anything I can open the bottle with?

@@EXAMPLE0@@To build the shelter, they had to make use of whatever bits of wood or plastic they could find.

@@EXAMPLE0@@The Romans made use of volcanic ash to produce concrete.

@@EXAMPLE0@@Who were the first to make use of pigeons as messengers?

@@EXAMPLE0@@Once you get used to a routine, it's hard to change.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Paul had finally gotten used to Heidi's mood swings.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@get used to (doing) something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Mary never really got used to living on her own after her husband died.
@@EXAMPLE1@@It took me a while to get used to the casual atmosphere in the office.
@@PHRASE1@@become/grow accustomed to
@@DEFINE@@to get used to something
@@EXAMPLE0@@After a while Edward's eyes grew accustomed to the dark.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Living so near the airport, they've grown accustomed to the sound of planes overhead.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@become/grow accustomed to doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@She had become accustomed to cooking for everyone in the house.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Larry remained completely relaxed - he was accustomed to dealing with difficult customers.
@@PHRASE2@@adjust to
@@DEFINE@@to get gradually used to a new situation, by changing your attitudes or the way you do things
@@EXAMPLE0@@It took us a while to adjust to the tropical climate.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Some of the staff found it hard to adjust to all the changes in technology and working methods.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@adjust to doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Kids need help to adjust to having a new baby in the house.
@@PHRASE3@@adapt to
@@DEFINE@@to gradually change your behaviour and attitudes, so that you get used to a new situation and can deal with it effectively
@@EXAMPLE0@@Slowly the country is adapting to the new market economy.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@adapt to doing something
@@EXAMPLE0@@She adapted remarkably well to eating a limited diet, and she's lost a great deal of weight.
@@EXAMPLE1@@After living in a house with a garden, it's hard to adapt to living in a flat.
@@PHRASE4@@acclimatize/become acclimatized
@@VARIANT@@acclimatise/become acclimatised
@@VARIANT@@acclimate/become acclimated
@@DEFINE@@to get used to a new place or a different type of weather
@@EXAMPLE0@@When first arriving in the Himalayas, mountaineers must give themselves time to acclimatize.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@acclimatize/become acclimatized to
@@EXAMPLE0@@As the immigrants became acclimatized to life in America, they abandoned some of their old traditions.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I flew to Hong Kong a day early to give myself a chance to acclimatise to the time difference.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@get acclimatized/acclimatised/acclimated
@@EXAMPLE0@@The team wants to have a few practices to get acclimated to the ball park.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@acclimatize/acclimatise/acclimate yourself
@@EXAMPLE0@@After a while, if you acclimatise yourself to the heat, you can get by with two canteens of water a day.

@@EXAMPLE0@@The game was watched by over 50,000 spectators.
@@EXAMPLE1@@There are no facilities for spectators at the pool.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Someone was juggling in the street, and a small group of spectators had gathered to watch.
@@PHRASE1@@viewer
@@DEFINE@@someone who watches a television programme - used especially in newspapers and news reports
@@EXAMPLE0@@The concert was seen by 500 million viewers around the world.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Millions of television viewers tuned in to the president's speech.
@@PHRASE2@@audience
@@DEFINE@@a group of people who have come to a place to watch a play, concert, film etc
@@EXAMPLE0@@Actors, wearing masks, came down among the audience.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I'm not sure that this film will appeal to British audiences.
@@EXAMPLE2@@The show has delighted television audiences in the United States and Britain.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@in the audience
@@EXAMPLE0@@There seemed to be quite a lot of young people in the audience.
@@PHRASE3@@onlooker
@@DEFINE@@someone who is watching an event, especially when they did not come specially to watch it but just happened to see it
@@EXAMPLE0@@The child glanced fearfully around the small circle of onlookers.
@@EXAMPLE1@@The last few runners appeared, to an accompanying cheer from the crowd of onlookers.
@@PHRASE4@@observer
@@DEFINE@@someone who watches an event, activity, or situation, especially someone who has been officially sent there in order to report back about it to an organization or country
@@EXAMPLE0@@She's been sent as an observer to the UN aid conference.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Most political observers believe that the president will now have to resign.
@@EXAMPLE2@@Military observers have been allowed into the area to monitor the ceasefire.
always watching to see what happens
@@PHRASE0@@alert
@@DEFINE@@someone who is alert is always watching, and notices if anything strange or unusual happens
@@EXAMPLE0@@Passengers should try to stay alert at all times, and report any suspicious packages to the police immediately.
@@EXAMPLE1@@She owes her life to an alert farmer, who spotted her car in a ditch and called the emergency services.

@@EXAMPLE1@@We had to watch out for potholes in the road.

@@EXAMPLE1@@Journalists suspected that the army was acting in collusion with the terrorists.
@@PHRASE2@@be in cahoots (with)
@@DEFINE@@working secretly and closely with another person or group in order to do something dishonest or cheat someone
@@EXAMPLE0@@Assassins, in cahoots with the army, were sent to kill two top members of the parliament.
@@EXAMPLE1@@By the middle of the book we've learned that the church and the local politicians are in cahoots to try to slow Sonja's research.

@@DEFINE@@if one organization is hand in glove with another organization, they work together very closely in order to do something dishonest, or dishonestly get power

@@EXAMPLE0@@The memo had been initialled by the President.
@@EXAMPLE1@@If you alter something you have written on a cheque, you must initial the change.
@@PHRASE2@@countersign
@@DEFINE@@to write your signature on an official document, especially one that has already been signed by someone else, in order to approve it
@@EXAMPLE0@@You have to get your visa countersigned by someone at the embassy.
@@PHRASE3@@signature
@@DEFINE@@your name written by you, for example on a document or at the end of a letter, in order to prove who you are or show that you wrote it
@@EXAMPLE0@@Who's it from? I can't read the signature.
@@EXAMPLE1@@Put your signature here, then print your name underneath.
@@EXAMPLE2@@You have to get the signature of the child's parent or guardian.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@signature on
@@EXAMPLE0@@I just need your signature again on this last sheet here.
@@PHRASE4@@autograph
@@DEFINE@@the name of a famous person, written by them on a photograph, in a book etc for someone to keep
@@EXAMPLE0@@She has the autograph of every player in the team.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@sign autographs
@@GLOSS@@to sign your name for people when they ask
@@EXAMPLE0@@He refused to sign autographs at a charity event last year.
to write information on an official document
@@PHRASE0@@fill in something/fill out something
@@DEFINE@@to write information or answer questions on an official document, for example giving your name, address, and age
@@EXAMPLE0@@Passengers must fill in a boarding card before boarding the plane.
@@EXAMPLE1@@I must have filled out the order form incorrectly.
@@THESPROPFORM0@@fill something in/fill something out
@@EXAMPLE0@@You just fill it out, then send it in to the passport office.
@@PHRASE1@@write out/write
@@DEFINE@@to write information, such as your name, the date etc on something such as a cheque or a form
@@THESPROPFORM0@@write (out) something
@@EXAMPLE0@@I'll write out a cheque for $500 to cover expenses.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@write somebody (out) something
@@EXAMPLE0@@Why don't you get the doctor to write you a prescription for some painkillers?
@@THESPROPFORM2@@write something out
@@EXAMPLE0@@Write the information out here on this form, and I'll order the books for you.
@@PHRASE2@@make out
@@DEFINE@@to write the necessary details on an official document such as a cheque or ticket, including the name of the person or organization it should go to
@@THESPROPFORM0@@make out something
@@EXAMPLE0@@He made out a cheque for $100.
@@THESPROPFORM1@@make something out (for somebody)
@@EXAMPLE0@@Would you like me to make out a receipt for you?
@@EXAMPLE1@@He's just making the booking form out.
@@THESPROPFORM2@@make out a cheque to somebody
@@GLOSS@@write on a cheque the name of the person you are paying it to
@@EXAMPLE0@@Who should I make the cheque out to?
@@EXAMPLE1@@If you want to pay by check, make it out to GK Fisher.
